title: China’s Moonshot, Z.AI, and DeepSeek are challenging U.S. AI labs—and beating them on cost
description: “The AI ecosystem in China is probably much better than people thought."
fullText:
It was, perhaps, the worst-kept secret in the AI community.

In mid-July, online sleuths who obsessively track the internet for signs of new AI models started to whisper about the latest offering from Moonshot AI, the Beijing-based artificial intelligence startup behind the Kimi large language model: Something big was coming.

How are Chinese AI models competing with U.S. counterparts?

What geopolitical concerns arise from Chinese AI model adoption?

Why are Chinese AI models significantly cheaper than American alternatives?

What impact did U.S. export controls have on China's AI development?

Moonshot AI's latest model didn't just live up to the hype—it raised the stakes.

On July 16, Moonshot debuted Kimi K3, the largest open-source model ever released, and promised it could perform close to the level of Anthropic's Fable 5—perhaps the most powerful publicly available model on the market today—at a fraction of the cost. Moonshot's official benchmarks consistently rank K3 among the top three AI models; one independent benchmark from Arena.AI even pegged K3 as the best model currently available, ahead of Anthropic.

The launch was a triumph for the lab and its founder Yang Zhilin, a 34-year-old Tsinghua and Carnegie Mellon alumnus—and Pink Floyd fan—who based his startup's Chinese name on his favorite album, The Dark Side of the Moon.

But the release also rattled investors because it challenged the idea that U.S. firms could maintain their sizable lead in the global AI race simply by outspending Chinese rivals on computing power.

Markets sold off in Asia. The chip-focused Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 1.6%. Nvidia lost almost $600 billion in value and briefly lost its spot as the world's most valuable company to Apple.

Many observers, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, hadn't expected a Chinese AI lab to release a model that could approach the U.S.'s best offerings for at least another six months. Tesla CEO Elon Musk suggested it might happen by the first quarter of next year. Kimi K3 blew up the timeline: Chinese AI is now cheap enough and good enough that even U.S. startups and Fortune 500 companies are quietly plugging the models into their operations to rein in spiraling AI budgets. It's a remarkable closing of the gap that China achieved despite Washington imposing export controls to choke off China's access to the world's most advanced chips.

"The AI ecosystem in China is probably much better than people thought," says Paul Triolo, a partner at DGA–Albright Stonebridge Group.

Chinese developers have been working from a severe disadvantage for years.

The U.S. began to cut China off from top-tier AI processors, like those made by Nvidia, in 2022. By limiting the sale of the advanced chips used to train and run AI models—and the tools that could be used to make them—Washington planned to kneecap China's tech sector and preserve the U.S.'s AI lead.

title: Mexico economy likely rebounded in second quarter
description: MEXICO CITY, July 27 (Reuters) - Mexico's economy is likely to have recovered in the second quarter, driven mainly by a rebound in industrial activity, according to a Reuters poll on Monday.
fullText:
MEXICO CITY, July 27 (Reuters) - Mexico's economy is likely to have recovered in the second quarter, driven mainly by a ‌rebound in industrial activity, according to a Reuters poll on ‌Monday.

The median forecast of 11 analysts found gross domestic product likely grew 1.3% between ​April and June in seasonally adjusted figures, following a 0.6% contraction in the previous quarter.

What are the different GDP growth forecasts for Mexico?

What drove Mexico's expected economic recovery in Q2?

How does Mexico's Q2 GDP forecast compare historically?

Which sectors contributed to Mexico's economic rebound expectations?

Should this be confirmed, it would mark Mexico's best quarterly economic performance since the first quarter of 2022. Mexico's statistics agency will ‌release its preliminary estimate ⁠of second-quarter GDP on Thursday.

"The expected improvement reflects a rebound in industrial activity and continued, albeit moderate, growth ⁠in services, broadly consistent with recent monthly indicators," Itau said in a report.

Last week, a leading indicator for economic activity known as IOAE forecast an ​expansion ​in economic activity in June following ​a contraction in May.

The recovery ‌was likely driven by a revival in secondary sectors, including manufacturing, mining and construction, according to the IOAE.

On an annual basis, GDP is estimated to have grown at a rate of 1.5%, up from a 0.2% increase in the first quarter, according to the poll.

In early ‌July, the International Monetary Fund lowered its ​growth forecast for the Mexican economy this ​year to 1.2% from a ​previously estimated 1.6%. The government responded that it ‌expects a better performance than anticipated ​by the IMF.

The ​Ministry of Finance has estimated that GDP will grow between 1.8% and 2.8% this year, a projection that is also more optimistic ​than the market's ‌1.1% forecast.

title: If You Loved ‘I Will Find You,’ There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next
description: The Fugitive is a Harrison Ford classic that has all the pathos, twists, and action a fan of I Will Find You could want.
fullText:
No one dishes out shocking twists and emotionally powerful moments like Harlan Coben, and his partnership with Netflix just keeps delivering stories you can’t help but devour in one sitting. I Will Find You, starring Sam Worthington and Britt Lower, is no exception: The story of a father risking everything to prove he didn’t commit an unspeakable crime while searching for the son he thought lost forever is the sort of show you hop online immediately after the credits roll to see what people are saying. If you’ve already watched the series that give the same vibe and want more innocent people trying to get their lives back, unpredictable plot swerves, and emotionally charged stories of hard-won justice, look no further than 1993’s The Fugitive.

The Fugitive was a massive hit in 1993. Based on a 1960s television series (also called The Fugitive) that was itself a national phenomenon, it’s the story of Dr. Richard Kimble (Harrison Ford), who is convicted of the brutal murder of his wife, Helen (Sela Ward), despite his claims of witnessing a one-armed man committing the crime. When the bus transporting him to prison crashes, Kimble escapes and launches a desperate campaign to prove his innocence, identify the murderer, and evade the dogged pursuit of U.S. Marshal Samuel Gerard (Tommy Lee Jones) and his team.

The Fugitive scratches the precise innocent-man-on-the-run itch as I Will Find You, following Kimble as he uses his medical training and survival instincts to avoid capture while taking enormous risks. He poses as a janitor at a local hospital in order to conduct research on men with prosthetic arms and is almost caught several times by the smart and experienced Gerard (who famously tells Kimble that he doesn’t care when Kimble protests his innocence).

While the film doesn’t have the bonkers twists that Harlan Coben came up with for I Will Find You, there are plenty of unpredictable plot swerves as Kimble unravels a conspiracy that hits closer to home than he expects. Just like the Netflix series, the villain has violently self-serving motives, and the true story of what happened is a surprising reveal. And if your favorite part of I Will Find You was the interaction between father-daughter FBI agents Max Williams (Chi McBride) and Sarah Greer (Logan Browning) as they pursue David, you’ll absolutely love Sam Gerard and his team as they bicker, joke, and follow the trail with absolute dedication to their jobs.

Bottom line: The Fugitive is a big-budget, slightly less shocking Harrison Ford blockbuster that every fan of I Will Find You will love. You can rent The Fugitive on Prime Video.

Still craving twisty thrillers about innocent folks searching desperately for the truth? Here are a few more brilliant movies to check out.

You want more absolutely mind-blowing twists? Primal Fear has one of the most brilliant swerves in film history. Edward Norton’s film debut sees him playing Aaron Luke Stampler, a stuttering, shy altar boy accused of viciously murdering the beloved Archbishop Rushman. Vain, publicity-seeking attorney Martin Vail (Richard Gere) takes Aaron’s case, believing the weak, forgetful Stampler incapable of such atrocities—but the twisty story builds to one of the all-time great reveals, a scene that made Norton a star overnight. Stream Primal Fear on Fubo or Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

Was it the complexity of the setup that hooked you in I Will Find You? Gone Girl takes that to the next level. Based on Gillian Flynn’s smash novel, the story begins when Nick Dunne (Ben Affleck) comes home to find his wife, Amy (Rosamund Pike), is missing. The clues at the scene don’t look great for Nick, and as the sordid truth of his marriage emerges, things look worse—but nothing is exactly what it seems in this taut, clever mystery. If you were fascinated by the effort put into painting David as a heartless killer, you should know that Gone Girl takes that to the next level. Rent Gone Girl on Prime Video.

There’s something absolutely gripping about a story focused on an innocent person’s life ruined by a false accusation. The Next Three Days is a tense thrill ride based on that premise: John and Lara Brennan (Russel Crowe and Elizabeth Banks) are happily married with a young son. When Lara’s boss is murdered after Lara had an ugly, public confrontation with him, she’s convicted of his murder. As time passes and John can see her giving up all hope, he launches a desperate plot to break her out of prison and reclaim their lives. If you rooted for David to prove his innocence, you’ll root for John and Lara in the same way. Rent The Next Three Days on Prime Video.

Part of the thrill of I Will Find You is the slow, twisty route to justice—to finding the truth and punishing the truly guilty. That’s where Double Jeopardy lives. Ashley Judd stars as Elizabeth Parsons, who is convicted of murdering her husband, Nick (Bruce Greenwood), after she’s found with a bloody knife on their boat, his body presumably swept into the ocean. She loses custody of their son and despairs—but she eventually discovers that Nick faked his death and framed her for the murder. Her life becomes consumed with the need to reclaim her son and—when she realizes she cannot be charged with the same murder twice—to get a measure of revenge. Stream Double Jeopardy on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

One of the all-time classics in the “wronged person serving time” genre, The Shawshank Redemption is simultaneously an inspiring story of friendship, a stirring tale of surviving in the face of horrific loss and injustice, and one of the greatest twisty stories of all time. Its steady pacing and careful characterization let you really get to know the wrongly convicted man at its core, and the ending lets you appreciate how resolute and determined he was while experiencing the worst horrors a human can imagine. Rent The Shawshank Redemption on Prime Video.

title: How to Stop Browser Fingerprinting, the Latest Method for Tracking Your Activity Across the Internet
description: Browser fingerprinting lets websites see you even after you disable every cookie.
fullText:
Uninterrupted browsing used to be a lot simpler: Disable all third-party cookies, blacklist known tracking domains, and get an ad blocker. But now, online platforms can pick up on things like your screen resolution, basic hardware specs, time zone, and installed fonts to establish a fingerprint unique to your browser and device. Websites can query a lot of seemingly harmless data from your device without prompting any security reaction, which, over time, they can use to trace your browsing activity.

If you truly care about your privacy, disabling cookies is no longer enough to guarantee your anonymity on the internet. Luckily, browsers like Safari, Firefox, Brave, and others have evolved to address this problem using more privacy features that cost nothing to enable. Let’s take a look at how these work and what you can do to minimize your digital footprint.

Browser fingerprinting is an advanced tracking method where a website queries minute technical details about your device, anything from your operating system to the drivers used by your GPU, to create a unique digital identification for your browser. It then uses this ID to record your on-site sessions and trace your browsing activity across the web, completely bypassing the need for cookies. And while browsers now include powerful blockers preventing websites from installing cookies on your device, even dedicated security solutions like internet security apps, private browsing modes, and VPNs struggle to fully stop browser fingerprinting.

Unlike cookies, fingerprinting does not require a website to install files or extensions to your web browser. Instead, it uses server-side and JavaScript-executed signals to collect innocuous details about your device and setup, such as:

Canvas fingerprinting: A simple JavaScript command forces your browser to draw a hidden 2D image. It then hashes the pixel data to uncover specific details about your graphics card, operating system, hardware drivers, and so on.

WebGL rendering: Instead of rendering drawings on a 2D canvas, this forces the browser to render a 3D image in WebGL, revealing even more details about your graphics processor make and model.

Font enumeration: By rendering specific text strings and measuring bounding box layouts, APIs map out the entire font library installed on your system.

AudioContext cues: This processes a silent audio signal through your sound hardware, creating a soundwave signature that’s unique to your device.

Hardware details: Device hardware specifications are considered low-hanging fruit that most fingerprinting APIs can pull easily. Things like screen resolution, storage space, battery levels, processor cores, etc. can be cobbled together to craft a unique digital ID.

If you’re curious about what kind of data your browser might be leaking to websites, Cover Your Tracks lets you run free scans that show you exactly how exposed you are. You can also rerun this check as many times as you want after adjusting your privacy settings. The site generates an immediate report that tells you whether you have cookies or trackers enabled in your browser, along with the types of data your device is leaking that can be accessed by fingerprinting technology.

For example, scanning my Chromium-based Arc Browser revealed that I was leaking 18.26 bits of identifying information including my time zone, language preferences, font library, and privacy settings in the HTTP headers when accessing a site, as well as a unique fingerprint tied to my device through Canvas and WebGL rendering. This was after already disabling cookies or trackers at the browser level.

You can’t fully stop browser fingerprinting because the technology does not rely on a single point of access to collect your data. But that doesn’t mean you can’t make it harder for sites and trackers to get to you. Let’s take a look at how each browser handles fingerprinting, with step-by-step instructions on what you need to configure or enable manually:

Apple introduced Advanced Tracking and Fingerprinting Protection in Safari at the same time as the release of iOS 17 and macOS Sonoma. The company has also heavily expanded the feature since its original release. As long as you’re on Safari 17+, you can enable this opt-in feature for added privacy when browsing the web:

Navigate to Settings > Apps > Safari > Advanced.

Tap Advanced Tracking and Fingerprinting Protection.

Launch Safari. Then navigate to Safari > Settings from the menu bar.

Make sure to enable Use advanced tracking and fingerprinting protection and choose All browsing from the drop-down menu.

Microsoft Edge offers fingerprinting protection even at the lowest privacy settings, without requiring any action on your part. However, you can enhance the level of protection by following these steps.

Launch Edge on your Windows computer, click on the three dots in the upper right corner, and navigate to Settings > Privacy, search, and services.

Look for the section that reads Tracking prevention and opt for the Strict option for the maximum level of security from fingerprinting and cryptomining.

You can also scroll down to Exceptions to whitelist trusted websites that need tracking enabled to work properly.

Firefox bundles all its privacy features under Enhanced Tracking Protection, which covers both fingerprinting and cookies. There’s even a privacy.resistFingerprinting flag available for advanced users in the hidden config page, but that’s overkill for most regular users and can disrupt basic functionality on many modern websites.

For most internet users, enabling the following features should be sufficient protection against most fingerprinting APIs:

In Firefox, go to Settings > Privacy & Security.

Under Enhanced Tracking Protection, select Custom.

Make sure the boxes next to Cookies and Fingerprinters are both checked. Fingerprinter blocking should also be set to All windows to extend protection beyond incognito browsing.

For even stronger security, select the Strict option instead of Custom under Enhanced Tracking Protection for the most potent privacy settings.

Though it’s Chromium-based, Brave’s developers have gone out of their way to implement strong fingerprinting protection into the browser using the Shields component. This is one of the strongest out-of-the-box fingerprinting prevention settings that I have tested, and it's very easy to enable.

Click the lion icon in the address bar of your Brave browser window to access Brave Shields. You can also do this by navigating to Settings > Shields.

Make sure that Trackers & ads blocking is set to Standard or higher.

Fingerprint protection is now enabled. Brave Shields works by effectively scrambling any data collected by fingerprinting APIs, so trackers cannot obtain any consistent information to establish a profile for your browser.

Now for the elephant in the room: since Google shuttered its Privacy Sandbox component in April 2025, Chrome does not offer built-in fingerprinting protection. However, there are several third-party extensions you can use to add these features to your browser, with caveats.

Canvas Blocker: When a website uses the HTML canvas element to create a unique fingerprint for your device, Canvas Blocker adds some random noise to the data generated by the canvas element to confuse fingerprinting APIs. It’s relatively lightweight compared to similar extensions because it doesn’t block your canvas element entirely and instead uses subtle changes to confuse fingerprinting trackers.

Fingerprint Spoofer: A much more complete anti-fingerprinting extension, since this also blocks JavaScript and image-based fingerprinting and can spoof user agent or navigator values. It also entirely replaces the canvas image generated by your browser instead of making minor alterations to it, which makes canvas fingerprinting even trickier.

StealthHound: This is a premium anti-fingerprinting extension that stops websites from probing for your hardware details, blocks canvas fingerprinting attempts, disables tracking scripts, and even gives you a risk signal to indicate how aggressively a website is trying to identify you. StealthHound operates entirely on your local device without sending information to any cloud-based apps or platforms to protect data sovereignty.

However, Chrome has implemented certain limitations in its latest Manifest V3 extension framework that affect how useful these third-party services can be. It now actively prevents extensions from injecting code into a web page before that page has finished loading, which often gives fingerprinting technologies just enough time to get what they need before spoofing mechanisms kick in. If you truly care about fingerprinting protection, Google Chrome is not the best option for you. For a Chromium-based browser with thorough fingerprinting protection, consider Brave.

title: No, Bananas Don't Destroy the Nutrients in Smoothies
description: According to a study, you should never put a banana in your smoothie. But does it really say that?
fullText:
Who doesn't love a banana in their smoothie? It adds sweetness and does wonders for the texture. Well, not Rhonda Patrick, who proudly told her followers she does not put bananas in her smoothies because of a fear that it's breaking down polyphenols from blueberries. This belief is one that made the rounds on social media a few years ago, and its grain of truth has been blown way out of proportion. I'll break down where this myth comes from, and what you actually need to know.

The idea that you need to avoid bananas in your smoothies started in 2023, when a study published in the journal Food & Function found that bananas can reduce the bioavailability of flavon-3-ols in smoothies.

The study is real, and several of the TikTok clips that immediately popped up to discuss it described the study more or less accurately. Where they went wrong is concluding that we shouldn’t put bananas in our smoothies. That’s not what the scientists concluded. There’s no need to give up your bananas.

The press release announcing the study probably started this mess (it calls adding a banana to your smoothie a “mistake”) but it also mentions that the lead author of the study, Javier Ottaviani, “said bananas remain a great fruit to be eaten or consumed in smoothies.” So clearly the banana warnings are overblown.

The study wasn’t about the nutritional value of bananas or smoothies in general. It was looking at a particular question of biochemistry: Does an enzyme in bananas react with one particular type of antioxidant found in cocoa extract? (Note that Rhonda Patrick's recent videos are focused on polyphenols in blueberries; those weren't tested in the study.)

Antioxidants are a broad class of chemicals. For context, vitamin C is an antioxidant, but so are lycopene and resveratrol (compounds famously found in tomatoes and grapes) and so are anthocyanins, the red and blue pigments found in berries. The antioxidant studied here is not any of the above, but a different one found in tea and cocoa. It’s called (-)-epicatechin, and it’s part of the antioxidant family called flavon-3-ols.

In the study, eight healthy men recruited from around the UC Davis campus were given each of the following, on different days:

A smoothie made with bananas, almond milk, and an epicatechin-containing cocoa extract.

A smoothie made with the same cocoa extract plus strawberries, blueberries, blackberries, raspberries, almond milk, water, crushed ice, and yogurt (presumably the yogurt and ice were required for texture).

A glass of milk and a capsule containing the cocoa extract.

Bananas contain an enzyme called polyphenol oxidase (PPO), and the scientists wanted to find out if the PPO in a banana could affect the levels of (-)-epicatechin, one of those flavon-3-ols, in food such as smoothies.

Somewhat surprisingly, it did! Our bodies convert epicatechins into other chemicals in the same family, and the researchers took blood samples from the volunteers to look for these chemicals after each of the experiments. After drinking the berry smoothie or taking the capsule with milk, blood levels of these chemicals were elevated. But after drinking the banana smoothie, they weren’t.

This strongly suggests that the PPO in the banana had destroyed a lot of the epicatechins present in the cocoa extract. Further experiments described in same paper suggest that this chemical activity happens when the ingredients are sitting together in the smoothie glass, and it likely also happens in our stomachs.

The study did not test a berry smoothie with an added banana. None of the smoothies or experiments combined berries and bananas. The study did not test levels of antioxidants or other nutrients from berries. They were looking specifically at what happened to the antioxidants provided in the cocoa extract. The study also did not look at other aspects of nutrition besides this very specific chemical reaction (PPO from bananas plus (-)-epicatechins from cocoa extract).

Therefore, we cannot conclude that the banana in a mixed fruit smoothie “destroys” or “ruins” the nutrients or even the antioxidants from the berries. This is a study about a specific type of polyphenol that's found in tea and cocoa, and it was studied specifically in a cocoa extract. We can't use this data to say what happens to the antioxidants in berries.

If an enzyme in bananas can reduce the bioavailability of a certain family of antioxidants...what does that matter? Were you drinking smoothies for the express purpose of increasing your intake of flavon-3-ols? More likely you were trying to get some fruit in your diet and/or have a nice breakfast or snack because you were hungry.

Regardless of their PPO activity, bananas also provide fiber, which is good for you, and carbs, which are a macronutrient our bodies can use in many ways. A medium banana contains 20% of our vitamin B6 needs for the day, 17% of our vitamin C, and 8% of our magnesium. After getting backlash about the banana myth, Patrick made a video in which she points out that bananas also have more sugar than avocados (her preferred ingredient). That's a plus, in my opinion: A smoothie needs some sweetness, and carbs are good for you anyway.

The recent study did not take any of that away from you. You still get all of the benefits above, no matter what’s happening to the flavon-3-ols in your smoothie.

OK, but what if you really were looking forward to getting lots of good antioxidants in that fruit smoothie? After all, flavon-3-ols like (-)-epicatechin are so good for us that the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics (AND) issued a guideline for them, even though flavon-3-ols are a non-essential nutrient. The guideline tells us that there are heath benefits to be gained by consuming at least 400 milligrams of flavon-3-ols per day.

If you want to get more flavon-3-ols, the best thing you can do is drink some tea. You can hit that 400-milligram recommendation with just 10 ounces of green tea (two small cups), or 12 ounces of black tea. There are flavon-3-ols in berries, but in lesser amounts; it would take 6 cups of blackberries or 40 cups of blueberries to provide the same amount as those two cups of green tea.

title: 10 Shows Like 'Stuart Fails to Save the Universe' You Should Watch Next
description: More high-concept sci-fi shows featuring time travel, multiverses, and more.
fullText:
Not since Happy Days spun off into Mork and Mindy has there been a weirder TV franchise expansion than Stuart Fails to Save the Universe, which takes the relatively straightforward sitcom antics of The Big Bang Theory and expands them into the multiverse. It seems that, at some point after the conclusion of their show, Howard, Sheldon, and Leonard built a quantum something-or-other machine that went haywire and triggered a multiversal apocalypse that only comic book guy Stuart (Kevin Sussman) can stop.

It's early days yet, but the HBO series is pretty fun, making the most of the parent show's geeky bona fides and affection for genre tropes. If you're looking for more entertainment in the same nerdy vein, here are other shows that inject varying degrees of comedy into serious sci-fi scenarios.

Though less overtly comedic, there's an appealing goofiness to this quintessentially '90s bit of sci-fi, a show that anticipates the multiversal mayhem of the modern Marvel era. Jerry O'Connell is Quinn Mallory, who accidentally opens a portal that sends him and a rotating group of companions (including, initially, John Rhys-Davies as Quinn's mentor) through the multiverse. The device that he invents to get them all home is, inconveniently, an unreliable timer that keeps them stuck wherever they land for...well, however much time the story demands. Over the course of their adventures, they visit worlds where the Soviet Union won the Cold War, where antibiotics were never invented, and where Hillary Clinton is president (I swear!). Increasing serialization involving a whole species of mostly evil sliders doesn't really improve things as the show goes on, but it's still a pretty good time. Stream Sliders on Peacock and Tubi.

Josh Hutcherson plays Josh Futturman, a twenty-something janitor who lives with his parents and isn't good at much aside from video games. Though that's enough, as it turns out: He's the only person ever to finish the game Biotic Wars, a success that triggers the arrival of time-traveling soldiers from the future who recruit Josh for their war (yes, that's basically the plot of The Last Starfighter). The show succeeds by wearing its sci-fi influences on its sleeve, taking its world and backstory seriously before populating it with goofy, raunchy, and believably out-of-their-depth characters. Buy Future Man from Prime Video.

The subject here is outer-space sci-fi in the Star Trek mold, but it's still a beautifully irreverent sendup of the genre, with an amiable loser at its center. Craig Charles is Dave Lister, a well-meaning slob who holds the lowest job possible on the enormous mining ship Red Dwarf. When he sneaks a pregnant cat aboard, he's punished by being placed in suspension (without pay) for the rest of the trip. Which is a lot longer than anyone anticipated: When Dave wakes up, three million years have passed, and humanity is entirely extinct. The kittens survived and sired an inbred cat empire that's since risen and all but fallen, while the senile main computer has recreated Dave's hated roommate (Chris Barrie) as a hologram to keep him company. Soon joined by a prissy android, they spend the next 30+ years bumming about in space and stumbling into adventures. Stream Red Dwarf on Britbox.

In a depressingly straight and self-serious superhero-media landscape, Legends of Tomorrow soared past its rocky origins as a dumping ground for supporting characters from other DC shows to become something altogether weirder (and queerer). Initially recruited by a time traveller for a mission specifically because of their insignificance (their absences from the timeline won't affect a thing), the Legends go from screwups to reluctant heroes under the leadership of Sara Lance (Caity Lotz), putting things right in time and space. Blending solid character work with brilliant goofiness, the show saw plotlines involving a giant animatronic bear threatening the Old West, a season-ending fight scene set to "The Thong Song," and a character's nipple getting bitten off by a unicorn. Stream Legends of Tomorrow on Netflix.

I feel like Resident Alien flew a bit under the radar during its run, though it still managed a solid four-season run. Alan Tudyk (Serenity, Rogue One, Superman) stars as Dr. Harry Vanderspeigle, sort of: He's actually an alien with an unpronounceable name who crashed on Earth before killing the real Harry and assuming his identity. He's meant to scout the planet for a planned destruction, but, by assuming human form and integrating with the community in the tiny town of Patience, Colorado, he slowly begins to have second thoughts, even as he continues to be entirely repulsed by human culture. Tudyk is genuinely funny while managing to hit some moving emotional beats along his journey to not-wanting-to-kill-us-all-quite-as-much, and the supporting cast is similarly game. The fictional setting is set near the real Southern Ute Reservation, and offers up some impressive Indigenous representation, including Sara Tomko as Harry's bestie and occasional foil, Asta Twelvetrees. Stream Resident Alien on Peacock and Netflix.

The Librarians began life as a charming, Indiana Jones-light TV movie led by Noah Wylie way back in 2004, which spawned two sequels, the series in question, as well as a sequel show now entering its second season. While largely a standalone take on the mildly comedic premise (a secret annex of the New York Public Library that catalogs magical and occult objects), The Librarians finds Rebecca Romjin, John Larroquette, and Christian Kane leading a group of action-scholars who use their brains to save the world. They're not lovable losers in the Stuart mode, but are, nonetheless, a bunch of true nerds who become reluctant heroes. Stream The Librarians on Prime Video.

Creator Will Forte stars as Phil Miller, a former banker who believes, for about a year, that he’s the only survivor of a plague that wiped out humanity...until he meets Kristen Schaal, a notary from Delaware. The two don’t have much in common, but decide they’re responsible for repopulating the earth. Frequently genuinely funny, the show winds up striving for a larger purpose than parodying end-of-the-world narratives, exploring our obsession with the end times and what it means to live in a world where apocalyptic thinking winds up becoming self-fulfilling. Stream The Last Man on Earth on Hulu.

The tone of this sensational series is wildly different than that of Stuart, and yet it would feel like a disservice to not mention this weird sci-fi apocalypse from Breaking Bad's Vince Gilligan, which displays a very dark, very dry sense of humor. Rhea Seehorn plays Carol Sturka, a fantasy romance author and general grouch who becomes one of only 13 people on the planet immune to the "Joining"—the result of an alien virus that transforms the rest of humanity into a peaceful, perky, and perpetually content hive mind. Carol refuses to surrender her miserableness in the face of a loss of identity, fighting instead to restore humanity to its admittedly cruddy ways. Saving the world means saving the world for snobby misanthropes like herself. Thrilling, heartbreaking, and genuinely funny, the show manages to address some big questions about what it means to be human, and what we'd be willing to give up to change. Stream Pluribus on Apple TV.

Based on the ‘90s-era vehicular combat games that your parents probably hated (involving, as they do, a lot of wild, demolition-derby style action in which you smash and/or blow up your opponents), Twisted Metal stars Anthony Mackie as John Doe, a driver tasked with carrying a package across the entirely lawless Wasteland while dodging challenges that include a murderous clown in an ice cream truck. Alternately brutal and goofy, the show mostly does what it says on the tin, providing plenty of frenetic car-on-car action (and car-on-semi, car-on-hearse, -ice cream truck, etc.). If the over-the-top comedic violence of Stuart is your bag, you'll get plenty of that here. Stream Twisted Metal on Peacock.

New Queer Cinema pioneer Greg Araki followed up his neon-tinged cinematic apocalypse in Kaboom with Now Apocalypse, a successor in spirit. Avan Jogia plays Ulysses Zane, living in sun-soaked California with his best friend Carly (Kelli Berglund), a struggling actress and sex worker. He keeps having bizarre dreams about an alien invasion that feel increasingly like they might be premonitions, or possibly just anxiety delusions brought on by too much weed. The show only lasted one season and never quite made it to its own prophesied apocalypse, but it was definitely fun while it lasted, and definitely offers something a bit to the left of the typical dreary end-of-the-world. It's a comedy dystopia, just sweatier and hornier than usual. Stream Now Apocalypse on Tubi.

title: McClenaghan finishes sixth in pommel horse final
description: Olympic champion Rhys McClenaghan says his routine "didn't go to plan" as he finished sixth and missed out on a medal in the men's pommel horse final.
fullText:
Olympic champion Rhys McClenaghan said his routine "didn't go to plan" as he finished sixth and missed out on a medal in the men's pommel horse final.

McClenaghan scored 13.000 with his routine at the Glasgow International Arena as he failed to earn a medal at the Games for the first time after claiming gold in the Gold Coast in 2018 and silver in Birmingham four years ago.

The 27-year-old had qualified third with a score of 14.500 and the expectation heading into the final was that he would become Team Northern Ireland's third medallist of the Games and potentially claim their first gold.

But it all went wrong for the Newtownards man, who nearly came off the pommel horse at one stage towards the end of his routine that did not look right from the off.

His difficulty (5.200) and execution (7.800) scores plummeted from Friday's qualifying and he had an appeal for his score to be reviewed rejected.

"I didn't have a great start. They didn't count the first skill so that dismantled the whole routine. I tried to push through the rest of the routine and it was going well until the end and the leg splits happened," he told BBC Sport NI.

"If I had have went start to finish, if that first skill had been counted, and to the untrained eye, it is probably nothing, but the judges don't like to see that."

Canada's Jordan Carroll, who went in the first section of the final, set the bar high with his tremendous routine that scored 15.00 as he won the gold medal.

Scotland's Reuben Ward, who claimed gold in the men's all-round final, produced a big score of 14.966 to take silver while Cameron Lynn scored 13.833 and claimed bronze much to the delight of the large Scottish contingent in attendance.

Adam Tobin, who was part of the England team that took silver, slipped and fell off at the first attempt and scored 12.066 for his second attempt as he finished eighth.

Losing out in Glasgow brings to an end McClenaghan's remarkable run of five successive major championship wins after he claimed golds in the Worlds in 2022 and 2023, Europeans in 2023 and 2024 and culminated with the Olympic win in 2024.

It is the worst score he has recorded this year after registering 13.466 and 13.900 in the two World Cup competitions in Azerbaijan and Antalya as he made his comeback from injury earlier this year.

Despite his obvious frustration, McClenaghan was philosophical in reiterating this is only the start of a new cycle with the World and European Championships still to come this year and the ultimate goal of retaining the Olympic gold in Los Angeles still two years away.

"It's another stepping stone to what's to come. European Championships in a couple of weeks, World Championships in October and then we look to LA Olympics. This is the stepping stone," he added.

"If I had have come away with gold medal today it also would have been a stepping stone and I'm sure I would have taken as many lessons. It didn't go to plan.

"I'm mentioning these mistakes and they're the finest of margins in this sport. It's going to happen eventually, if it doesn't happen in training it will happen in competition.

"I treat them as the same, I'm going back to the gym to progress even more."

title: Porsche ramps up job cuts to 9,000 by 2035
description: German luxury carmaker Porsche will cut 9,000 jobs in total by 2035, it said on Monday, as parent Volkswagen and its brands restructure
fullText:
BERLIN, July 27 (Reuters) - German luxury carmaker Porsche will cut 9,000 jobs in total by 2035, it said ‌on Monday, as parent Volkswagen and its brands restructure in the face ‌of weak demand and stiff competition.

In a deal announced after months of negotiations, Porsche management and ​labour representatives agreed to 5,000 additional job cuts that avoid compulsory redundancies through measures like natural attrition and voluntary schemes.

What challenges is Porsche facing in China?

Why is Porsche cutting 9,000 jobs by 2035?

How will Porsche avoid compulsory redundancies?

What investments is Porsche making despite job cuts?

These measures follow a first package of 3,900 job cuts and another 500 announced by new CEO Michael Leiters earlier this year linked ‌to the closure of subsidiaries.

On ⁠becoming CEO at the start of the year, Leiters was tasked with overhauling the business after sales in Porsche's once highly ⁠lucrative China market collapsed and its EV strategy stalled.

Other German carmakers including Mercedes-Benz and BMW are also cutting costs as they navigate the shift to electric vehicles in ​a race ​with Chinese rivals while absorbing the impact ​of high tariffs.

The deal announced ‌by Porsche on Monday also includes guarantees to keep sites open for another five years, until the end of 2035, as well as €2.1 billion ($2.39 billion) in investments in its main factory of Stuttgart-Zuffenhausen and its R&D centre in Weissach, the company and the works council said in a statement.

The announcement followed a meeting of ‌Porsche's supervisory board last Wednesday, in which the ​committee gave its blessing to the additional cuts.

Leiters' ​predecessor Oliver Blume remains CEO ​of Volkswagen, having ended a dual leadership role that was ‌opposed by many investors.

Blume is now pushing ​for a doubling ​of job cuts across the Volkswagen group to 100,000, measures that he says are necessary to remain competitive as more Chinese brands come to Europe.

He ​has also warned that ‌four of the group's factories, including one belonging to premium brand Audi, ​are threatened with closure after 2030.

title: No, Miami isn’t more expensive than New York. But it may be less ‘affordable’
description: "Now they're having affordability issues, and I think that's really making people think twice about leaving New York," broker Michelle Griffith said.
fullText:
You may have seen the headline on your social media feeds this week, or some instance of it: Miami is now more expensive than New York City. The source of the headline is based on Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) data, which details the cost of living in Miami as greater than New York's for the first time ever.

How does Miami's cost of living compare to New York's?

What are the real estate price differences between cities?

What factors are driving Miami's affordability challenges?

How do job markets differ between Miami and New York?

The thing is, "expensive" is all relative. A locale's cost of living isn't a measure of raw prices—it's prices weighted against what local residents earn. The BEA finding doesn't mean that an apartment in Miami costs more than a comparable one in Manhattan. In fact, Manhattan's median listing price per square foot was $1,489 in May 2026, more than three times Miami-Dade County's $465, according to data retrieved via the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. What's changed is that Miami's prices have climbed further, relative to what the average Miami resident earns, compared to how New York's prices have climbed relative to what New Yorkers earn. And truth be told, both cities are viciously expensive.

That distinction also explains why the comparison misses how people actually live in each city. Cost-of-living indexes fold in categories that barely register for a Manhattan renter but hit Miami households hard, chief among them car ownership, along with rising insurance premiums, private school tuition and restaurant costs that have all climbed there over the past year. South Florida's consumer price index has risen 36% since 2019, more than any metro area tracked by the government, except Tampa. None of that has much to do with the price of Manhattan real estate.

Michelle Griffith, a broker at Douglas Elliman, has been fielding questions about the report since it published. It's really about that one word: affordability. "Affordability now in Miami, especially—and listen, I feel really badly for the people who were living in Miami [before this influx of new residents], and now all of a sudden the restaurant costs are going up, the transportation costs are going up, insurance costs are going up, rent is going up, tuition to send your kids to school is going up." That's a genuine problem for Miami residents, she added, but there isn't evidence that Miami has caught up to New York on the numbers that actually move real estate.

"When we really break down the numbers, the jobs are based in New York City," Griffith said. New York City's metro area added 86,800 jobs over the year through December 2025, more than double Miami's total and more than the combined job gains in Dallas, Philadelphia, and Atlanta, according to the NYCEDC's monthly economic snapshot. In contrast, Miami's metro area only added 42,600 jobs over the same 12-month stretch, according to BLS regional employment data, less than half of New York's total, despite Miami posting the faster percentage growth rate of the two metros.

title: In deep-red Iowa, rural voters consider voting for Democrat Rob Sand
description: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand, fueled by an $18 million war chest, welcomes Republicans on his 100-county tour of Iowa.
fullText:
SANBORN, IA — About 40 minutes into Rob Sand's town hall in rural northwest Iowa, resident Chuck Virgil takes the microphone.

"There's a lot of things I'd like to talk about," the 78-year-old lifelong Republican said, launching into a conversation about eminent domain and a proposed carbon capture pipeline slated to cut across the area.

As he reaches the end of his comments, Virgil tells the small crowd he's "this close" to supporting Sand, a Democrat, for governor.

Virgil is just one person and one vote. But Sand is hoping it's interactions like this one, multiplied many, many times over, that will lay the foundation for success in even the reddest parts of the state as he looks to reverse Democrats' long losing streak in November.

Sand is set to face Republican nominee Zach Lahn in what analysts are calling one of the most competitive governor contests in the country.

Fueled by record-breaking campaign donations that have netted him an $18 million war chest, Sand is now nearly halfway through his second 100-stop statewide town hall tour of the election cycle.

His July 21 schedule took him through five counties in rural, highly conservative northwest Iowa, where he drew crowds that his campaign said were often twice as large as previous events.

Sand started his day in O'Brien County, where voters backed Republican President Donald Trump by a 61 percentage-point margin over Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024. About 70 people attended.

Democrats don't expect Sand to flip counties like this one from Republicans on Election Day. But to win a governor's race for the first time since 2006, the party needs to prevent Republicans from running up the vote margin in these dark-red pockets.

Across Iowa, data from the Secretary of State's Office show registered Republicans outnumber Democrats by more than 180,000 people. In the 4th Congressional District, which is home to O'Brien County, there are about 117,000 more registered Republicans than registered Democrats.

But Sand said his approach here is no different than anywhere else in the state.

He expects "a good mix of Iowans from across the political spectrum who care who the next governor's going to be and are willing to take the time to come out and meet someone who's willing to meet them."

During his previous round of town halls, Sand always asked Republicans and independent voters to raise their hands to be applauded and welcomed to the event.

This time around, he's driving the point home even further by also handing his microphone over to one of those Republicans and asking them to share a question or comment.

"We can talk a lot about including each other, but a more important thing to do is to be judged by our actions, not just our words," Sand said during the event in Sanborn before giving Virgil the microphone.

After the event, Virgil told the Des Moines Register that he's a "very likely Sand voter" in November.

"I feel betrayed by the Republican Party," he said. "Absolutely betrayed."

He said Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds' veto of legislation that would have blocked the use of eminent domain for the carbon capture pipeline project is a major reason. He also wishes Republicans would better regulate the aerial application of agriculture chemicals, especially as the state's cancer rates climb.

"To me, as a lifelong Republican, really the whole crux of the matter is the Republican Party has run amok," he said. "I don't have a lot of confidence in the Democratic Party, but I do want to put some confidence in someone. And if that someone is Rob Sand, I want to give him a chance."

In his remarks, Sand worked to smooth the transition for Republicans and independents like Virgil who might remain skeptical of the Democratic Party — even if they're Sand-curious.

"At the end of the day, I think the Democratic Party tends to be the party that does a better job of representing the little guy," he said in Sanborn. "Maybe that's not true as much now as it used to be. Maybe you don't think that's true at all. I'm just telling you what I thought when I signed up as a Democrat. And I know my values haven't changed, even if the parties' may have moved."

Lahn and other Republicans have criticized Sand for what they say is a hypocritical approach to his town halls.

They've circulated a video showing Sand's staff denying entry to someone who says she is a Republican. A staffer in a Sand T-shirt says the event is "private."

"Is it because I worked for Adam Steen? That's the policy?" the person filming the video says. Steen competed in the Republican primary for governor.

"Our policy is just, if you have worked for opposition candidates who have been running against us, then we're just going to ask you to leave," the Sand staffer says.

Kollin Crompton, communications director for the Republican Governors Association, posted the video to social media, criticizing Sand for holding open events "unless you are a Republican with a question."

Asked about the incident, Sand told the Register the campaign expects to host more than 10,000 people across its 100 town halls this year.

"I think the vast majority of Iowans are reasonable people that would understand that some folks don't behave in a way that gets them in the front door," he said.

Lahn has also criticized Sand for conducting town halls instead of being in the auditor's office.

"Thursday at 3:30 p.m. during a workday," he wrote, sharing one of the Sand campaign's recent posts about a mid-week town hall. "Out Of Office. Rob Sand Doesn't Work."

But Sand said he would continue to do a 100-stop public town hall tour even if he's elected governor. Current Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds does not hold public town halls.

"Don't these people deserve that?" he told the Register. "I mean, aren't we supposed to have a political system where people know that no matter who they are, they might at least have a opportunity to meet and to question the people that have been elected to lead their state? I understand that that's a big undertaking, but I think that's the way it's supposed to be done."

He said his truck is equipped with satellite internet, so he can work everywhere he goes, especially if someone drives him.

"I can be on the phone, I can be reading reports, I can be emailing, I can be on Zoom," he said.

Sand also criticized Lahn, who has held one publicly advised campaign event since winning the nomination and didn't publicly answer questions from attendees or take questions from reporters who attended. Lahn has said he stayed after the event to talk to Iowans directly. He also has attended parades, other private events and party functions.

"That's not leadership," Sand told reporters at an event in Spencer. "You don't get these questions and these issues resolved without being willing to lead."

Kelly Nieuwenhuis, a 67-year-old Primghar Republican, also attended the town hall in Sanborn. He said he previously voted for Sand for state auditor "because I like checks and balances."

"I haven't totally decided, but I'm leaning very hard towards voting for Rob," he said. "And it's just mainly because I really like his campaign slogan of not redder or bluer, but better and truer."

Nieuwenhuis said he's served on the Iowa Corn Board of the National Corn Growers Association for nine years, and he has come to appreciate that being an independent thinker open to working with all sides can help advance a cause.

He said Republican U.S. Rep. Randy Feenstra was his first choice in the Republican primary, but he's not a Lahn fan. He said he's skeptical of the time Lahn spent out of state before moving back to Iowa.

"I just don't know him that well," he said. "I know Rob better."

Brianne Pfannenstiel is the chief politics reporter for the Des Moines Register. She writes about campaigns, elections and the Iowa Caucuses. Reach her at bpfann@dmreg.com or 515-284-8244. Follow her on X at @brianneDMR.

This article originally appeared on Des Moines Register: In deep-red Iowa, rural voters consider voting for Democrat Rob Sand

title: 'This is just the start': India's Gen Z protesters force out a minister, but what next?
description: The education minister's resignation, a rare setback for the Modi government, brings hope to many young protesters that their voices will be heard.
fullText:
In 12 years of Narendra Modi's rule in India , only one cabinet minister had previously resigned - over allegations of sexual misconduct.

So the resignation of education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, on Saturday after more than a week of intense street demonstrations was a defining moment – and one which many young people were quick to celebrate.

In the words of 22-year-old Sakhi, a student activist in Delhi, "for the first time, it felt like we can make things happen through protests".

Soon after Pradhan quit, social media seized on an old video of a senior Modi minister boasting that "resignations do not happen in our government", reflecting the confidence of the nationwide youth movement that had demanded his exit.

Sakhi says they grew up reading textbooks that spoke about the importance of dissent in a democracy, "but I did not see that around me in the Modi years".

On Instagram, Sakhi posted photos and videos of police assaults and detentions alongside reels mocking officers standing beside them. Many have been viewed millions of times.

Sakhi says the government failed to grasp the movement's momentum because it was out of touch with the language and platforms of the protests. "The government has a hold on mainstream media, Facebook and WhatsApp. But it missed Instagram."

The latest education protests erupted in May after NEET, India's biggest medical entrance exam, was cancelled following a question paper leak, forcing nearly two million students to retake the test. More than 20 students died by suicide, with their families blaming the scandal.

The outrage was channelled by the satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), an online campaign launched after India's chief justice likened unemployed people with "fake and bogus degrees" to cockroaches. Its founders staged a sit-in in Delhi, demanding Pradhan's resignation, education reforms and compensation for the bereaved families.

Initially, the protest drew little attention. That changed on 18 July when Delhi police forcibly removed and hospitalised hunger-striking educator Sonam Wangchuk.

Two days later, tens of thousands marched on parliament at the CJP's call, triggering a police crackdown. Videos of baton charges, tear gas and pellet guns spread rapidly online, fuelling public anger and swelling the protests instead of suppressing them.

The discontent among India's youth and the courage to voice it on the streets spread to other parts of the country.

Somaya Korde was detained at home after urging people online to join a 20 July protest in Mumbai, but went on to attend multiple demonstrations in the days that followed.

Pradhan's resignation, says the 26-year-old, "is not the end, but just the beginning".

"For this generation, this is the first time many of us have stepped out to protest. But there are larger issues to talk about, and we will talk about them," she says.

Korde, the first woman in her family to graduate in law and a recent civic election candidate, comes from a community officially classified as "backward" because of its historic social and economic disadvantage.

Like many young Indians, she saw education as her path to a better life, but says the NEET paper leak shattered her faith in a system that promised hard work would be rewarded.

"Schools and colleges are being privatised, paper leaks are happening, even if you finish education, there are not enough jobs. In a democracy, all this raises questions of accountability against the government," she says.

Her frustration is indicative of a larger picture.

India has the world's largest youth population, yet unemployment among 15- to 29-year-olds rose to 16.2% in June from 13.8% a year earlier, according to government data.

Even graduates are struggling: a 2026 Azim Premji University study found fewer than 7% of jobseekers secured permanent salaried work within a year, and fewer than 4% landed white-collar jobs.

The protests became a rallying point for young people to shed their caution and voice their frustration. Among them was 18-year-old Harshvardhan Kadam, who took a part-time job selling laptops after finishing school to help support his mother following his father's death last year.

On 23 July, a video Harshvardhan filmed during a protest march in Mumbai went viral. In the Instagram reel, now viewed 10 million times, a policeman is seen threatening to frame him in a fake drugs case while detaining him in a police van. The constable has since been suspended.

"I did not wish him to be suspended," Kadam told the BBC, "I just wanted to document how the police were treating me for participating in a peaceful protest." Now, reflecting on Pradhan's resignation he says: "This is just the start. This shows that next time the government will be scared when we raise our voices."

Swaraj Priyo, a 29-year-old screenwriter from Guwahati, says years of protesting under the Modi government had left him disillusioned by the lack of change. But this movement, he says, has restored hope: "This movement has brought back space for question and dissent and the reality check that all is not over."

A growing sense that the Modi government is on the back foot is palpable. Protest sites across the country now display posters declaring: "Pradhan was just an example. It's Modi's turn next".

But alongside this bullishness comes some apprehension.

Varuni Poorva, a 30-year-old aspiring professor from Patna and a student activist for nearly a decade, says Pradhan's resignation shows the Modi government can be "brought to its knees".

But she fears a "witch hunt" against protesters despite the government's pledge not to act against those who organised or joined the demonstrations.

Over the past week, she has sought anticipatory bail to guard against possible arrest. Police have charged more than 100 protesters with offences including attempted murder, and arrested more than 40.

The organisation Human Rights Watch says that under Modi, Indian authorities have "routinely prosecuted activists, journalists, and peaceful protesters on fabricated counterterrorism and hate speech laws".

Despite fears of a crackdown, shared by many students' parents, Poorva believes the protests have given young people newfound confidence. With their deeper frustrations unresolved, she says, it will be difficult for the government to return to "business as usual".

At one protest site in Delhi, graffiti captures the mood: "We do not have jobs. If you wipe this out, we will come back tomorrow".

title: Funeral director breached families' trust 'on industrial scale'
description: The sentencing hearing of Robert Bush hears how the funeral parlour was likened to a "horror scene".
fullText:
A funeral director who failed to bury people and gave out wrong ashes has breached the trust of bereaved families "on an almost industrial scale", a court has heard.

Some 35 bodies and more than 100 sets of ashes were found by police raiding Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull in March 2024.

Owner Robert Bush previously admitted 67 offences, including 30 counts of preventing a lawful and decent burial, and theft from 12 charities.

At the start of his five-day sentencing hearing on Monday, family members watching proceedings at Hull Crown Court gasped and were in tears as details of the "horror scene" at the parlour were described by prosecutors.

This story contains details some might find distressing.

Chris Paxton KC told the packed court bodies had been discovered "on the racks" of a cold storage area and one was found on a stretcher on the floor.

The vast majority were "uncovered and in varying states of decomposition", including one of a stillborn baby.

Bush, 48, was "entrusted by hundreds of bereaved families" but had "breached that trust on an almost industrial scale in a myriad of ways", Paxton said.

Paxton said the scale of Bush's offending was discovered by chance when, while he was on holiday in the US, he asked two funeral directors from another firm to remove a body from a care home.

Patrick Moore, a casual worker at Legacy, had been told by Bush "not to bring anyone back to Legacy", Paxton said.

The court heard the undertakers became suspicious and asked Moore how many bodies were at the site.

Paxton said Moore counted up to 29 bodies and described it as something from a "horror scene", adding: "You two don't know the half of it, bodies have been there for years."

The undertakers were "shaken" and flagged down a passing police car, the court was told.

During searches, officers found a brown paper bag containing a tiny item they initially thought was a baby bird.

They then saw two hospital wristbands wrapped around the waist that read "Baby of Jasmine Beverley, born on 13/05/22 at 05:04", Paxton said.

The funeral home was also described as "dirty and unkempt", with flowers, teddies and cards strewn on the floor - items "loved ones would have wanted" for their deceased family members.

Bush, of Otley, West Yorkshire, was arrested when he landed at Heathrow Airport days later.

He told officers his daughter, with whom he was travelling, was "unaware" of what had happened and said, "I have deceived everyone".

Of the remains discovered at the Hessle Road premises, most were "of older people above the age of 60" and about six bodies were waiting to be cremated.

One of the bodies had been at the site for a year.

Hundreds of victim impact statements are expected to be read over the course of the week.

The first was from Karen King, whose father Norman Bridger's body was recovered 10 months after his death.

Her statement described how she had lockets made for her and her mother containing the ashes given to her by Bush.

"I now feel violated that I have had some unknown person's ashes so close to me," she wrote.

The moment Robert Bush is arrested at Heathrow airport

Kathryn Howard, who used Legacy after her 73-year-old partner Jonathan Butler died, told the court her "world fell apart all over again" when she learned his body had been left at the site.

She said an apology "would not be enough for me" and wanted Bush to know that she will "never, ever, get over this".

Byron Lill had to pause at times while he read out his statement. He said his mother Muriel Winning died from cancer in July 2023 and he was given ashes by Bush, which he placed on his windowsill.

"Bush took advantage of us when we were at our most vulnerable. He abused his position of trust. Why?"

Through floods of tears, Christina George read out her statement which detailed how the body of her fisherman brother, Raymond Dagnall, was "left on a rack wearing a soiled hospital gown and still with hospital tubes in his body".

George thought she had scattered his ashes at Bridlington Harbour, as per his wishes, and said the discovery had made "me feel sick and the hairs prickle on the back of my neck".

John Banyard arranged for a cremation and funeral for his 77-year-old friend John Carlill, the £970 cost of which was paid for from the estate.

When he went to see his friend, Bush told Banyard the deceased "didn't look good", so the lid of the casket was kept down.

In a statement, Banyard described the former funeral director as the "lowest of the low".

"Bush shook my hand and was saying 'God bless' to me," he said.

"If you can't trust a funeral undertaker, who can you trust? How can someone be so callous, cold and calculated?"

Reading her statement, Mollie Finn described the devastating emotional and psychological impact of learning the body of her grandfather, Graham Finn, had been found at the home.

"There are no words to fully capture the disgust I feel. Every time I see this case in the news, it feels like an out-of-body experience, like it's not real - like this couldn't possibly be happening to us."

The 23-year-old said she "despised" Bush.

"I hope that for the rest of his life, he is haunted by what he has done."

She added: "Justice must be served, not just for our family, but for every single person affected by this appalling crime."

Jade Munro, whose father Tony Munro's body was recovered four months after his death, told the court she was angered that "there are no regulations in the funeral business".

She quickly became upset as she read out her statement, in which she said: "We've been to hell and back".

The court also heard how families had to go through a second funeral, with several questioning whether it had been legitimate.

How memories of my grandma are tainted by funeral boss's crimes

Funeral fraudster motivated by money, says ex-worker

The court heard that between March 2017 and April 2024, more than £3m was paid into Bush's accounts. He also transferred more than £879,000 to his wife, who was on the "payroll for tax purposes".

When questioned, Bush told police he had debts of about £90,000, Paxton said.

The prosecutor told the court: "In respect of the older bodies that had not been cremated due to cash flow issues, his plan had been to generate more business and clear the backlog within two to three months."

A single cremation cost about £500, Paxton added, but Bush "chose not to deal with those bodies entrusted to him but to operate as he chose and spend the money on himself and others".

"The financial situation within the business was not dire, but likely mismanaged, and the expenditure reflected Mr Bush's priorities and not those whom he was meant to be serving."

Ashes recovered from Legacy funeral home reburied

'I'm trying to forgive undertaker who kept my dead baby'

title: Wales' Pawlett out of Commonwealth heptathlon
description: The 22-year-old follows Katarina Johnson-Thompson in pulling out of the competition but still competes in the 200m.
fullText:
Welsh athlete Abi Pawlett has pulled out of the heptathlon event at the Commonwealth Games.

The 22-year-old follows Katarina Johnson-Thompson in withdrawing from the competition.

Pawlett has been recovering from an Achilles injury that forced her out of the World Indoor Championships in March, just weeks after claiming the British 60m hurdles indoor title and a personal pentathlon best in February.

She will still compete in the 200m in Glasgow, but the workload of seven events in the heptathlon is too much.

Pawlett is Wales' only female 200m sprinter after national record holder Hannah Brier was controversially not selected after missing the cut-off date to run the qualification time.

Brier later complained Wales' deadline was too early compared to other nations.

title: China's industrial profit growth moderates as exports cushion uneven recovery
description: BEIJING, July 27 () - Profits at China's industrial firms grew at a solid, though slower, pace as resilient exports helped cushion sluggish domestic demand, highlighting ‌the economy's uneven recovery despite policymakers' efforts to spur consumption. Exports and industrial production ‌have done much of the heavy lifting for the world's second-largest economy.
fullText:
BEIJING, July 27 (Reuters) - Profits at China's industrial firms grew at a solid, though slower, pace as resilient exports helped cushion sluggish domestic demand, highlighting ‌the economy's uneven recovery despite policymakers' efforts to spur consumption.

Exports and industrial production ‌have done much of the heavy lifting for the world's second-largest economy. Persistent weakness in consumption and the ​property sector, however, helped drag second-quarter growth to its slowest pace in more than three years, keeping calls alive for further policy support to address economic imbalances.

What drove China's industrial profit growth in June?

Why did automobile manufacturing profits decline significantly?

What policy support measures might China consider next?

How are exports supporting China's economic recovery?

Industrial profit growth eased to 15.1% in June from 21.1% in May, while first-half profits rose 18.7% from a ‌year earlier, compared with an ⁠18.8% increase in the January-to-May period, data from the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) showed on Monday.

"If this recovery can be sustained, it will ⁠be a good sign for the rest of the economy, as a return of profits growth could give companies room to resume wage growth," said Lynn Song, chief economist of Greater ​China at ​ING.

The figures add to evidence of a two-speed ​recovery in the world's second-largest economy, ‌where manufacturers have benefited from robust overseas demand, while sectors tied to domestic spending continue to struggle.

"The external environment remains complex and international commodity prices uncertain," NBS statistician Yu Weining said. "Industrial firms also face weak demand and cash flow pressures."

Underlining strains in the domestic market, automobile manufacturing profits fell 19.5% in the first half of the year, NBS ‌data showed, as car sales declined for a ninth ​consecutive month in June.

Market reaction was muted with ​Chinese stocks and the yuan slightly ​firmer following the data.

Attention is now turning to the Communist Party's Politburo ‌meeting at the end of July, ​a key policy-setting gathering ​where investors will look for signals on additional support measures.

Expectations for a broad-based stimulus package have been tempered, however, by resilient exports and Beijing's preference for targeted ​easing.

Industrial profit figures cover firms ‌with annual revenue of at least 20 million yuan ($2.95 million) from their ​main operations.

title: Study documents a precipitous decline in the number of languages
description: Globally, people currently use roughly 7,500 languages, with English, Mandarin Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, Arabic and French the most common, counting
fullText:
WASHINGTON, July 27 (Reuters) - Globally, people currently use roughly 7,500 languages, with English, Mandarin Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, Arabic and French the most common, counting native and nonnative speakers. That is a lot of languages. But it is a far cry from the peak number historically.

Researchers used mathematical modeling and ‌insights from anthropology, linguistics and demography to estimate the number of languages used globally dating back about 12,000 years to around the end of the last Ice ‌Age, covering a chapter in time called the Holocene epoch. They identified a period spanning the first millennium BC and first millennium AD when humankind may have spoken tens of thousands of different languages.

The researchers also charted ​a major decline since this linguistic "golden age," due to language replacement driven by factors such as the expansion of large empires in antiquity and European colonialism in the past several centuries.

"Languages are meaningful to their communities. They carry knowledge, associations and memories," said Claire Bowern, a professor of linguistics and anthropology at Yale University in Connecticut, and a leader of the study published in the journal Science.

"For scientists, languages carry huge amounts of information about the past, from where people lived to what they ate, and what they talked about. They also give us a window into ‌the human mind," Bowern said.

Many language families arose and evolved, with ⁠written language eventually emerging, first in Mesopotamia — Sumerian written in cuneiform script — during the fourth millennium BC, and separately in places like Egypt, China and Mesoamerica. The researchers estimated that the number topped out in a range from 30,000 to potentially more than 75,000 different languages used worldwide ⁠at any one time.

"We rarely appreciate that, until just a few thousand years ago, humanity inhabited a vastly more diverse cultural world than the one we know today," said study lead author Damian Blasi, a cognitive scientist and evolutionary anthropologist at the Catalan Institution for Research and Advanced Studies in Spain.

The researchers used some ingenuity in reaching their estimates.

"There's no direct evidence for language numbers until ​very ​recently. We cannot rely on the extremely patchy records from antiquity. But because we know a lot about ​the relationships between languages and societies, we can use a couple ‌of assumptions to make a simulation model of language diversification through time," Bowern said.

The researchers used data spanning 171 extant hunter-gatherer societies in Africa, South America and Southeast Asia to assess the size of ethnolinguistic groups — each representing a distinct language — near the beginning of the Holocene. They applied that to estimates of the human population at the time.

People were dispersed in small bands around the world living as nomadic hunter-gatherers, with the onset of agriculture and the establishment of permanent settlements and more complex cultures yet to come. The researchers estimated that these scattered populations some 12,000 years ago spoke perhaps 4,500 to 6,200 languages.

As the global population gradually grew over subsequent millennia and human society changed, the number of languages expanded.

"The situation where ‌populations are increasing and using agriculture creates more sedentary communities and is ideal for the fostering of ​many, many small languages," Bowern said.

Numerous major and minor languages have come and gone. Just a few examples ​include the Sumerian, Hittite, Akkadian and Etruscan languages, various languages used in ancient Egypt ​and ancient China, and some African click languages.

Bowern described some ways languages disappear.

"The people who speak that language are killed or the people who ‌speak that language shift — or are forced to shift — to another language," ​Bowern said.

Bowern also noted that old languages can ​evolve into new languages, as Latin, the tongue of ancient Rome, morphed into languages including French, Italian and Spanish in the centuries after the Western Roman Empire expired in 476 AD.

Colonial powers often pursued linguistic imperialism. For instance, England cracked down on the Irish language in Ireland, Spain banned indigenous languages in the Americas and ​Portugal barred indigenous languages in Brazil. Other examples include France prescribing ‌French in its African colonies and Japan suppressing Korean in Korea.

Some managed to persist. For instance, languages of the Inca, Maya and Aztecs survived Spanish suppression ​efforts.

About half of languages used today are deemed endangered.

Bowern said that "90% of the world's population speaks 10% of the world's languages, so there are many, many ​languages with small numbers of speakers and signers."

title: Nevada man dies at famed Sequoia National Park trail after sudden emergency
description: An elderly Nevada hiker died after a suffering from a medical emergency on a popular hiking trail in Sequoia National Park on Thursday.
fullText:
An elderly man reportedly died Thursday after suffering a medical emergency on a popular hiking trail in California's Sequoia National Park.

The victim was identified as 79-year-old John Francis Oliver of Henderson, Nevada, a suburb of Las Vegas, the Tulare County Sheriff's Office said, according to Your Central Valley.

Oliver was found along the General Sherman Tree Trail, a one-mile path that leads to the world's largest living tree, the General Sherman Tree, according to the outlet, citing the National Park Service (NPS).

First responders rendered emergency medical aid to Oliver at the scene, but the man was eventually pronounced dead in the park, according to SFGATE.

Cause Of Death Revealed For Big Sur Hiker Whose Body Was Found Naked On Remote California Trail

The Tulare County Sheriff's Office declined to release additional details about what led to the medical emergency or the circumstances surrounding Oliver's death "out of respect for the family," SFGATE reported.

The man's cause of death has also not yet been determined.

Park Visitors Face Flood Danger Out West While Severe Storms Rip Through Ny, Nj

The incident came as temperatures in the region climbed into the upper 90s, according to the National Weather Service.

An extreme heat warning was also in effect Thursday for portions of the nearby Mojave Desert and Indian Wells Valley.

Thursday's death marks the latest in a string of fatal incidents at Sequoia National Park and nearby areas in recent months.

Lone Survivor Rescued After Fatal Fall Kills Three Climbers On Mount Mckinley

In June, a 17-year-old girl died after slipping into a fast-moving river during her first visit to Sequoia National Park, according to a GoFundMe.

In neighboring Kings Canyon National Park, a San Mateo couple drowned at Roaring River Falls in May, according to Fox 2 San Francisco.

Last summer, NPS also said a local missing hiker, 36, was found dead in Sequoia National Park.

Fox News Digital contacted the National Park Services and the Sequoia National Park
