title: 'Every country wants to beat Nigeria' - Super Falcons hunt 11th Wafcon title
description: Nigeria face Malawi, Zambia and Egypt at the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations, looking to defend their crown and claim an 11th title.
fullText:
Nigeria arrived in Morocco for the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations (Wafcon) carrying a familiar burden of expectation.

Having claimed a record-extending 10th title in the North African kingdom last July - a campaign dubbed "Mission X" - the Super Falcons remain the benchmark in African women's football.

The challenge now is to retain their crown, something they last managed in 2018, the culmination of a hat-trick of titles.

"Now that we are champions, every other team will want to draw you down," head coach Justin Madugu, who masterminded last year's title charge which concluded in a 3-2 victory over the hosts, told BBC Sport Africa

"It's not going to be easy. We are quite aware of that and we are going to be fully ready."

Nigeria begin against debutants Malawi on Tuesday before also facing Zambia and Egypt in Group C.

"Every country wants to beat Nigeria," said assistant coach Ann Chiejine, a four-time Wafcon winner as a player.

"That is why we must up our game by making sure we train harder."

The squad contains some of the most recognisable names in African football.

Captain Rasheedat Ajibade, named best player at last year's tournament, Chiamaka Nnadozie, the current African goalkeeper of the year, and six-time African player of the year Asisat Oshoala will provide experience and leadership.

But Madugu has also chosen to weave in a number of young players, including striker Joy Omewa, who plays her club football in Sweden and observed last year's Wafcon triumph from afar.

"The last one was really exciting to watch. All the games were really good.

"I think this year it's going to be even bigger."

All you need to know about Wafcon 2026

Nigeria are one of only three nations to lift the Wafcon trophy.

Their dominance is such that they have claimed 10 of the 13 titles dating back to 1998, with only Equatorial Guinea (2008 and 2012) and South Africa (2022) able to break their stranglehold.

This time around they face greater competition, if only by weight of numbers after the tournament was expanded from 12 to 16 teams.

There is also more at stake because Wafcon doubles as a qualifying competition for next year's Fifa Women's World Cup in Brazil, with the four semi-finalists all guaranteed a place in Brazil.

"Our first target is to qualify for the World Cup. After that we can think of defending our title," winger Francisca Ordega told BBC Sport Africa.

"We are not under any kind of pressure. We can hold our own against any team across Africa."

Nigeria have represented the continent at all nine World Cups since the first was held in China in 1991.

In 2023, a record four nations travelled to Australia and New Zealand, with the West Africans being joined by South Africa and debutants Morocco and Zambia.

"We have come of age," said Cheijine when discussing improvements in the African game.

"If we are now being beaten by penalty shootout, or 1-0, 2-0, it means that the graph is rising."

In Morocco, Cape Verde and Malawi are the two countries making their maiden Wafcon appearances.

Malawi may be ranked 153rd in the world, compared to Nigeria in 36th, but the Scorchers boast a fearsome attack with proven pedigree in the form of the Chawinga sisters, Tabitha and Temwa.

Older sister Tabitha scored the goals which fired Lyon to a fifth consecutive league title in France last season.

Temwa, meanwhile, has won the National Women's Soccer League golden boot and MVP awards in both of her two full seasons with Kansas City Current.

Nigeria will also have to be on their guard against Zambia's experienced strike duo Barbra Banda and Racheal Kundananji, both of whom also play in the USA.

"You don't want to undermine or underestimate what anybody can do, Madugu said on the eve of the team's opening fixture, with Ajibade cautioning that Malawi's qualification shows "the progress they're making".

Seven stars to watch at Wafcon 2026 and why

'Motherhood should not be the end of anyone's story'

While previous Wafcons have seen Nigeria's preparation time limited, Madugu and his staff have had the luxury of multiple friendlies to run the rule over the current squad.

A double-header against Cameroon in the early months of the year was followed by two warm-up matches against Senegal in June and a victory over Tanzania last week.

Twenty-one-year-old goalkeeper Comfort Erhabor, the backup to Nnadozie, is among the fresh faces brought in by Madugu.

Born in the Netherlands and raised in England, she made her debut against Cameroon.

"The trust he [Madugu] puts in us young players is something I respect a lot," she said.

"I didn't expect to get along so quickly and so well with the team. But they received me with open arms."

Erhabor currently plays in the third tier of English football for Portsmouth, a city just over an hour's drive along the south coast to Brighton, which is where Nnadozie plies her trade.

Describing Nigeria's number one as like "a big sister" who she hangs out with, she says it was a "no brainer" when it came to choosing her international allegiance.

"It's in my blood, so I felt like there is no greater honour than to represent my roots, make my parents proud as well.

"I love the culture, and one big thing for me was how open everyone here is with Christianity and religion, because I felt that would allow me to come into the team, faith-based, and express myself."

As Madugu searches for a heavenly blend of youth and experience, Omewa describes the stellar names she now trains alongside as "golden", as opposed to older.

"Without them we wouldn't be here today.

"With them coming into the team, teaching us how to do it, we learn from those people."

Fellow striker Oshoala, who is chasing her fifth Wafcon title, is one of those Omewa is thankful to.

"She's a really remarkable person. She's a person who you can talk to, share experiences with and she tells you things she has gone through.

"I think she's a really good mentor."

Nigeria do not have all of their stars available, with centre-back Ashleigh Plumptre, a central figure in last year's Wafcon campaign, out with a foot injury.

The squad has also been unsettled after falling victim to thefts after landing in Morocco, with forward Esther Okoronkwo, player of the match in last year's final, reportedly losing hundreds of dollars.

When it comes to prize money, the pot for this year's tournament has been doubled, with the winners picking up $2m (£1.5m) - an increase indicative of the continued growth in African women's football.

But despite the increasing level of competition, Nigeria remain the team to beat.

title: Bell stays cool as Brave win last-ball thriller
description: Lauren Bell holds her nerve as Southern Brave win a last-ball thriller against MI London to maintain their 100% start to this year's edition of The Hundred.
fullText:
The Hundred women's competition, Utilita Bowl

Southern Brave 126-7 (100 balls): Wolvaardt 35 (30); Matthews 4-22

MI London 125-3 (100 balls): Wyatt-Hodge 52* (42); Wong 1-20

Lauren Bell held her nerve as Southern Brave won a last-ball thriller against MI London to maintain their 100% start to this year's edition of The Hundred.

With eight runs required off the final five deliveries of the match, Bell kept her cool as MI fell one run short of Brave's total of 126-7.

Danni Wyatt-Hodge had laid the foundation for MI's chase with an unbeaten half-century, but with four needed off Bell's final delivery she was unable to find a boundary.

Bell was mobbed by her Brave team-mates as they made it three wins from their opening three fixtures to remain top of the standings while winless MI were left to rue how they made such a hash of the chase.

Earlier, Maia Bouchier had given Brave's innings some early impetus with a breezy 31 off 22 balls before she was caught slog-sweeping Hayley Matthews to deep mid-wicket.

South Africa batter Laura Wolvaardt then shared a 60-run stand for the third wicket with the more fluent Jemimah Rodrigues, who made 32 off 22 deliveries only to be snared by Matthews.

But Brave's innings faded away towards the end in the face of some tight bowling from MI as Matthews finished with 4-22.

West Indies all-rounder Matthews then gave MI a solid platform in the chase, smacking four fours in her 32 off 28 deliveries only to miss a straight one from Issy Wong.

Wyatt-Hodge and MI skipper Holly Armitage looked to have things under control only for the latter to depart for 27 after feathering an edge off Sarah Glenn into the gloves of Lizelle Lee.

MI then struggled to find the middle of the bat as Wong and Sophie Molineux bowled tightly to ramp up the pressure further.

Victory still appeared within reach for MI when Bell stepped up to bowl the final set for Brave, but neither Wyatt-Hodge nor Nicola Carey could find the clean strike required to beat the fielders as they fell agonisingly short.

The focus switches to Headingley in The Hundred on Tuesday, where Sunrisers Leeds host Manchester Super Giants in a double header.

In the women's competition, the unbeaten Super Giants will hope to cut Southern Brave's lead at the top of the table when they face the Sunrisers at 15:00 BST.

The Super Giants' men are bidding to make it three wins from their opening three fixtures against their rivals from across the Pennines at 18:30 BST.

title: Kremlin says it has seen nothing tangible on any new Ukraine peace proposals
description: MOSCOW, July 27 (Reuters) - The Kremlin said on Monday that it had not seen any specific information regarding new proposals for a peace settlement in Ukraine ahead of a meeting in Washington between
fullText:
MOSCOW, July 27 (Reuters) - The Kremlin said on Monday that it had not seen ‌any specific information regarding new proposals for ‌a peace settlement in Ukraine ahead of a meeting ​in Washington between U.S. President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy.

Trump and Zelenskiy are due to hold talks in Washington on Tuesday.

A Ukrainian ‌source said last ⁠week that U.S. and Ukrainian officials had been discussing a proposal for ⁠an air ceasefire to take to Russian counterparts as part of a new round of peace ​talks.

"It is ​true that this ​information emerged a few ‌days ago, but so far it is nothing more than media speculation. There are no specific details on this matter, nor are there any specific details regarding any new proposals or ‌suggestions," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov ​told reporters.

Peskov also declined ​to comment on ​an assertion by Zelenskiy that Moscow ‌was preparing to receive 30,000 ​North Korean ​troops in Russia's Voronezh region.

"I don't think it's necessary to comment on them (Zelenskiy's remarks)," ​said Peskov. "It's ‌not for Zelenskiy to talk about our ​plans."

title: Europe's huge wildfires strain waterbomber capacity, aerial firefighting firm Avincis says
description: (Refiles story to remove erroneous spelling of company name in paragraph 5)  PARIS, July 27 (Reuters) - Europe's largest aerial emergency services firm Avincis is warning Europe is not ready for longe...
fullText:
(Refiles story to remove erroneous spelling of company name in paragraph 5)

PARIS, July 27 (Reuters) - Europe's largest aerial emergency services firm Avincis is warning Europe is not ready for longer and more extreme wildfire ‌seasons, with the company's chief executive telling Reuters that its firefighting aircraft are now needed almost year-round.

CEO John ‌Boag said longer European wildfire seasons and bureaucratic obstacles have exacerbated regional shortages of both aircraft and the experienced pilots needed to fly them.

"Globally, fire seasons ​are getting longer, aircraft are not moving between areas and pilots are becoming harder and harder to get," Boag said in an interview.

The comments by Boag, a helicopter pilot who began his career herding cattle in Australia's outback in a Bell 47 chopper in 1985, come as France and Spain battle historic wildfires after weeks of drought turned forests into major fire risks.

Lisbon-based Avincis says Europe is ‌under strain in part because the extra months ⁠of firefighting narrow the window for moving capacity between hemispheres, leaving gaps in capacity.

"Originally the peak period of the year over the summer was three or four months ... Now we have aircraft starting ⁠in March and April and going through to October," Boag said.

Wet winters only make the problem worse by increasing the growth of vegetal matter that can later turn into tinder. Just as concerning is the spread of fire risk further North.

"You're at a point where governments ​are going ​to have to be able to afford to have the aircraft ​available to cover a 12-month period, because commercial companies ‌can't go to the South (southern hemisphere) and earn more revenue over the off-season," Boag said.

Avincis has a fleet of 180 helicopters and 40 fixed-wing planes worldwide, including 22 Canadair waterbombers.

In Spain and Portugal, where it uses 47 aircraft, Avincis has flown more than 5,000 hours in firefighting operations so far this year, more than double the same period in 2025.

Europe has already made a collective purchase of 22 of the rugged water-scooping Canadairs from Toronto-based De Havilland Canada. After a decade-long production halt, ‌a new model is coming but won't reach its first customer, Greece, ​until 2028.

The Airbus A400M military plane has joined firefighting in France, ​dropping 20 tonnes of retardant. Others including China's Comac ​touted potential plane variants at last week's Farnborough Airshow and a French startup, HYNAERO, is in the ‌early design phase of an amphibious plane to be ​ready in 2032.

Firefighting is demanding, ​relying on low-level, precision flying in the face of unpredictable air currents. Experts say there is a shortage of experienced pilots and technicians.

Boag faulted European rules that require pilots to re-sit civil aviation exams if coming from abroad or ​the military.

"We need a pathway to be ‌able to get people into Europe quickly without the bureaucracy," Boag said. "The aerodynamics on a helicopter are the same ​in the military and the civilian world."

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency had no immediate comment on ​its pilot licensing rules.

title: Scotland's Lynn surprises himself to join Ward on pommel podium
description: Scotland's Cammy Lynn surprises himself to join compatriot Reuben Ward on the pommel horse podium at the Commonwealth Games.
fullText:
On Sunday, Reuben Ward and Cammy Lynn were bouncing around fuelled by an intoxicating mix of testosterone and joy after the former made history by becoming Scotland's first ever men's all-around Commonwealth Games champion.

That Lynn had finished 10th in the same event did not dillute his delight.

But 24 hours on, the Saltire-swaddled pair bounded around the Glasgow International Arena again belting out 'No Scotland, No Party' with a medal each around their necks after a tense pommel horse competition.

That Ward added silver to Sunday's gold was no great surprise - this is, after all, considered his strongest discipline - but not many expected Lynn to join him on the podium. Not least the 23-year-old himself.

The Stirling native was the sixth to go in the eight-man competition. Jordan Carroll of Canada had already posted a mark that would ultimately earn him gold - with Ward falling just short immediately after him - when Lynn had his shot at it

And on the big occasion - an occasion in which the Scot was clearly revelling - he delivered one of his best ever routines to move into third, just one place behind his team-mate.

Gymnast Ward goes from Glasgow dreamer to gold medallist

All the latest from Team Scotland at the Games

It left Scotland in silver and bronze position but Northern Ireland's Olympic champion Rhys McClenaghan and Australia's Ritam Malik were still to go. Surely at least one Scot was going to be disappointed? And Lynn was the most likely.

"I mean, it's Rhys McClenaghan, right? He's the Olympic champion," Lynn told BBC Sport Scotland. "So, as he's stepping up, I'm just buzzing that I've scored a 13.8 and I didn't really think much of it other than that.

"I mean, that guy's the Olympic champion. And Ritam's an amazing gymnast as well, so I was just thinking 'oh, a little top-five finish might be quite nice'."

A few minutes later, Lynn had much, much more than that - even after the Northern Irish team lodged an ultimately-pointless protest against McClenagahan's mark.

And nobody was happier for him than his pal Ward, who could be forgiven for having his senses scrambled after the 24 hours he has had.

A gold medal. More attention than he's ever had before. Emotional exhaustion. Then returning here the on Monday for the Floor event, which culminated in him scudding his face off the floor while trying to execute an ambitious dismount.

The 21-year-old's pommel routine was hugely impressive in the aftermath of that, though, albeit it fell just 0.34 points shy of Carroll's stunning effort.

"I expected to be up really late last night, but I was just drained," Ward told BBC Sport Scotland. "I'd been through so many emotions and I was just so tired.

"I woke up in the morning and thought 'I've got a new day today'. I really went for it on the floor and just missed out, then went to the pommel and thought, 'I've just got to give it my all'.

"And to get two out of three on the podium for Scotland, and to do it with one of my best friends is a feeling I can't describe."

title: Someone cosplaying online as Ukraine's new top general has already fooled thousands
description: The account on X, @Drapatyi_M, has posted 22 times in the last five days, mimicking the run-of-the-mill updates one would expect from an official.
fullText:
An X account claiming to be Ukraine's new commander in chief already has close to 7,000 followers.

But it's not a parody or fan account; instead, it appears to be impersonating Mykhailo Drapatyi.

Ukraine's armed forces had to officially list out the real social media pages for Drapatyi.

Less than a week after Ukraine appointed its new commander in chief, a premium X account posing as the popular general has already racked up nearly 7,000 followers.

The account @Drapatyi_M, which was created this month, has been on a tear since Maj. Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi was named Ukraine's new military chief on Tuesday, posting at least 22 times in the last five days.

Ukraine's General Staff of the Armed Forces confirmed on Sunday that the account was illegitimate and posted a list of Drapatyi's "only official pages." @Drapatyi_M wasn't among them.

Повідомляємо, що єдиними офіційними сторінками Головнокомандувача Збройних Сил України генерал-майора Михайла Драпатого в соціальних мережах є:⬇️ pic.twitter.com/zpgI7yfETA

— Генеральний штаб ЗСУ (@GeneralStaffUA) July 26, 2026

X permits parody or satirical accounts of celebrities or major figures on its platform, but generally marks them with a "parody label" to denote they aren't the real deal.

@Drapatyi_M, however, doesn't appear to be posting for a laugh.

The X account has been mimicking the run-of-the-mill updates that Kyiv's leaders tend to publish, ranging from thanking Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for a meeting to an apparent discussion with Raytheon executives about Patriot missiles.

"We are bringing the war to the territory of Russia and intensifying strikes with long-range weapons," it wrote in a July 22 caption of a photo showing Drapatyi and Ukraine's acting defense minister, Yevhen Khmara, grasping hands in greeting.

Then on Sunday, one of its posts drew the attention — and ire — of several Ukrainian figures. @Drapatyi_M had announced that an "audit" of Ukraine's forces was underway, saying that there would be no "untouchables" in the investigation.

To be fair to @Drapatyi_M, it wouldn't be absurd for the actual general to announce an investigation. Mykhailo Fedorov, who was until recently the country's defense minister, had announced a similar audit before his ousting, and Drapatyi is known to have agreed with many of Fedorov's decisions.

But Serhii Sternenko, who runs one of Ukraine's most famous fundraising groups for combat drones, called out the account on Sunday.

"Mykhailo Drapatyi does not currently have a Twitter page. The statement circulating on social media is fake," Sternenko wrote.

It was a snub to @Drapatyi_M; Sternenko's was one of the 15 accounts the fake general's page followed.

As of Sunday evening, @Drapatyi_M had just under 7,000 followers.

X provides a blue check mark to accounts that pay for its $8 monthly premium service, but has said before that the check mark doesn't mean an account is ID-verified. There's historically been confusion, however, over whether the badge denotes legitimacy because it was how the platform marked verified accounts during its days as Twitter.

Official government accounts are typically given a gray checkmark instead.

Notably, X pays creators for posting on its platform if they have at least 500 verified followers or 5 million organic impressions over three months.

Zelenskyy appointed Drapatyi, a rising star in Ukraine's armed forces, as commander in chief on Tuesday amid widespread protests about Fedorov's removal. Demonstrators had demanded that the commander in chief at the time, Oleksandr Syrskyi, be removed instead.

Drapatyi was the popular favorite to take over the position.

title: Identical twins win gymnastics medals on same day
description: Abigail and Emily Roper create a piece of Team Wales history by both winning bronze at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
fullText:
The identical Roper twins created a slice of Wales team history as the gymnasts both won Commonwealth Games bronze in Glasgow within a couple of hours of each other.

Abigail secured third place in the women's vault, one place ahead of sister Emily, who then claimed her own medal later in the afternoon by finishing third in the uneven bars.

"I can't even put into words how crazy it is," said Abigail.

"I went into this final with no expectations, it was my first final at a major tournament and I was just happy to make it.

"To come away with a bronze medal is just insane."

Wales' Pawlett out of Commonwealth heptathlon

Follow Wales at the Commonwealth Games

Emily outlined how she recovered from her disappointment of finishing fourth to clinch her bronze.

"Coming back from the vault was disappointing but I was super proud for Ab," said Emily.

"It was about doing my own thing on the bars and this result was just amazing. I just needed to regather my emotions and just know I knew what I could do."

"Going from vault straight to bars, it wasn't that long a time. So being resilient obviously helped a lot and I'm glad it paid off."

Welsh gymnast Jemima Taylor, who came in for Ruby Evans, finished seventh. Australia's Kate McDonald won gold and Canada's Ellie Black picked up silver.

Wales have now claimed six medals in Glasgow, with five bronze and one silver so far.

title: England netball team returns to winning ways
description: England bounce back from a difficult loss to world number one side Australia with a 73-38 victory over Malawi at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
fullText:
England bounced back from a difficult loss to world number one side Australia with a 73-38 victory over Malawi at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

There was no hangover from the 66-47 loss to Australia as England cruised into a 18-9 lead in the first quarter.

England consistently kept their advantage throughout before stepping it up in the final quarter to allow Malawi just five points to the Roses' 18.

Goal shooter Eleanor Cardwell proved to be an influential substitution, scoring all of her 21 shots following her introduction in the second half.

"After yesterday's loss, we've definitely turned things around and fixed some of the things we got wrong," said vice-captain Amy Carter.

"At the start of a tournament, a loss isn't actually a bad thing to have. In the last 24 hours, we've looked at video, righted some of the wrongs, connected as a group, had a games night and just spent time together as team-mates.

"We didn't get too bogged down by it because we've got to look forward."

The Roses are third in Pool A behind reigning champions Australia and South Africa.

They will next face Tonga on Wednesday at 16:00 BST before playing South Africa - their rivals for a place in the semi-finals - on Thursday at 21:00 BST.

England are looking to regain the gold they won in 2018 but have had a rocky preparation for the tournament.

Jess Thirlby stepped down as head coach in March for family reasons, leaving assistant Anna Stembridge in interim charge, while injuries to Helen Housby and Natalie Metcalf mean 10 of the Roses' 12-player squad have made their Commonwealth debuts in Glasgow.

Tonga recorded their first ever Commonwealth Games win as they beat Northern Ireland 58-52 in an enthralling game at the Hydro.

After two defeats from their first two games, Tonga started well on Monday and led 15-11 after a clinical first quarter.

It was a more competitive second quarter as the Warriors, who had also suffered two losses from their first two games, fought back but they still trailed 31-26 at the half-time break.

Tonga pulled away again in the third period to lead 45-37 and closed out the victory despite Northern Ireland outscoring them in the final quarter.

The result leaves Northern Ireland bottom of Pool A before a tough game against South Africa on Tuesday at 14:00.

title: Salah, Stones & Sancho - who are the Premier League free agents?
description: BBC Sport takes a look at some of the notable out-of-contract players who playing in the English top flight last season.
fullText:
The 2026-27 Premier League season is fast approaching but there are still plenty of players yet to secure their club futures.

Whether by choice or force, contracts have been run down and career paths changed.

BBC Sport takes a look at some of the notable out-of-contract players who were playing for a club in the English top flight last season.

John Stones, 32 (Last club: Manchester City)

Stones now left City after a decade at the club in which he won 15 major trophies. Picked for England by Thomas Tuchel despite recent injury issues, Stones has most recently been linked with former club Everton and Italian giants AC Milan.

Mohamed Salah, 33 (Last club: Liverpool)

Salah's last few months at Anfield were not easy as his relationship with boss Arne Slot appeared to disintegrate. Both have now left Liverpool. It was widely expected Salah would move to the Saudi Pro League once the World Cup was over but he has since been linked with a move to Turkish club Besiktas.

Jadon Sancho, 26 (Last club: Manchester United)

It has been a turbulent few years for Sancho since joining United from Borussia Dortmund for £73m in 2021 and he has spent the last two and-a-half years playing elsewhere on loan, most recently at Aston Villa following a lacklustre period at Chelsea. Sancho made just 30 Premier League appearances for United but has reportedly received an offer from Qatari side Al-Rayyan.

Yves Bissouma, 29 (Last club: Tottenham Hotspur)

Mali midfielder Bissouma made just 11 top-flight appearances last season as he struggled with injury and off-field issues at Spurs. He is reportedly keen on staying in the Premier League, with Fulham said to be interested.

Stefan Ortega, 33 (Last club: Nottingham Forest)

Former Manchester City number two goalkeeper Ortega made 10 appearances across all competitions for Forest last season. A move to Greek side Olympiacos is potentially close.

Tyrell Malacia, 26 (Last club: Manchester United)

A difficult four-year spell at United for the Dutch left-back was marred by injuries and long stints on the sidelines. A chronic knee issue requiring surgery kept him out for over 500 days, causing him to miss the entire 2023–24 campaign. He has made just 11 appearances across all competitions since.

Adama Traore, 30 (Last club: West Ham)

Traore was released by the Hammers in the wake of their relegation to the Championship after just six months at the club. The powerful Spanish winger has been linked with a move back to Wolves, where he spent five years.

Other Premier League players who are out of contract:

Adam Webster, 31 (Last club: Brighton & Hove Albion)

title: O'Sullivan makes winning start to season in Shanghai
description: Ronnie O'Sullivan makes a comfortable start to the new snooker season as he wins in the first round of the Shanghai Masters.
fullText:
Ronnie O'Sullivan made a comfortable start to the new snooker season as he won in the first round of the Shanghai Masters.

Playing in his first major event of 2026-27, the seven-time world champion claimed a 6-1 win over 18-year-old Chinese amateur Liu Linhao, who was a wildcard entry.

The 50-year-old Englishman made four breaks of more than 50 as he set up a meeting with top seed and defending champion Kyren Wilson in the last 16 on Tuesday.

England's four-time world champion Mark Selby suffered an early exit as the world number nine was beaten 6-5 by Zhou Yuelong.

The 28-year-old local favourite, currently ranked 22 in the world, hit breaks of 83 and then 107 to fight back from 5-4 down.

Barry Hawkins beat Lei Peifan 6-4 to reach the last 16 while fellow Englishman Chris Wakelin cruised through 6-0 against Hewen Tang.

Hawkins will face world number one Judd Trump next in Tuesday's second-round matches, while Hawkins takes on Mark Williams and world number two Neil Robertson meets Xiao Guodong.

title: Former JPMorgan Chase banker expands lurid sexual harassment, racism lawsuit
description: NEW YORK, July 27 (Reuters) - The former JPMorgan Chase banker whose lurid sexual harassment lawsuit went viral added new claims and defendants on Monday, saying the largest U. bank's acceptance of racism and sexual coercion irreparably destroyed his ‌career.
fullText:
NEW YORK, July 27 (Reuters) - The former JPMorgan Chase banker whose lurid sexual harassment lawsuit went viral added new claims and defendants on Monday, saying the largest U.S. bank's acceptance of racism and sexual coercion irreparably destroyed his ‌career.

Chirayu Rana said racism was ingrained in the culture of his otherwise all-white leveraged finance team, where his South Asian heritage "became ‌the punchline for a stream of degrading jokes," including calling him a "monkey" and "brown boy."

What legal claims is Rana pursuing against JPMorgan?

What are the new allegations in Rana's expanded lawsuit?

How has this case affected JPMorgan's public reputation?

Who are the new defendants added to the lawsuit?

JPMorgan has said it believed Rana's allegations were meritless. Neither the bank nor its lawyers had ​an immediate comment.

In an 82-page complaint, Rana, who is of Nepali descent, added allegations that colleagues suggested he transact in rupees, and one texted that he should "run before we call ICEE {sic} on your family," referring to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Rana also renewed allegations that the defendant Lorna Hajdini, a JPMorgan executive director, coerced him into sex and demanded his submissiveness as a condition of advancing his career, repeatedly saying she "owned" him.

Once a "leading" deal originator paid "well ‌over" $2 million a year, Rana has been "effectively blackballed," ⁠the complaint said. "His reputation has been destroyed, his professional relationships shattered, and the career he spent years building reduced to rubble. This was not an unintended consequence of defendants' misconduct. It was its intended result."

MULTIPLE CASES BRING UNWANTED ⁠ATTENTION

Hajdini has also denied Rana's claims and countersued him for defamation, saying his lies "wreaked havoc" on her life, subjected her to around-the-clock ridicule, and were designed to attract maximum press coverage.

Lawyers for Hajdini did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The case is one of several matters involving JPMorgan employees to permeate ​social ​media this year, generating unwanted attention for a bank that generated $37.6 billion of profit ​in the first half of 2026.

JPMorgan is challenging a $4.25 ‌million arbitration award to a former wealth manager who was fired after expensing a Super Bowl platter, while a former employee was caught on video dumping out and then walking away with a commemorative trash can during a parade for the NBA champion New York Knicks.

Rana filed his lawsuit in Manhattan federal court, after a state judge on July 16 dismissed a version filed in April so Rana and his new lawyers could add claims.

title: Hodgkinson & Asher-Smith in GB squad for Europeans
description: Keely Hodgkinson, Dina Asher-Smith and Katarina Johnson-Thompson are named in the Great Britain squad for next month's European Championships in Birmingham.
fullText:
Keely Hodgkinson, Dina Asher-Smith and Katarina Johnson-Thompson have been named in Great Britain's 98-strong squad for the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham.

The trio were among a number of high-profile British athletes who skipped the ongoing Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Olympic champion Hodgkinson (800m) and Asher-Smith (100m) will look to defend their European titles at Alexander Stadium next month, when Britain hosts the championships for the first time.

Johnson-Thompson, who was forced to withdraw from the 2024 edition with an injury, will return to compete in the heptathlon, having claimed silver at the Paris Olympics.

Birmingham-born Matt Hudson-Smith, the 400m Olympic silver medallist and a four-time European champion, will take part in the men's 400m at the venue where he has a stand named after him.

Georgia Hunter Bell, a 2024 European silver medallist and world indoor champion, will compete in the women's 1500m alongside 2022 champion Laura Muir.

The GB squad also includes former 1500m world champion Jake Wightman and world indoor 400m champion Amber Anning.

Jake Heyward, who set a new one-mile Welsh record at the London Diamond League this month, is part of the squad but Scotland's Josh Kerr, who set a world record in the same race, has opted out.

"To compete at a major championship is always a tremendous achievement, and it makes the occasion even more special with the event taking place on home soil," said performance director Paula Dunn.

"This team reflects the strength and depth of talent we have across track and field, bringing together established international medallists alongside an exciting group of emerging athletes.

"I have every confidence that this team will rise to the occasion."

Meanwhile, Norway's two-time Olympic gold medallist Jakob Ingebrigtsen appears set to make his return from injury at next month's championships, which run from 10 to 16 August.

Ingebrigtsen has not raced in 2026 after having Achilles surgery earlier this year, but strongly hinted at his participation with a post on Instagram, external that read: "I've heard Birmingham is nice this time of year."

The 25-year-old has enjoyed significant success at the European Championships, winning the 1500m and 5,000m double at each of the past three editions - in Berlin, Munich and Rome.

title: Cycling in rude health thanks to awesome Pogacar and stringent testing
description: Tour de France fans were spoilt for choice in Paris when it came to drinking in the drama of cycling's greatest race.
fullText:
Tour de France fans were spoilt for choice in Paris when it came to drinking in the drama of cycling's greatest race.

Should their attention be all on Tadej's Pogacar's crowning as the joint most successful rider of all time, with five Tour titles?

But then what about Mathieu van der Poel's superhero-style victory on the final stage, climaxing magnificently on the Champs-Elysees?

Or would the focus be on the sheer passion of a huge, fervent crowd which lined the streets on Montmartre and around Sacre-Coeur?

That last element illustrated a sport in rude health and again raised the question of why organisers had not run the traditional closing stage over the scenic cobbled hill before its debut visit last year.

Pogacar, the rarely beaten 27-year-old Slovenian, is widely regarded now as cycling's greatest of all time.

The fifth Tour win helps in that respect, matching fellow greats Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Indurain – but Pogacar can also point to his many successes elsewhere in cycling's other huge events, such as one-day monuments.

Brutal Belgian Merckx stood alone as the sport's greatest before now, thanks to a similar versatility on the bike – capable, like Pogacar, of winning in all formats: time trials, cobbles, high mountains and even some sprints.

But perhaps what elevates Pogacar to the top now is his respectful demeanour, paying tribute as he did in Paris to every one of his domestiques by name, before thanking his family.

He also shepherded his young UAE-Team Emirates-XRG team-mate Isaac del Toro across the line on more than one occasion during this year's race when his own job was done.

The fact Pogacar achieved what he did while most of his team-mates - and possibly even himself - suffered sickness across the second half of the Tour is even more remarkable.

The Tour de France still is, after all, one of the hardest events in elite sport.

The Tour de France has a chequered history that cannot be forgotten.

"He knows what the record is," Lance Armstrong said on social media following Sunday's result, referring to Pogacar.

The American's record of seven Tour de France victories between 1999 and 2005 has long since been wiped from the record books following the revelation of his systematic doping.

And those in the sport have fairly diligently avoided mentioning his name since.

But the night-time anti-doping tests during this year's Tour, which the International Testing Agency (ITA) told BBC Sport were undertaken as an "exceptional operation" and because time was of the essence, once again raised questions in a sport which doesn't need them, thanks to that dark past.

Testing at such anti-social hours is rare and requires additional permission, and some suspect it may have been a factor in Jonas Vingegaard's Tour-ending crash after he was woken at 2am the previous night, and Pogacar himself at 5am.

Others were tested at night, too, and all riders were tested during the race. But what were the ITA looking for?

They wouldn't say, specifically, but one possible explanation for night-time testing of professional cyclists appears to be to gather as much information as possible to try to understand micro-dosing. That is where an athlete could take performance-enhancing drugs, such as red blood cell stimulant EPO or anabolic steroids, in very small quantities to evade detection on the Athlete Biological Passport, which is endorsed by the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada) and used across cycling.

There is no suggestion of wrongdoing in the case of Pogacar, Vingegaard or any of those tested at night this year.

Past findings produced by Wada suggest micro-dosing could evade detection methods, and so the scope to cheat in professional sport remains, meaning all efforts must be taken to ensure nobody beats the system.

The ITA cannot confirm when the results of the Tour tests will be made public, but EF Education-Easypost boss Jonathan Vaughters told BBC Sport: "Doubts? Actually [those tests] solve my doubts."

Vaughters, who doped during his riding career, is now reformed.

He said during this year's race: "If we had 24-hour testing in 2001 when EPO tests were first introduced we would have had a huge number of riders excluded from the sport, including me. And it would have saved 25 years of drama.

"So I mean we wouldn't have had to go through Lance Armstrong... The problem would have been solved immediately in 2000.

"If you introduce a low enough dose of a peptide hormone, the clearance time can be four hours - if you take it at 11 it'll be out of the system at 3am, so it makes a difference. The testing technology is evolving quickly.

"If you want to watch a clean sport, watch cycling, most other sports' testing is a complete joke.

"Why is cycling so hyper-focused? History. This is human F1 car racing; this is edge of human performance; boundaries are always going to be pushed."

Many riders and team bosses won't go near the 'D' word, and the consensus is 'believe what you are seeing' when Pogacar accelerates away and wins by, at times, a matter of minutes, and when others perform their own remarkable feats in the saddle.

Huge numbers of people do believe what they see.

About 500,000 spectators turned out in Paris on Sunday, with 180,000 around Montmartre alone.

And it doesn't stop at the Tour de France, as many of the bigger races on the calendar are seeing notably bigger numbers.

"You can't get to certain parts to watch it any more, everyone has been there all day. Especially this year," said one journalist at Paris-Roubaix in April.

"There's so much traffic and so many people."

And many fans have noticed the increase in numbers.

Another 500,000 people were estimated to have lined the roads up to Alpe d'Huez last Friday, as videos emerged on social media of crowds setting up camp days before, drinking and partying prior to the race arriving.

At the end of Friday's stage, Movistar's Colombian climber Einer Rubio was even involved in a harrowing incident when he crashed, face-first, into the back of one of the service cars belonging to Pogacar's team, breaking the glass.

The car had been forced to stop abruptly when a spectator fell immediately into its path.

Rubio was forced to abandon the race after being given 20 stitches in hospital.

The presence of Britain's women's Tour winner Lizzie Deignan and record Tour stage win holder Mark Cavendish on the Champs-Elysees on Sunday was a timely reminder that Britain will hosts six stages of the men's and women's Tour de France races next summer.

It will be summer when British fans hope Netcompany Ineos Cycling's new injection of investment will pay dividends – after they failed to win a stage in this year's race – and riders such as Tom Pidcock can light up the race on home soil.

Some 30.2m people cycled at least once in Britain in the past year, according to British Cycling, which is the highest number it has been since 2019-20.

While Pogacar will probably prevent it happening in 2027, many thousands of Britons are still expected to flock to witness the race in motion.

title: 'Give him his passport' - Hearn backs British champion's citizenship fight
description: British champion Bilal Fawaz has lived in the UK for more than 20 years but is fighting for British citizenship - his story features in a new BBC documentary.
fullText:
The UK government should be "embarrassed" that boxing champion Bilal Fawaz does not have a British passport after living in the country for more than 20 years, says his promoter Eddie Hearn.

Fawaz, 38, was trafficked to the United Kingdom at the age of 14 and has not travelled outside the country since.

The London-based light-middleweight represented England as an amateur before turning professional after receiving a work permit.

He has since become British and Commonwealth champion, but his immigration status prevents him from fighting abroad - or taking his family on holiday.

"What on earth is the hold-up?" asked Hearn.

"You want to go down to Number 10 [Downing Street] and bang on the door and say: 'Any chance of dealing with this?' It's the most ridiculous thing I've ever heard.

"If you were them, you'd almost be embarrassed. Someone should look at it and go, 'What are you guys doing? Give him his passport.'"

A Home Office spokesperson told BBC Sport it does not routinely comment on individual cases.

Fawaz's remarkable story is explored in the new BBC documentary Fighting for Freedom, which followed him as he prepared to defend his British title against Ryan Kelly in Wolverhampton in May.

Fighting For Freedom - Bilal Fawaz

Born in Nigeria to a Beninese mother and Lebanese father, Fawaz says his childhood was shaped by abuse, neglect and a persistent feeling he did not belong.

He was sent to live with relatives before being taken to London, believing he would be reunited with his father. Instead, he claims he was confined in a house, forced to work and prevented from attending school or mixing with other children.

"My best friend was the window," he says. "I could see people walking and kids outside playing, but I wasn't allowed to play with them."

After escaping, he entered the care system and received convictions for minor offences - including cannabis possession and graffiti - during his youth. Fawaz says he was a vulnerable teenager who needed guidance rather than punishment.

"I've never robbed anything," he says. "I've never beaten anyone up. I've never done anything that's atrocious.

"I was just a kid who needed guidance and I never had that. Somebody should have taken care of me and fixed my whole life before I turned 18."

Fawaz found stability at the All Stars Boxing Club in west London. He became an English amateur champion and represented England six times, but was unable to pursue Olympic qualification or accept professional contracts because he did not have permission to work or travel.

He was twice held in immigration detention and threatened with deportation before a judge ruled there were no lawful grounds to detain him. He was released and found himself effectively stateless.

Fawaz received a work permit at the age of 33, by which point many professional fighters are approaching retirement.

After turning professional he made up for lost time by beating Junaid Bostan to win the English light-middleweight title, then defeating Ishmael Davis to become British and Commonwealth champion.

"Boxing saved me," he says. "It's my addiction. Boxing gave me the feeling that I deserve more. I've worked hard. When will I get the dues and respect that I deserve?"

The documentary follows Fawaz inside the gym and at home with his family, as well as on the dancefloor during one of his regular salsa sessions.

It also explores how his childhood has shaped him as a father.

"The only way I can fill the void is by being there for my family and my sons," he says. "That's healing."

Fawaz has a British partner and British children, but says he continues to feel as though the authorities do not recognise his contribution to the country.

"I am in prison," he says. "I've been in this country for 24 beautiful years and I've never travelled. I was being used. 'Fight for us... but you're not British'. I fought for them six times as an amateur. I was bleeding in the ring.

"They don't view me as important or someone who is trying to make an honest living. I am a Commonwealth champion who can never take my belt to another country."

Fawaz is on a 10-year 'route to settlement' and will be 43 before becoming eligible for British citizenship.

Under this route, people must complete 10 years of lawful residence before applying for indefinite leave to remain. The granting of that status allows them to stay in the UK without immigration restrictions.

British citizenship can then be applied for - if relevant requirements are met.

The UK has shorter settlement routes, including five-year routes available to people who meet the requirements of certain immigration categories.

The route someone follows depends on the basis of their immigration status and their individual circumstances, including factors such as family life, work, length of residence and private life in the UK.

It is not clear whether the 10-year route was the only option available to Fawaz or why that route applied in his case.

The Home Office previously said the decision to place Fawaz on a 10-year route to settlement was not made by the department.

Without a passport, Fawaz cannot accept potentially lucrative fights in countries such as Saudi Arabia or the United States. He can, however, take up such opportunities in the UK.

He believes he could already have become a world champion had he received a passport in his early 20s.

"The government are denying him that opportunity, which is so wrong," says Hearn, who would also stand to benefit from being able to get Fawaz fights overseas.

"I could get him a big fight in America. I could get him a fight in Saudi. This is a story that resonates in any part of the world. How can you not be allowed to travel?"

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, you can visit BBC Action Line.

title: Chelsea open talks to sign Henderson and Welbeck
description: Chelsea are in talks to sign Brentford midfielder Jordan Henderson and Brighton striker Danny Welbeck.
fullText:
Chelsea are in talks to sign Brentford's Jordan Henderson and Brighton's Danny Welbeck.

England midfielder Henderson, 36, has a year left on his Brentford contract but the Bees are willing to let him leave on a free transfer.

Ex-England striker Welbeck, 35, is keen on moving to Stamford Bridge and there is optimism from Chelsea's side that a deal can be concluded.

The Blues are looking for experience because of an acceptance that their model of signing young players needs a "tweak" - according to influential owner Behdad Eghbali in April.

Welbeck scored a career-high 13 league goals in 37 games for Brighton last season, taking his tally to 51 goals in 201 matches since joining from Watford in 2020.

Brighton have declined to comment.

Welbeck signed a 12-month contract extension in March, with his current deal running until the end of the 2026-27 season.

Henderson made 34 appearances in all competitions for Brentford last season after joining from Ajax.

He made one substitute appearance for England at the World Cup before breaking his arm falling over advertising hoardings while celebrating their last-16 win over Mexico.

The Chelsea academy stars looking to break through

Alonso expects 'movement' on transfers - what can Chelsea achieve this season?

Chelsea will be 'different' - Colwill says Blues 'ready' to compete with Arsenal

There are questions over the futures of several Chelsea forwards, with Joao Pedro regarded as the club's first-choice option.

Chelsea also have Liam Delap, Emmanuel Emegha, Marc Guiu and Nicolas Jackson on their books.

Guiu is understood to be available for a permanent transfer or a loan move, with Chelsea valuing him at about £25m.

Jackson, who has returned from a loan spell at Bayern Munich, was expected to remain at Stamford Bridge but is open to leaving amid interest from Aston Villa.

Delap was keen to establish himself under new manager Xabi Alonso, just a year after a £30m move from Ipswich, but he is increasingly expected to depart.

There is also uncertainty surrounding the future of Dutch striker Emegha, despite having only recently joined Chelsea from Strasbourg, a club within the same ownership group.

Chelsea have signed attacker Morgan Rogers for a club record £117m, full-back Marco Palestra and are closing in on a move for centre-back Maxence Lacroix this summer.

Welbeck and Henderson joining Chelsea would be another sign of a shift in strategy this summer.

Their move for the duo follows attempts to sign 33-year-old midfielder Granit Xhaka from Sunderland, with the Black Cats refusing to sell the Switzerland captain.

Although the arrival of Rogers, 23, fits the club's preferred policy of signing younger players, he brings significant Premier League experience.

The Blues are also expected to complete a £52m move for Crystal Palace defender Lacroix, 26, to add further Premier League-ready experience.

However, Welbeck's arrival would leave Chelsea with an abundance of attacking options despite not being involved in European competition.

At his age, Welbeck may be content to provide cover for Joao Pedro, but the move would represent bad news for several other forwards.

Jackson is open to leaving, while Delap and Emegha had hoped to establish themselves under Alonso.

Nevertheless, the Chelsea manager is getting what he wants: experience and strong personalities to address shortcomings that contributed to the team's 10th-place finish in the Premier League last season.

It says everything about Welbeck that senior figures at Brighton were convinced England should have taken the veteran striker to the World Cup as a back-up.

Forget about his age. Welbeck featured in 37 out of Brighton's 38 Premier League games last season. His 13 goals put him joint-ninth in the list of top scorers, with only three Englishmen bettering that tally.

Those statistics show him to still be a top forward.

Then there is his overall game - his ability to hold the ball up, bring team-mates into play or buy his defence some valuable time.

Finally, there is Welbeck's presence behind the scenes. He is someone who drives standards, makes demands of team-mates; someone for younger players - of which Chelsea have plenty - to learn from.

Manchester United tried to bring him back to Old Trafford in the past but it did not quite work out. Welbeck is the kind of forward they need now.

But it is Chelsea who have acted first. One of the most surprising deals of the summer could turn out to be one of the most astute.

title: Liverpool's centre-back situation and why Iraola must act
description: BBC Sport looks at Liverpool's issues at centre-back, and what Andoni Iraola might do to fix them.
fullText:
Two centre-backs caught the eye of Liverpool's scouting department at the U17 World Cup in Qatar last November.

Within weeks, the club spent a combined £3.5m on the pair: Senegal's Mor Talla Ndiaye and Austria's Ifeanyi Ndukwe.

Under Matt Newberry, Liverpool's director of global talent, this was evidence of future planning in full flow.

Yet surely no-one inside the club would have expected the teenage duo to be the centre-back pairing for most of Liverpool's opening pre-season fixture.

With Joe Gomez forced off by injury in the eighth minute against Sunderland, and neither Jeremy Jacquet or Giovanni Leoni fit to play still, Liverpool have a problem at the heart of their defence.

Looking at the long term is one thing, but they need reinforcements in the here and now.

Even before the injury, new head coach Andoni Iraola said his squad was "very thin" defensively.

Gomez was absent from Liverpool's training session in Chicago on Sunday and an update on the severity of his injury is expected this week.

He is Liverpool's longest-serving current player but has now missed 225 games because of injury, according to Transfermarkt, since signing from Charlton in 2015.

Virgil van Dijk is the club's only fit senior centre-back. The Liverpool captain is 35 and played every minute in the Premier League last season, but he is not the force that he used to be.

The Dutchman, like Gomez, is also into the last year of his contract at Anfield. There is a possibility both players will move on next summer.

One of the reasons why Liverpool allowed Ibrahima Konate to leave on a free transfer and join Real Madrid was because they felt Jacquet, 21, and Leoni, 19, whose transfers weighed in at £60m and £26m respectively, were the best young centre-backs in France and Italy.

Perhaps they will prove inspired signings, with Jacquet in line to make his debut against Leeds on Sunday.

Liverpool will give them every opportunity to fulfil their potential, but right now, just like Ndiaye and Ndukwe, both are far from the finished product.

"We need players. It's fairly obvious," former Liverpool striker Robbie Fowler told BBC Sport in New York, where the Reds take on Wrexham on Wednesday.

"I'm very sad for Joe Gomez, who has been so unfortunate with injuries. This could have been a real chance to cement his place and for him to show that we don't need another centre-half.

"We've spent money on Jacquet and Leoni and the guidance that Joe and Virgil can give from their experience to the young lads is telling.

"We won't see the best version of the young lads yet, but you do need that experience in the squad. And yes, the manager's been on record saying that we need players and I would not be surprised if another centre-half is in that conversation."

Is 'special talent' Jacquet the future of Liverpool's defence?

From the outside, Liverpool's failure to seal a move for Marc Guehi last summer looks even more interesting now.

They have a buyback clause with Jarell Quansah, who left for Bayer Leverkusen for £35m last July, but there are no current plans for Quansah to return.

Sources stress that if Liverpool bring in Bradley Barcola, who Paris St-Germain value in excess of £100m, then there will be limitations to what more they can do in the market.

Deals for Jacquet and Victor Munoz have cost a combined £94.5m.

Without any major outgoings from Iraola's squad, there is an understanding that this summer will not be like last summer when a club record £450m was spent.

Fowler, who scored 183 times for the Reds, said: "When you look at Liverpool across the last decade, one of the problems that we've had is that the first 11 is more than capable but the argument that people have is the squad depth.

"I'm a big believer in getting the squad right because it gives everyone a lift and keeps people on their toes, knowing that if you're not performing, someone else could do the job.

"Go back to the days of Phil Neal and he'll tell you stories about how players would never want to get injured because they knew that if someone else came, they wouldn't get their place back.

"You need that mentality and I think that has a real knock-on effect on standards."

In six months from last summer through to January 2026, Liverpool agreed deals for five centre-backs who were aged 20 or under at the time - Leoni, Ndiaye, Ndukwe, Noah Adekoya and Jacquet.

It is worth noting that Ndukwe, who was impressive against Sunderland, must go out on loan this year as he does not yet meet the criteria for a UK work permit.

The long-term potential of centre-backs is not a concern at Anfield.

But experience is in short supply - a glaring gap in this Liverpool squad and one that needs to be addressed.

title: Why did a $154 billion CEO just endorse stripping most Americans of voting rights—and taking us back to the 19th century?
description: Should how much you pay in taxes determine how much your vote counts? Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke seems to think so.
fullText:
Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke, whose company commands a market capitalization near $154 billion, told his social media followers this week that a tax-tiered voting system—one that would strip voting rights from anyone who pays no income tax—would be a "good system."

That two-word endorsement, dropped into a viral thread, has reignited a debate over wealth, power, and democracy that most Americans thought was settled more than a century ago.

The proposal would invert the founding American principle of "no taxation without representation" into something closer to "no representation without taxation"—and specifically, high taxation. Reactions online split sharply: Some framed it as a provocative thought experiment about aligning fiscal responsibility with political voice, while others called it a naked attempt to legitimize plutocracy by giving billionaires and multimillionaires a formal, multiplied vote over the laws that govern everyone else.

But it also revealed that America is grappling with a political economy debate, as a frozen housing market and an entrenched wealthy baby boomer demographic have many, not just Lütke, arguing that something big needs to change.

The exchange began with a provocation from Lütke: Pension recipients should have their financial futures "locked in and guaranteed," but in return would be reclassified as "dependents" and lose the right to vote—the same way minors can't vote. A reply from "Eric Thor," who claimed to be a retired banking executive as well as "armchair economist and policy wonk," proposed a sliding scale: zero votes for anyone who pays no income tax, one vote for those earning $1–100K, two votes for $100–200K, scaling up in that pattern to a hard cap of five votes for anyone earning $500K or more. The pitch was framed as fairness—reward "representation" for those who "foot the bill" through taxation.

That was the good system that Lütke endorsed.

To be clear, under this proposed system, the disenfranchised bloc would be enormous. It would encompass all retirees living on Social Security and pension income, students, caregivers, disabled Americans, and millions of low-wage workers who owe no net federal income tax after deductions and credits. Meanwhile, a small population of high earners would receive up to five votes each—a fivefold multiplier on political power concentrated in the hands of people already holding disproportionate economic power.

Tying the right to vote to wealth or tax contribution has a name: "census suffrage," or property-qualified voting. In fact, it was the dominant system for the majority of early modern history. Across much of 19th-century Europe and in parts of the early United States, only property owners or taxpayers above a certain threshold could cast a ballot. The earliest democracies in history, in ancient Greece and ancient Rome, likewise limited voting to property owners.

The dawning of the 20th century, though, coincided with several universal suffrage movements that spent decades dismantling those systems precisely because they entrenched the political power of the already wealthy and locked out workers, women, and minorities from any say in the laws governing them. Jessica Lautz, deputy chief economist of the National Association of Realtors, told Fortune recently that the housing market showed signs of returning to an "early 1900s" status quo, but this surely was not what she meant.

Perhaps ironically, Lütke's tweetstorm began as a response to Jordan Grimes bemoaning the current crisis conditions in the housing market. The San Francisco Chronicle's Laura Waxmann had reported on classic NIMBY (not in my backyard) activism as hundreds of San Francisco Marina residents swamped a town hall to protest what for them was an "uncomfortably tall, 22 & 18 story project at the low-slung neighborhood's waterfront." The excessive influence of old homeowners has been dubbed an "oldigarchy" by Yale professor Samuel Moyn, who advocated in his recent book Gerontocracy in America for something like the reverse of Lütke's policy: extending the voting age down to an ever-younger population to counterbalance the tyranny of NIMBY boomers.

Lütke's own track record with voting rights makes the endorsement especially pointed. In 2022, Shopify shareholders approved a "Founder Share" structure that guarantees Lütke at least 40% of the company's voting power regardless of how much equity he actually owns—a mechanism governance watchdogs criticized as an entrenchment device that decouples voting power from ownership stake. Glass Lewis, a proxy advisory firm, publicly flagged the structure as controversial when it went to a shareholder vote.

In other words, Lütke secured himself outsize, guaranteed control over his own company's decisions—then publicly praised a system that would strip voting power from the majority of ordinary Americans in the political sphere.

Shopify did not immediately respond to Fortune's request for comment.

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: Rohingya schools in Malaysia face closures amid online surge in hate speech
description: Nur is a 12-year-old Rohingya Muslim refugee in Malaysia who has stopped going to school since June, after two men threatened to beat her on her way
fullText:
KUALA LUMPUR, July 27 (Reuters) - Nur is a 12-year-old Rohingya Muslim refugee in Malaysia who has stopped going to school since June, after two men threatened to beat her on her way to class.

"Why do you want to go to school? Do you want to take over our country?" they asked, according to Nur, whose family declined use of her full name for fear of repercussion.

Nur ‌is just one of many Rohingya children to face harassment and threats that have prompted refugee schools across Malaysia to close, say rights groups and educators.

"Children are so scared that they're afraid to leave the house," ‌said Sharifah Shakirah, a Rohingya community activist brought up in the southeast Asian nation.

"You're not just harassing a child for a day or two, you're creating a lasting trauma."

At least nine schools have shut nationwide, Reuters checks show, after online hate speech and misinformation targeting the Rohingya led to tougher ​controls on the community and raised tech regulation concerns.

The home affairs ministry did not respond to a request for comment on the school closures or hate speech campaign.

Malaysia does not officially recognise the Rohingya as refugees, branding them illegal migrants, though about 120,000 are registered with the United Nations refugee agency.

Muslim-majority Malaysia has long sympathised with the persecuted minority from Myanmar, but opinion soured during the COVID-19 pandemic amid accusations refugees were spreading the virus, disrepecting cultural norms and competing for jobs.

Malaysians "have begun feeling burdened by issues arising from managing the Rohingya community", Deputy Foreign Minister Lukanisman Awang Sauni told parliament last week.

Fresh invective spread in May on social media run by Meta Platforms Inc, as well as Bytedance's TikTok, after hygiene concerns linked to the Muslim ritual of ‌cattle slaughter by one Rohingya group.

A viral online petition urging the government to "remove" Rohingya refugees ⁠was taken down in June after rights groups raised the alarm, but not before it garnered nearly half a million signatures.

"What we're seeing now is 100 times worse than it was during COVID," said Sharifah, the community activist.

Some posts reviewed by Reuters exhorted violence against Rohingya refugees, including children. One sub-topic on Meta-owned Threads was titled "Lempang Rohingya", or "Slap Rohingya" in Malay, for example.

Some ⁠influencers encouraged users to film Rohingya communities and report their locations to authorities.

Despite social media sentiment, the government cannot arbitrarily deport refugees, Home Minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail said in June, adding it would respond by "balancing national security with humanitarian values".

Free speech advocacy group Article 19 said the online campaign had boosted scrutiny of Rohingya communities, leading to investigations, raids and school closures.

But it did not observe any human rights-based approaches towards tackling attacks, a spokesperson said, adding, "The government's punitive measures are causing more harm than reducing tension and ​harassment."

The ​U.N. refugee agency said it was concerned by rising online hate speech, disinformation and dehumanising narratives targeting Rohingya and other refugees.

"We continue to ​monitor the situation closely and to support measures that reduce risks for refugees and host ‌communities," it added in a statement, without mentioning the school closures.

Authorities have shut down Rohingya-linked businesses and schools they say are operating illegally.

Refugees cannot legally work in Malaysia, and their children are barred from the national education system, leaving many dependent on schools run by non-government bodies or informal learning centres.

After Nur's experience, her teacher and the school's operator suspended classes indefinitely on safety concerns. Two nearby refugee schools also closed.

Rohingya children have been chased off public playgrounds, said the teacher, who founded the school in 2022 to offer young people a basic education to prepare for possible re-settlement elsewhere or a safe return home.

Himself a Rohingya refugee, he rejected accusations that the school was encouraging refugees to settle permanently in Malaysia or take jobs from locals.

"Many accuse us of breaking Malaysian laws," said the school founder, who sought anonymity for reasons of security. "For me, starting this school is one way I can teach others how to understand and obey the law."

Authorities closed a school ‌in the northern state of Kedah this month for lacking proper permits after videos of its premises were posted online, said one of ​its teachers, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

At least nine schools teaching Rohingya children have closed for safety reasons or were shut by authorities ​after complaints on social media, said teachers and community leaders who declined to be interviewed, fearing repercussions.

Teachers at three ​schools still operating said they took precautions to avoid being targeted, including telling students not to wear uniforms and cancelling outdoor activities.

The longer-term impact of school closures will be to worsen social ‌problems, such as child marriage among Rohingya girls and vagrancy, said activist Sharifah.

"Many people complain ​about Rohingya children begging for money on the streets," she added. "There ​will only be more of them if schools are closed."

RENEWED CONCERNS OVER ONLINE MODERATION

Activists say the online campaign has revived questions over social media platforms' ability to curb hate speech and violent rhetoric.

Some posts flagged to Meta and TikTok were removed, Article 19 said, but much remained online. Meta removed seven of 10 items flagged to it by Reuters across Facebook, Instagram and Threads, while TikTok removed eight of 11.

Despite policies on harmful content, ​enforcement by the social media firms is inconsistent, Article 19's spokesperson said, adding that AI ‌moderation tools often struggle with coded language, visual content and linguistic nuances.

Meta and TikTok use a combination of automated detection and human review to enforce policies against hate speech and conduct on their platforms. ​TikTok also has safety features reminding users to reconsider potentially harmful comments.

For now, the children denied classes have few options, with a tearful Nur telling Reuters, "If I don't go to school, I won't be able ​to learn anything, and I can't become anything."

title: ABC, NBC, CBS, CNN and MS NOW ignore Fauci diary entries that reveal fixation on fame during COVID
description: Anthony Fauci's diary entries revealed his celebrity fixation during COVID-19, yet ABC News, NBC News, CBS News and CNN all ignored the story on the air.
fullText:
Eye-popping diary entries written by Dr. Anthony Fauci reveal the former White House COVID advisor was fixated on his newfound celebrity at the height of the global pandemic, but anyone who relies on legacy media outlets for news and information may not be aware.

ABC News, NBC News, CBS News, CNN and MS NOW's on-air broadcasts ignored Fauci's diary entries from the time they were released on Saturday afternoon through Monday at 9 a.m. ET when flagship morning shows had concluded, according to a search of transcripts using Grabien Media.

Released by Senate Homeland Security Committee Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., the journals chronicle Fauci's day-to-day role during the COVID-19 crisis through conversations with President Donald Trump, governors and world leaders, media appearances, and his personal observations as the pandemic unfolded in 2020.

Fauci's Newly Released Covid Diaries Reveal Bizarre Fixation On Fame As Pandemic Deaths Mounted

Paul, a longtime Fauci critic who frequently clashed with him over the federal response and the origins of the virus, made the diaries public as part of the committee's ongoing oversight investigation. The diary entries document Fauci's fondness of his newfound fame, cozy relationships with a variety of legacy media personalities, his growing frustration with the Trump White House and the suggestion that it was "not hyperbole" to say he was "the most famous and talked about person in the country."

The diary entries exploded on social media but appear to have been ignored by mainstream news networks.

"NBC Nightly News" failed to mention the story over the weekend and NBC continued to look the other way Monday morning on "Today," according to Grabien transcripts. On ABC, "World News Tonight" and "Good Morning America" followed the same pattern, while "CBS' Evening News" and "CBS Mornings" didn't find anything newsworthy, either.

Sunday affairs programs such as ABC's "This Week," NBC's "Meet the Press" and CBS' "Face the Nation" also declined to cover Fauci's diary.

Inside Fauci's Private Diary: What He Wrote About Trump, Tv Personalities And Celebrities

It was much of the same on cable news, as CNN and MS NOW both ignored the story on linear television through Monday morning. The word "Fauci" was not mentioned once, according to Grabien Media.

CNN's on-air blackout came despite anchor Jake Tapper appearing repeatedly throughout the private diary entries as Fauci documented phone calls, text exchanges and dinners at the Tappers' Washington home amid their growing friendship.

Fauci wrote that Tapper privately checked to make sure a CNN interview hadn't caused problems with the White House. When The Atlantic's Peter Nicholas suggested Fauci had been "humiliated" over a canceled Tapper interview, Fauci fired back in his diary: "F--- you, Peter."

After Fauci's heated exchange with GOP Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan in April 2021, Fauci wrote that CNN's Dana Bash texted him, telling him he was "a better man" and relaying that fellow CNN anchor Wolf Blitzer had joked no one would have blamed Fauci if he had told Jordan to "go f--- yourself."

Conservative Groups Urge Fcc To Back Off Abc License Review, Warning It Could Hurt Right-leaning Media

Fox News chief political analyst Brit Hume took notice of the media blackout.

"This is not getting the coverage it deserves," Hume wrote on X. "Is that because so many media luminaries were so chummy with the man at the center of a major medical controversy?"

ABC, NBC, CBS and CNN did not immediately respond to a request for comment. MS NOW declined comment.

The diary release came days before Fauci is scheduled to testify before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee after being subpoenaed by Paul. Several network insiders have suggested the news broke during a busy news cycle and there is still time to cover it before Wednesday's hearing.

Fox News Digital's Amanda Macias contributed to this report.

title: CEO of the top-rated hiring platform says the job market is so bad that candidates are paying $20 to mass apply and driving bosses crazy with spam
description: Job seekers are spamming every job with AI. Employers are using AI to filter them out. Greenhouse's CEO says it's created a doom loop for everyone.
fullText:
Job seekers are exhausted. Tired of shooting résumés into the void and getting ghosted, many have started paying for AI tools that blast their application out to every open role they can find. But according to Greenhouse CEO Daniel Chait, employers are just as miserable—and he's got a name for the hiring nightmare: an AI doom loop.

What alternatives help job seekers stand out today?

What is the AI doom loop in hiring?

What solutions is Greenhouse offering to fix hiring?

How are AI tools affecting job application volumes?

"This is the first time when really both sides have been unhappy," Chait told Fortune. "The market just isn't working for either side."

Job seekers, he says, are "piling more and more job applications into the black hole and not getting any progress." It doesn't matter how many they send—they "just don't get anywhere."

So they've turned to AI tools that make the process less painful. "You can go search on Google, and there are tools that advertise, use AI to automatically apply to every Greenhouse job," the jobs board boss said. "Someone goes and buys that tool, it's like 20 bucks, and now they can just shoot out job applications willy-nilly to as many jobs as they want."

On the other side of the inbox, recruiters are drowning. There are currently 175,000 live jobs on Greenhouse's platform—and on average, for every job ad posted, around 254 job seekers are applying, pushing applications per recruiter up by 412%.

"They'll often get hundreds or thousands of applications in just a day or two, and they're not able to keep up with it," Chait said. Worse, because so many of those applications are AI-generated, "they all start to look the same"—so candidates can no longer tell who is seriously interested from someone who has auto-applied to a thousand jobs overnight.

It leaves employers turning to AI just to survive the flood of applications, while candidates who keep getting overlooked respond the only way they know how: applying to even more jobs.

"We've called that the AI doom loop," he added. "Everyone's using their own AI to solve their own problem, but it's making the whole system worse," he said.

The data backs up how broken things have gotten. More than 1.2 million applications were submitted last year in the U.K. alone for fewer than 17,000 graduate roles. One young man with a master's degree applied to thousands of positions for over six months without a single callback. And it could get even worse: Goodwill's CEO Steve Preston has said the job center is bracing for an influx of jobless young people as AI eats into entry-level roles.

description: Four-star defensive lineman Maleek Lee transferred to Palmetto from Booker. Last season, he led the Tornadoes with 69 tackles and 39 tackles for loss.
fullText:
Four-star defensive lineman Maleek Lee confirmed with The Herald-Tribune on Monday, July 27, that he will play his senior season at Palmetto, transferring from Booker.

In 2025, the Georgia Tech commit led the 12-2 Tornadoes with 69 tackles and 39 tackles for loss. Last season, Palmetto finished 10-2 under head coach Eric Sanders, who has helped the Tigers to a 19-4 record since taking over in 2024.
