title: PFF: Saints free agent loss one of offseason's most underrated moves
description: PFF highlighted the New Orleans Saints losing Luke Fortner among the offseason's most underrated moves. Do they have a backup plan behind Erik McCoy?
fullText:
A New Orleans Saints offseason departure was recently named to Pro Football Focus' list of this spring's five most underappreciated acquisitions -- someone who stepped into a starting role last season and did an admirable job replacing a Pro Bowl center Erik McCoy due to injury. After signing with the division-rival Carolina Panthers in free agency, he now has the opportunity to solidify the middle of Carolina's offensive line and prove that his breakout 2025 campaign was no fluke.

Panthers brass did its part to upgrade a below-average defense, making two splash moves by signing Devin Lloyd and Jaelan Phillips. Yet the addition of Fortner was quietly a savvy one as well.

After playing only 13 offensive snaps in 2024, Fortner enjoyed a strong 2025 campaign with New Orleans. Across 678 snaps, Fortner permitted three sacks but just 11 pressures, good for a 72.5 PFF pass-blocking grade to rank third among qualified centers. Moreover, Fortner was his best in the run game yet with a career-high 65.3 PFF run-blocking grade, including the 61st percentile for gap concepts.

Utilizing both Cade Mays and Austin Corbett, the Panthers earned just the 23rd-ranked overall PFF grade at center last season. With both departing this spring, Fortner figures to not only assume command, but has the tools to upgrade the position along a high-potential offensive line.

Locker views Fortner as one of the more overlooked additions from this offseason, highlighting the tremendous strides he made during his tenure in New Orleans in limited action. His grades via PFF are a direct reflection of that, earning the 3rd highest pass-blocking grade among centers, while also posting career-high numbers in the run game. With a clear path to the starting job in Carolina, Fortner has the opportunity to build on his breakout season and make a career for himself as one of the league's most reliable players at his position.

This article originally appeared on Saints Wire: PFF: Saints free agent loss one of offseason's most underrated moves

title: As Carlos Beltran enters Hall of Fame, could managing Mets be next?
description: Carlos Beltran is headed to Cooperstown and remains deeply involved with the Mets' future. Could a managerial role be ahead?
fullText:
Carlos Beltran had more options than most as he stewed on the decision about which team would adorn his cap on his bronze plaque in the National Baseball Hall of Fame.

The nine-time All-Star outfielder, with three Gold Gloves, two Silver Sluggers and a World Series crown to his credit, could have picked any of the seven teams across his 20-year career. After being elected in his fourth year on the Baseball Writers Association of America ballot, Beltran settled on the New York Mets.

As the five-tool center fielder was inducted in Cooperstown on Sunday afternoon, he shared the reasoning why after spending seven of his seasons between 2005-11 in Flushing.

"Every organization shapes your career. New York shaped my life," Beltran said during his speech. "It was here where I achieved my greatest success and some of my greatest challenges. Playing for the Mets made me a better man and a better leader.

"Many of the most meaningful relationships that I was able to build in my career I did it wearing a Mets uniform. So the Mets cap what it represents to me is growth and it represents a place where I became the best version of myself."

Beltran also paid a debt of gratitude to his upbringing in Manati, Puerto Rico, for paving his path toward the ultimate distinction in professional baseball.

He pulled a Puerto Rican flag out of his jacket pocket and waved it toward the crowd. That is where the story of Beltran's career and his desire to leave baseball in a better place than where he left it began.

"When I was growing up in Manati, Puerto Rico, many of these guys were teaching me the game of baseball," Beltran said. "I know some of you guys opened a lot of doors and went through a lot of situations in your careers, that my generation was able to walk through those doors because you opened the path for us, so I just want to say thank you for making this game better.

"I feel very blessed, and I hope our generation have done the same for the ones who are already playing the game."

Beltran has tried to carry that responsibility as his career evolved. Francisco Lindor, a fellow Puerto Rican and potential future Hall of Famer, counts Beltran as one of his mentors in the sport.

And as a special assistant to Mets president of baseball operations David Stearns in the front office, interim manager Andy Green, the club's senior vice president for player development, sees an icon who is willing to take a step behind the scenes and counsel the next generation of Mets players.

"It's one thing when you show up around the big league clubhouse and live the big league life. It's another thing when you're willing to go down and talk to our minor league players and invest in them," Green said. "That's where respect grows. This is not just an elite performer, but this is an elite person."

As Beltran was enshrined, he thanked the writers who voted for him and those who did not for the "perspective" they provided.

The triumphs and challenges within New York have been wound into Beltran's DNA. And the boos helped steer him toward greatness.

"If baseball has really taught me something, I want to say that I hope in life we continue to measure ourself by the same standard we have used to measure others," Beltran said.

Beltran will see his No. 15 lifted to the rafters at Citi Field later this season.

And the Mets will soon be looking for a new manager as Green steps back into his role as farm director. Beltran was hired as the team's manager once before, back in 2020, but resigned after his role in the Astros' sign-stealing scandal came to light.

Beltran is entrenched in helping to broker a strong direction into the future and has grown further and further entrenched in the direction of the franchise. Might it be in the manager's seat in the future? Time will tell. For now, Beltran is reveling in his opportunity to be an agent for growth and possibility, just as the previous generation was for him.

"To Steve and Alex Cohen, I have to tell you guys that I know this year might not look pretty, but what makes me proud is the culture that you have been able to create," Beltran said. "Making players, families and employee valued and especially myself, having the experience to experience different chapters in the Mets organization, I have to tell you guys that I have never been prouder to call myself a Met."

Jeff Kent will be remembered for his triumphs with the Giants organization, including a National League MVP and four of his five All-Star selections, but he did not forget where his baseball roots began during his induction speech.

The Hall of Fame second baseman, who was elected by the Contemporary Baseball Era Committee, made sure to mention his early days in Flushing, where he was traded in 1992 and played until 1996, mostly under manager Dallas Green.

"New York was something that I was not prepared for," Kent said in his speech. "You learn about pressure, accountability and responsibility really fast in that city, and if you don’t, it will chew you up, but I am without a doubt grateful for every minute of it."

Kent was particularly endeared to Eddie Murray, who late in his own Hall of Fame career taught him about "keeping things simple." And Green was able to begin to harness Kent's fiery passion.

"He coached us by playing with your head and heart and that there will be no excuses for failure," Kent said. "If you are prepared and competed, he had your back and that helped shape the understanding that respect in this game comes from effort and accountability, not talk."

This article originally appeared on NorthJersey.com: As Carlos Beltran enters Hall of Fame, could managing Mets be next?

title: Italy’s Sports minister slams Azzurri’s Andrea Pirlo mess-up
description: Italian football finds itself in the middle of a crisis again, as Andrea Pirlo’s candidacy for the Azzurri role has gone up in smoke. There have been increasing doubts about the future of Paolo Mald...
fullText:
Italian football finds itself in the middle of a crisis again, as Andrea Pirlo’s candidacy for the Azzurri role has gone up in smoke. There have been increasing doubts about the future of Paolo Maldini too and now, Italy’s sports minister Andrea Abodi has made his views clear about the matter.

Now, Pirlo will definitely not be the next manager of the national team. This is largely due to his links with a FonBet, a Russian betting company and this didn’t sit well with many at FIGC, even if it went against the technical director Maldini’s wishes.

Now, Abodi has been asked about the matter and he has made it clear that things like these shouldn’t be happening in Calcio.

He told Piacenza Hub Network – via Di Marzio: Pirlo’s resignation from the Azzurri bench? It’s news that speaks for itself. It’s a situation we would have liked to have changed with greater speed and with a shared purpose that hasn’t materialised. Now we have to make up for a poor showing.”

The outcome of the Pirlo saga is arguably something that can only unfold in Italian football, embarrassingly enough. It is a classic case of putting politics over sport, while hiring a sporting figure who should be backed to the helm. This is what lets Italian football down – from top to bottom, and it has happened again.

title: Yanees Trade Idea Cuts Ties With Anthony Volpe For New Catcher
description: The New York Yankees need an upgrade at catcher
fullText:
The New York Yankees are reportedly in the market for a new catcher and could find one by dumping Anthony Volpe.

Volpe has not panned out in New York and continues to struggle offensively. With top prospect George Lombard Jr. making a strong case to debut soon, Volpe's clock may be ticking. The Athletic's Chris Kirschner proposed this trade that would send Volpe to the Minnesota Twins:

Twins receive: Anthony Volpe and Camilo Doval

"Ryan Jeffers is the most logical catching target for the Yankees because of his relationship with Tanner Swanson, the club’s director of catching. Swanson was a key figure in the Minnesota Twins’ decision to draft Jeffers in 2018," Kirschner wrote on Monday. "Jeffers will be a free agent after this season, so this move would also give the Yankees a stretch run to determine if he could also be a longer-term fit. In return, the Twins would get two change-of-scenery candidates in Volpe and Doval."

Looking for the perfect gift for a baseball player in your life? Check out our brand new baseball lifestyle brand!

MLB insider Jim Bowden weighed in on the trade and felt that this would be a deal that both sides would accept.

"Volpe, 25, needs a change of scenery, and with more than two years of remaining club control, it’s a risk worth taking for the Twins, especially considering Jeffers is an impending free agent," wrote Bowden. "From the Yankees’ standpoint, Lombard is ready for a promotion to replace Volpe, and they would still have José Caballero as an option at shortstop."

This deal could knock out two birds with one stone for the Yankees. It would open the door for Lombard and finally get rid of Volpe, while also drastically improving at catcher.

title: UNC Puts Football GM Michael Lombardi on ‘Administrative Leave’
description: The beleaguered football program led by Bill Belichick faces yet another controversy.
fullText:
Ahead of the 2026 season, UNC football faces yet another controversy.

Football general manager Mike Lombardi has been placed on paid administrative leave, the university announced Monday. His leave is effective immediately.

The release did not provide any details or reason for his suspension. But the announcement came from UNC vice chancellor for communications and marketing Dean Stoyer, not an official within the athletic department.

“As is standard procedure with personnel matters, leadership, staff, and student-athletes are prohibited from addressing this topic further, and has no reflection on the merits,” Stoyer said.

Before taking up the GM role in Chapel Hill, Lombardi spent several decades coaching in the NFL, winning three Super Bowls during his career. He joined Belichick at UNC in December 2024, and earns a salary of $1.5 million.

Belichick, 74, had a tumultuous debut in college football last season that looked nothing like his illustrious NFL coaching career. The beginning of his tenure was marred by off-field tumult including the involvement of his 25-year-old girlfriend, Jordon Hudson. Then, the Tar Heels went 4-8, and did not qualify for a bowl game.

The post UNC Puts Football GM Michael Lombardi on ‘Administrative Leave’ appeared first on Front Office Sports.

title: Report: Commanders dismissed TE coach Ben Steele for violating team policy

fullText:
The Commanders announced the departure of tight ends coach Ben Steele on Monday morning and declined further comment about why the offseason addition to Dan Quinn's staff was leaving the team just before the start of training camp.

Nicki Jhabvala of TheAthletic.com reports that Steele was dismissed due to a violation of team policy. Jhabvala also reports that Steele was arrested on suspicion driving while intoxicated on June 7 and faces additional charges for refusing to take a blood/breath test and obstructing or resisting an officer without force.

title: Arsenal set to break British transfer record if they insist on Vinicius

fullText:
Arsenal are interested in adding Vinicius Junior to their squad this summer, and the move would represent one of the biggest transfers of the window, despite many supporters doubting whether the club can complete such a deal.

Vinicius has entered the final year of his contract at Real Madrid, and the Spanish giants would reportedly rather sell him than risk losing him on a free transfer next year. The Brazilian has also enjoyed outstanding form in recent months and was the standout performer for Brazil during the 2026 World Cup.

According to Sport, Real Madrid have opened the door to Vinicius leaving the club because they are unwilling to allow him to run down his contract. The report adds that the Spanish side have already set an asking price for the attacker.

Vinicius appeared determined to demonstrate that he deserves the salary he has been requesting from Real Madrid throughout the summer. However, the club have still not reached an agreement with him over a new contract, leaving uncertainty surrounding his long-term future.

His entourage are reportedly exploring the possibility of a departure, and Arsenal are eager to take advantage of the situation. The Gunners view the Brazilian as a player capable of transforming their squad and believe signing him would be a major statement of intent.

Real Madrid are expected to demand 160m euros for Vinicius, reflecting both his quality and his importance to the club. Any team hoping to secure his signature would therefore need to make a significant financial commitment.

If Arsenal continue to pursue the transfer, they are set to break the British transfer record to complete the deal. The club would have to meet Real Madrid’s valuation while also convincing the Brazilian that the Emirates Stadium is the right destination for the next stage of his career.

Although completing the transfer will be extremely challenging, Arsenal remain interested in the winger and will continue to monitor developments. The coming weeks are expected to determine whether the Gunners can turn their ambitious pursuit into one of the biggest transfers of the summer.

title: Chelsea open talks to sign Brighton striker Welbeck
description: Chelsea are in talks to sign Brighton & Hove Albion striker Danny Welbeck, with the 35-year-old keen to join new manager Xabi Alonso at Stamford Bridge.
fullText:
Chelsea are in talks to sign Brighton striker Danny Welbeck.

The 35-year-old is keen on moving to Stamford Bridge and there is optimism from Chelsea's side that a deal can be concluded.

The Blues are looking for experience because of an acceptance that their model of signing young players needs a "tweak" - according to influential owner Behdad Eghbali in April - and Welbeck could be a good fit.

He scored a career-high 13 league goals in 37 games for Brighton last season, taking his tally to 51 goals in 201 matches since joining from Watford in 2020.

Brighton have declined to comment.

Welbeck signed a 12-month contract extension in March, with his current deal running until the end of the 2026-27 season.

There are questions over the futures of several Chelsea forwards, with Joao Pedro regarded as the club's first-choice option.

Chelsea also have Liam Delap, Emmanuel Emegha, Marc Guiu and Nicolas Jackson on their books.

Guiu is understood to be available for a permanent transfer or a loan move, with Chelsea valuing him at about £25m.

Jackson, who has returned from a loan spell at Bayern Munich, was expected to remain at Stamford Bridge but is open to leaving amid interest from Aston Villa.

Delap was keen to establish himself under new manager Xabi Alonso, just a year after a £30m move from Ipswich, but he is increasingly expected to depart.

There is also uncertainty surrounding the future of Dutch striker Emegha, despite having only recently joined Chelsea from Strasbourg, a club within the same ownership group.

Chelsea have signed club-record £117m attacker Morgan Rogers, full-back Marco Palestra and are closing in on a move for centre-back Maxence Lacroix this summer.

Alonso expects 'movement' on transfers - what can Chelsea achieve this season?

Chelsea will be 'different' - Colwill says Blues 'ready' to compete with Arsenal

Welbeck joining Chelsea would be another sign of a shift in strategy this summer.

Their move for him follows attempts to sign 33-year-old midfielder Granit Xhaka from Sunderland, with the Black Cats refusing to sell the Switzerland captain.

Although the arrival of Rogers, 23, fits the club's preferred policy of signing younger players, he brings significant Premier League experience.

The Blues are also expected to complete a £52m move for Crystal Palace defender Lacroix, 26, to add further Premier League-ready experience.

However, Welbeck's arrival would leave Chelsea with an abundance of attacking options despite not being involved in European competition.

At his age, Welbeck may be content to provide cover for Joao Pedro, but the move would represent bad news for several other forwards.

Jackson is open to leaving, while Delap and Emegha had hoped to establish themselves under Alonso.

Nevertheless, the Chelsea manager is getting what he wants: experience and strong personalities to address shortcomings that contributed to the team's 10th-place finish in the Premier League last season.

title: 10 Biggest Chiefs Questions: Can Mahomes play with fewer scrambles?
description: How does Kansas City’s quarterback adjust to an assumed lack of scrambling ability this season?
fullText:
There are many qualities that make Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes a special player. His arm strength is incredible. Mahomes’ ability to change his arm angle is arguably the best the NFL has ever seen. He can adjust his throw to hit any throwing window. Mahomes’ feel for space and coverage is some of the best ever.

However, the first thing I think about in Mahomes’ game is all the plays outside the pocket or scrambling over his career. Mahomes has the arm strength and flexibility to make a throw from any platform, even while sprinting. He forces defenses to cover every blade of grass behind the line of scrimmage, since Mahomes is a threat to throw from any position.

He also has the speed to create explosive runs with his legs. Mahomes’ feel in the pocket for small openings has bailed the Chiefs out many times. Mahomes has made countless crucial first downs with his rushing ability.

As the Chiefs’ offensive infrastructure and talent have decreased in recent years, Mahomes’s ability to scramble to create throwing or rushing windows has become even more important. The Chiefs’ wide receivers have needed more time to get open downfield against man coverage, and Mahomes gives them that with his scrambles.

Arguably, the Chiefs best answer on third down in recent years has been Mahomes scrambles. His ability to get just enough for a first down has kept the offense buoyant.

While this has been a major weapon for the Chiefs, this need for Mahomes to create so much with his legs caught up to him. The floor fell out for the Chiefs’ offense last season. The team couldn’t run the ball at all, and the wide receivers struggled to do anything downfield. The offense was cramped and could not string together drives often.

“There was so much pressure on Mahomes to carry things. … The Kansas City Chiefs must find a way to make life easier for [Patrick Mahomes].”@tthasselbeck and @minakimes on how the Chiefs should handle Mahomes' return from injury 🏈 pic.twitter.com/I2jaGDTKEu

— NFL on ESPN (@ESPNNFL) July 24, 2026

In an attempt to overcome this, Mahomes had to scramble more often. By the end of the season, despite Mahomes’s best heroics, he wasn’t able to lift the offense with his playmaking.

To make matters worse, Mahomes tore his ACL against the Los Angeles Chargers during the fourth quarter of Week 15. Not only was that the final conclusion of a rough season, but it affects this coming season too.

Mahomes has proven over the years to be able to come back from an injury quicker than others, and he’s doing that again. Despite only tearing his ACL seven months ago, Mahomes has been a full participant in training camp.

It’s remarkable that Mahomes is going to even be able to play that shortly after his injury. Just having Mahomes back, even if he’s limited, is a major boost to the offense. However, Mahomes is going to have to alter his playing style to account for his injury, mainly running less.

Mahomes acknowledged this in a recent press conference about running less this season.

If anyone could come back in that short amount of time and still be able to run, it is Mahomes. However, the most likely outcome is that Mahomes is going to need to scramble less after the injury.

That will materially change the offense. What could that look like?

Patrick Mahomes (knee) on changes to his play this season:

"I think I ran a little bit too much last season… If all else fails, I'll just hand it off to K9 and let him go to work." pic.twitter.com/dLlhbMqdc2

— Underdog NFL (@UnderdogNFL) July 24, 2026

As Mahomes mentioned, having running back Kenneth Walker as a nearby weapon should help with that. Walker gives the Chiefs a credible run threat that defenses have to account for. He’s also potentially their best avenue to creating explosive plays, particularly if Mahomes is limited in his running.

A byproduct of running the ball more might be going under center. Going under center can help the run game by unlocking easier angles to block and allowing extra blockers into the play.

Another benefit of going under center is that the Chiefs can keep Mahomes in the pocket while giving him more protection. There can be extra bodies dedicated to protection.

Having the threat of a run will make those play actions look easier, and it also helps the receivers in this offense. Using condensed formations from under center can get the receivers free releases and more space to run into. Mahomes can also manipulate zone defenders from his eyes. It would be an easy transition for Mahomes to be more of a play-action quarterback.

Still, the question is about third-and-long situations. The Chiefs can’t mitigate the primary receiver issues on these snaps, as defenses aren’t going to fear the run. Teams will play man coverage without strong proof that Kansas City’s receivers strike fear in one-on-one situations.

Mahomes has long helped this issue with his legs. If that’s off the table, how will the Chiefs be able to compensate for that?

The offense will need receivers to step up in these situations to help Mahomes out. I’m skeptical.

The Chiefs will likely struggle to move the chains on third-and-long if Mahomes has to stay within the pocket, but having a stronger run game can mitigate how many of those situations you’re put in.

Another thing the Chiefs could do is throw short of the sticks on third down and be more aggressive on fourth down. If a third-and-8 can become a fourth-and-short, the play calling can rely on short-pass concepts that help the receivers.

The hope is that the Chiefs are able to adapt the offense to more under-center formations early in the season as Mahomes gets comfortable. The best-case scenario is that as the season goes on, Mahomes becomes more capable and willing to scramble and run. If the offense can spend the early part of the season developing the run game, that is a formula that could be dangerous by the playoffs, when Mahomes is potentially hitting a physical stride

But until Mahomes is fully comfortable with scrambling again, the Chiefs are going to need to adapt the offense, or the team could really struggle to move the ball. It’s on the staff to adapt the scheme to account for this.

title: Braves Minor League Recap: Conor Essenburg’s huge game helps fuels GreenJackets offense
description: (43-56) Iowa Cubs 7, (52-48) Gwinnett Stripers 3 Box Score The Stripers were unable to overcome rough starting pitching en route to their loss to the Iowa Cubs. JR Ritchie got the start and struggled out of the gate – struggling to generate whiffs and spot his pitches in the first inning, which ultimately was […]
fullText:
Patrick Clohisy, CF: 2-for-5, R, .488/.523/.829

Sean Murphy, DH: 2-for-4, RBI, 2B, .244/.326/.317

Ha-Seong Kim, SS: 0-for-3, BB, SB, .239/.352/.348

Jair Camargo, C: 2-for-4, HR, RBI, R, .233/.270/.365

JR Ritchie, SP: 4IP 7H 5ER 1BB 3K, 3.88 ERA

The Stripers were unable to overcome rough starting pitching en route to their loss to the Iowa Cubs.

JR Ritchie got the start and struggled out of the gate – struggling to generate whiffs and spot his pitches in the first inning, which ultimately was too much for Gwinnett to handle. After giving up a lead off single JR was able to strikeout the next batter before giving up a two run home run. He would then surrender a triple, and hit by pitch before giving up the third run of the inning – a sacrifice fly. JR would get through the next two innings unscathed before surrendering two more runs in the fourth inning, giving Iowa five on the game. He would be replaced by Drue Hackenberg (3.1IP 5H 2ER 2BB 0K) who gave up three extra-base hits himself, as well as two walks, and two earned runs. He would come out of the game with a runner on first and be replaced by Rolddy Muñoz (0.2IP 0H 0R 0BB 0K) who needed just eight pitches to get through the rest of the 8th inning. Joel Payamps (1IP 0H 0R 1BB 1K) pitched the final inning, struggling with his command, but ultimately getting the job done.

Offensively, the Stripers were held to just six hits, going 0-for-8 with runners in scoring position and stranding seven on base. They got two on in the first inning with zero out before Ha-Seong Kim drove in a run on a double play to put the Stripers on board. They would then be held scoreless until the seventh inning when Jair Camargo got a hold of one, driving the ball 398’ with an exit velocity of 108.9 to give the Stripers their second run of the game. Luke Williams would then walk right after it, before eventually coming into score on a roped run scoring double by Sean Murphy who scalded a ball to right-center for the Stripers third run of the game. Unfortunately the rally would promptly end with shortstop Ha-Seong Kim striking out.

Dalton McIntyre, CF: 1-for-2, BB, R, 2B, .257/.375/.378

Jordan Groshans, 1B: 2-for-3, 2B, RBI, .262/.335/.524

Colby Jones, 3B: 1-for-3, 3B, R, .182/.302/.455

Shay Schanaman, SP: 2IP 1H 1ER 1BB 2K, 5.44 ERA

The Clingstones were unable to overcome a rough hitting performance on their way to a close 4-2 loss to the Blue Wahoos.

Shay Schanaman took to the mound in a bullpen game for the Clingstones and gave up a single run across two innings pitched that came via a double that brought in a runner who was on second. After pitching a scoreless second inning he was replaced by Riley Frey (2IP 1H 0R 0BB 3K) who was extremely strong, pounding the zone and attacking hitters – striking out three across his two innings of work. He would be replaced by Owen Hackman (2IP 3H 3ER 0BB 1K) who fell victim to what was a game altering three run home run that put the Blue Wahoos in the lead. Anderson Pilar (1IP 0H 0R 0BB 2K) and Blane Abeyta (1IP 2H 0R 0BB 1K) pitched the final two innings, holding the Blue Wahoos scoreless – giving the offense a chance to see if they could stage a comeback.

Unfortunately, the offense as a whole struggled against the Blue Wahoos pitching staff getting just six hits while striking out nine. Much like the Stripers, the Clingstones went 0-for-8 with runners in scoring position, stranding four on base. Jordan Groshans who has been one of the Clingstones, if not the entire organizations, best players was the only Clingstones player to register a multi-hit game. He drove in the first run of the game, driving in Dalton McIntyre who doubled to start the game.

Ahead Early pic.twitter.com/bAD1qDtNT2

— Columbus Clingstones (@GoClingstones) July 26, 2026

The Clingstones would be held scoreless until the fifth inning when Colby Jones led off the inning with a triple. He was driven in by Matt Scannell who grounded out to first but drove in Colby to give the Clingstones their second, and final run of the game. At the time of the play this put the Clingstones up ahead 2-1, but ultimately not being able to get anything else going offensively led to their defeat.

Tate Southisene, SS: 1-for-4, R, .255/.379/.428

John Gil, 2B: 0-for-1, 3 BB, 2 R, .241/.342/.372

Eric Hartman, CF: 1-for-2, R, BB, RBI, .269/.358/.517

Owen Carey, LF: 1-for-4, 3 RBI, R, .268/.333/.459

Dixon Williams, 1B: 1-for-4, 2 RBI, .216/.328/.405

Cade Kuehler, SP: 5IP 5H 2ER 4BB 2K, 5.42 ERA

The Emperors were able to overcome a an up-and-down starting pitching performance on their way to capturing their 45th win of the season thanks to some extremely strong work by the bullpen.

Cade Kuehler got the start and was a bit up and down with his performance, walking four and surrendering five hits across his five innings of work. Cade would surrender just two runs but dealt with a lot of traffic as he struggled to consistently land in the zone. He would be replaced by Ray Kerr (1IP 1H 0R 0BB 1K), who looked strong in his third rehab appearance for the Rome Emperors. Jacob Kroeger (1IP 1H 0R 0BB 2K) would work around a single and would strike out two in his very strong inning of work. Logan Samuels (1IP 0H 0R 1BB 2K), and Tyler Schoff (1IP 1H 0R 0BB 0K) would work the games final two innings without allowing a run to score.

Offensively for the Emperors all their damage came in a pair of innings, the first and the seventh. After drawing a walk in the first John Gil would steal second and take third on an errant throw to set the tone. Eric Hartman would then walk to put two on and Owen Carey would triple them both in to put the Emperors up 2-1.

Owen Carey clears the bases and the Emperors lead! pic.twitter.com/4r35aBEMLr

— Rome Emperors (@GoEmperors) July 26, 2026

Owen would then come into score when Dixon Williams would ground out to the pitcher and drive in Owen to score the Emperors third run of the game. While the offense would threaten by getting runners on second in a pair of innings, they were largely held in check until the seventh inning when they scored an additional three runs to really put the game away. After loading the bases to start the inning Eric Hartman drove in the fourth run of the game with a sacrifice fly. Owen Carey would follow that up with a ground out to second that scored Tate Southisene to give the Emperors their fifth run of the game. The final run came with the next batter, Dixon Williams, who singled in John Gil to push the lead to 6-2. The Emperors would go 1-2-3 in the eighth inning before ending the game in the top of the ninth.

Luis Guanipa, CF: 3-for-5, 3 R, RBI, R, .302/.358/.456

Conor Essenburg, RF: 3-for-5, 3 RBI, HR, 3 R, BB, .267/.407/.500

Alex Lodise, SS: 2-for-5, HR, 2 R, RBI, BB, .256/.343/.483

Austin Machado, C: 1-for-2, 2 R, RBI, 4 BB, .216/.554/.243

Junior Garcia, LF: 2-for-4, 2 RBI, R, BB, .201/.326/.296

Carter Holton, SP: 4IP 2H 2ER 6BB 1K, 5.08 ERA

An offensive explosion, and some incredible luck on the mound helped fuel the GreenJackets massive 13-4 win on the road.

Carter Holton got the start and survived, giving up a pair of runs across four innings of work. Carter surrendered just two hits, but walked a staggering six batters as he had a rough 51% strike rate. To his credit, he navigated through all of the runners on base and surrendered just two earned runs, but it definitely wasn’t one of his best starts. Ryan Heppner (1.2IP 4H 0R 0BB 1K) replaced Carter in the fifth inning and got into some danger himself, allowing four hits across those innings pitched, but registered 1.2 clean innings. Kade Woods (1.1IP 2H 1ER 2BB 1K) relieved Heppner and gave up a pair of hits and walks in his work. Cristobal Abreu (2IP 0H 0R 2BB 2K) pitched the final two innings, walking two but giving up zero hits.

Offensively it was a massive night for the GreenJackets as they had nearly as many runs (13) as they did hits (14). The starting pitcher for the RidgeYaks had a game to forget as he gave up six earned runs in just .1 innings of work. Those six runs in the first came on two bases loaded walks, a hit by pitch with the bases loaded, a sacrifice fly, and two run single. The GreenJackets would tack on another run in the third, before bursting for six runs over the games sixth, and seventh innings. In the sixth, Luis Guanipa led it off the inning with a single, before Conor Essenburg connected on a towering home run to put the GreenJackets ahead 9-2.

Conor Essenburg into a different AREA CODE! pic.twitter.com/QBJzLZf0sr

— Augusta GreenJackets (@GreenJackets) July 26, 2026

Not to be out done, Alex Lodise followed him up with a solo home run, his 21st of the season.

And Alex Lodise goes back to back! pic.twitter.com/3EjenvZyhv

— Augusta GreenJackets (@GreenJackets) July 26, 2026

In the seventh it was Luis Guanipa who drove in Junior Garcia for the GreenJackets 11th run of the game, followed up by a Conor Essenburg double that drove in Guanipa for the games 12th run. After moving over to third on a single by Alex Lodise, Essenburg would come into score on a Cody Miller sacrifice fly for the games final run.

title: Phillies on the Pharm: 7/27/2026
description: Painter looks good in his start for Lehigh Valley
fullText:
It was yet another day evaluate what Andrew Painter on the mound and it turned out to be something very positive. How the kids did:

Lehigh Valley 9. Indianapolis 8

With Painter on the mound for the IronPigs, he was going to draw most of the focus and for the better part, he was very good. Six innings of only allowing a run on a home run, striking out six and getting quite a bit of swing and miss on his fastball is a step forward for the young man. He still isn’t being mentioned much as an option to cure the fifth starter’s spot, which is interesting to think about, but the team looks comfortable simply letting him continue working on things in Lehigh Valley.

As for the rest of the game, Keaton Anthony led the offense with three hits while several hitters – Liover Peguero, Dylan Moore and Carter Kieboom – all had two RBI on a day where the bat woke up a little bit. One might wonder where all the runs came from if everyone was performing so well, but it really was just some shoddy fielding in the ninth inning that allowed Indianapolis to score a few unearned runs to make it closer than it actually was.

Bryan Rincon continues his year that has seen him start to show off some power, hitting his 16th dinger on the season to pace a Fightin’ Phils team that is surging a bit. Rincon hasn’t had this much over the fence power in his career yet and maybe it’s a side effect of playing half the games of the year in Reading, but it’s a nice piece of player development that he is getting going a bit more. Luke Ritter joined him as the hitting star of the day, going four for four, all singles and scoring a run.

There were at least two hitters that had decent days for the BlueClaws in Wuilfredo Antunez (two doubles) and Trent Farquhar (two for two off the bench, including a double), but it was again more of the same. The pitching had a bullpen game where no one was really anything of note, the lack of offensive talent showed up and another loss was registered.

Cole Gilley was good in his four innings for the Threshers, but the star was Mark Kolozsvary. A grand slam in the fourth inning was the big blow that helped lead the offense to a win. Robert Phelps, Alirio Ferrebus, Lyle Miller-Green and Victor Cardoza also had an RBI a piece for the offense.

title: Kaden Elliss could be the key to Brandon Staley’s Saints defense
description: Why Kaden Elliss more than just another starter.
fullText:
As the New Orleans Saints prepare to open the 2026 season on the road against the Detroit Lions, much of the attention has centered on defensive coordinator Brandon Staley and how he’ll fill the void of Demario Davis. According to New Orleans Football Network’s Nick Underhill, one player could be more important to that transition than anyone else: veteran LB Kaden Elliss.

Speaking alongside Mike Triplett, Underhill explained why he believes Elliss is the focal point of what Staley wants to accomplish defensively.

“Elliss is interesting because I think that he is the piece Staley’s looking at as the straw that stirs the drink a little bit,” Underhill said. “I think he views him as like, here’s my first handpicked chess piece. Like I can do all this stuff with him.”

Underhill believes Elliss’ versatility makes him uniquely valuable in Staley’s defensive scheme, which has historically relied on defenders capable of filling multiple roles. Whether it’s rushing the passer, dropping into coverage or lining up in different spots across the front seven, Elliss gives Staley the flexibility to disguise looks and create favorable matchups.

“I think he opens up the defense and gives them versatility that if he disappeared, I don’t know what you would… I don’t know how that would change,” Underhill continued. “That is a big one because it does feel like he is a little bit more so, positional value aside, like a Jenga block on the defense and that, like if he vanishes, where do you go?”

The comparison stresses just how critical Elliss is to the Saints’ defensive identity, especially following the departure of Demario Davis this offseason in free agency. Rather than simply replacing his production if an injury were to occur, losing Elliss would force Staley to rethink how he deploys the entire defense.

As training camp gets underway, all eyes will be on how Staley utilizes Elliss. If Underhill’s assessment proves accurate, the linebacker won’t just be another starter, but could be the player who makes the Saints’ defensive scheme come to fruition.

title: Nick Saban opens up on his advice to Lane Kiffin
description: Saban revealed the guidance he gave Kiffin before he accepted the LSU head coaching job.
fullText:
Former Alabama head coach Nick Saban recently shared new details about the advice he gave Lane Kiffin before Kiffin accepted the LSU Tigers head coaching job.

Speaking during SEC Media Days, Saban said Kiffin reached out while weighing his options and asked for guidance. Rather than telling him what decision to make, Saban said he asked Kiffin what he ultimately wanted to accomplish. When Kiffin responded that his goal was to win a national championship, Saban pointed to LSU as a program with the resources and tradition to make that a possibility.

Saban also emphasized one of LSU’s biggest advantages, which is recruiting. He noted that Louisiana consistently produces elite NFL level talent on a regular basis and that many of the state’s top players grow up wanting to play for the Tigers. That built-in recruiting edge, combined with LSU’s history of postseason success, made Baton Rouge an attractive destination for Kiffin.

While Saban acknowledged he believed LSU offered Kiffin an ideal opportunity, he stopped short of saying he told him to take the job. Instead, he stressed that if winning a national title was Kiffin’s priority, LSU gave him the best chance to achieve that goal, as long as everyone within the program is on the same page.

title: Pellegrini to sign new Roma contract before Wales preseason
description: Lorenzo Pellegrini is waiting to sign his contract renewal with Roma. His teammates are eagerly awaiting him, as Cristante made clear a few days ago: “I’ve spoken to him, we’re waiting for him w...
fullText:
Lorenzo Pellegrini is waiting to sign his contract renewal with Roma.

His teammates are eagerly awaiting him, as Cristante made clear a few days ago: “I’ve spoken to him, we’re waiting for him with open arms and hope he returns to the team as soon as possible.”

The Giallorossi number 7 is recovering from an injury, so Gasperini may need to work on his fitness, given that he hasn’t found consistency since April.

Pellegrini has always prioritized his contract renewal with Roma, and further developments are expected in the coming hours.

As reported by Il Tempo, the player’s goal is to join the team for Wales. The midfielder, who grew up in Trigoria, is expected to sign a two-year contract with an option for a third year worth €2.5 million plus bonuses.

Pellegrini remains an important asset for Gasperini on and off the pitch, which is why he pushed for his renewal. Decisive developments are expected.

title: Dana White confirms Conor McGregor injury return timetable
description: Dana White doesn’t expect to see Conor McGregor fight for a while
fullText:
Conor McGregor definitely isn’t fighting again for a long time.

“Notorious” made a disappointing return to action at UFC 329, lasting just 69 seconds against longtime rival Max Holloway before a McGregor knee injury forced the bout to be stopped. It was McGregor’s first in-cage appearance since July 2026, when he broke his leg in a loss to Dustin Poirier.

Since his latest injury, McGregor has stated he plans to fight again in summer 2027, and though he recently shared a video that appeared to show him already doing leg exercises, UFC CEO Dana White doubts that changes the current prognosis.

“I have no idea,” White said at a post-Zuffa Boxing event press conference Sunday when asked about the video. “We had him on FaceTime tonight, ringside, but you know, Conor McGregor’s out for a year.”

In McGregor’s previous statement, he pointed out that he previously tore his ACL in a fight with Holloway back in 2013 and returned to competition nine months later, so he is optimistic that “With today’s regenerative medicine advancements and improved training methods it is well within my realm to return by next summer.”

McGregor, 38, has said repeatedly that his goal is to fight out the final fight of his UFC contract. Following the loss to Holloway, he is now without a victory since January 2020.

title: Arizona Diamondbacks News, 7/27: Snakes driven out of Washington
description: Recaps [AZ Central] Perdomo eyeing pitching upgrade as Diamondbacks fall to Nationals – It is understandable why starting pitching would be on Perdomo’s mind. Over the past two days, the Diamondbacks have handed the ball to a pair of rookie lefties in Mitch Bratt and Kohl Drake. Bratt got through five innings on Saturday, July […]
fullText:
[AZ Central] Perdomo eyeing pitching upgrade as Diamondbacks fall to Nationals – It is understandable why starting pitching would be on Perdomo’s mind. Over the past two days, the Diamondbacks have handed the ball to a pair of rookie lefties in Mitch Bratt and Kohl Drake. Bratt got through five innings on Saturday, July 25, but he allowed five runs and walked five batters. Drake on Sunday allowed four runs in four-plus innings. “I think sometimes it’s a lot for them,” Perdomo said of young starters being thrust into a pennant race. “They don’t have so much experience. They have been doing the best they can do. They work hard every single time. Bratt and Drake, they (empty their tanks). Whatever has happened in the games, it’s tough for them, but at least we get some fight from them.”

[Dbacks.com] D-backs drop rubber game to fellow Wild Card contender as Deadline looms – Making his second Major League start on Sunday, Drake was given three leads but surrendered each one, allowing consistent hard contact. Ahead 4-2 in the fifth, he issued a leadoff walk to Nasim Nuñez and James Wood followed with a two-run homer to tie it. “The most important inning in baseball is the inning after you score, right?” Lovullo said. “Shutdown inning. I think the walk to start the fifth was very critical.” The poor pitching performances negated a solid afternoon for the the top of the lineup one day after Lovullo switched things up. The manager moved Ketel Marte down into the cleanup spot and Gabriel Moreno up to number three behind Corbin Carroll and Perdomo. The group combined to go 5-for-14 with five walks and six runs scored.

[SI] Ugly Loss to Nationals is a Wake-Up Call for D-backs’ Deadline Needs – As obvious as it may have been already, the Diamondbacks simply won’t be able to make a deep postseason run with the rotation in its current state, and the team cannot bank on the return of injured players in that category. Arizona trotted out two of its rookie arms in Mitch Bratt and Kohl Drake. Both of those starters have shown some potential in the majors, but both were hammered by a strong Washington offense. Meanwhile, Merrill Kelly still has an ERA in the 5.00s with inconsistent command. Zac Gallen, when healthy, had the worst qualified ERA in baseball. Ryne Nelson may not be able to fully ramp back up, and Corbin Burnes isn’t expected back until early September, and his effectiveness is anything but guaranteed coming off both Tommy John surgery and a shoulder injury.

[MLB Trade Rumors] Diamondbacks Interested In Extension With Gabriel Moreno – The five-year, $99.4MM extension Cal Raleigh signed with the Mariners in advance of his 60-homer 2025 season might very well be a target point for Moreno’s agents at Klutch Sports. Raleigh inked his deal heading into his age-28 season (whereas Moreno will be 27), and with one of his three arb years already in the books. While Raleigh’s power numbers were superior to Moreno’s, their overall offensive production was pretty similar. Moreno has a career 114 wrC+ from 1429 career PA and counting, whereas Raleigh had a 111 wRC+ from 1760 PA at the time of his extension.

[Arizona Sports] The Athletic’s Bowden lists Angels pitcher Jose Soriano as trade target fit for Diamondbacks – Bowden noted the Diamondbacks’ need for a starting pitcher and his control beyond 2026 as the main reasons for the 27-year-old righty’s potential fit in Arizona. In 21 starts, Soriano has posted an 8-6 record with a 3.43 ERA, 122 strikeouts and a 1.25 WHIP. Soriano had a strong outing in his most recent start against the St. Louis Cardinals on Monday, pitching seven innings with just one run surrendered on four hits and seven strikeouts. With Soriano under control through 2028, he would also give the D-backs an option in the rotation beyond this season, as several starters are set to become free agents, including Michael Soroka and Zac Gallen. Corbin Burnes also has an opt-out clause in his contract.

[Noozhawk] A McCann-Do Attitude Has Arizona Diamondbacks Pointed Toward Playoffs – That Major League Baseball team trusts no one more with its pitchers than James McCann, a Dos Pueblos High School graduate who turned 36 last month. Diamondbacks manager Torey Lovullo has described McCann’s mentorship of the team’s young mound staff as being “on a Ph.D. level.”“You could probably target the day he got here and take a look at our ERA and do some of the reverse math on your own,” Lovullo said. “I know it’s been very good since he’s gotten here.“I think he’s had a strong input as to the success that we’ve had overall as a pitching staff.”

[MLB.com] Sun-splashed and spirited crowd watching, Beltrán, Andruw, Kent enshrined in Hall – The three new members bring the Hall’s count to 354, of which 281 are players. Beltrán and Jones are just the third and fourth center fielders elected by the Baseball Writers’ Association of America in nearly half a century. Since Duke Snider went in with the Class of 1980, only Kirby Puckett (2001) and Ken Griffey Jr. (2016) were counted as center fielders elected by the BBWAA until this year. Kent, who was elected by the Contemporary Baseball Era Committee at the Winter Meetings last December, is the first second baseman to join the Hall since another Astro: Craig Biggio in 2015.

[Deseret News] The name for Utah’s potential future MLB team? It has to be ‘Trappers’ – Utah’s current sports branding is top tier. The Jazz name is iconic, “Mammoth” has quickly proven to be a popular choice and Real Salt Lake and Utah Royals FC have slick identities as well. Thus, the bar will be high for an MLB team name. They can’t afford to get it wrong. Scrolling through social media, some of the most popular name proposals include the Utah Outlaws, Utah Gulls, Utah Cutthroats, Utah Black Diamonds AND Utah Pioneers. Some have suggested the longtime minor league Bees brand get called up to the majors. But there’s a different minor league team that should be chosen for an MLB name: the legendary Salt Lake City Trappers.

There have certainly been bigger nautical disasters than HMS Titanic. The wartime sinking of the Wilhelm Gustloff resulted in the loss of over nine thousand lives, roughly six times as many. But none has made such an indelible mark on pop culture. Purely in the cinema, there have been dozens of films based on or inspired by it. The first came out less than a month after Titanic sank, and starred actress Dorothy Gibson, who was actually a survivor of the event. Most famously, of course, is James Cameron’s Titanic, which remains the second-biggest movie worldwide, almost thirty years after its release. Tapping into this interest, an exhibition recently opened in Scottsdale, promising to “tell the story of the RMS Titanic like never before.” So, does it?

title: 3 positions of need remaining for Michigan Football’s 2027 recruiting class
description: The Wolverines already have a strong 2027 recruiting class, but they still have needs to fill. Here are Michigan Football’s 3 top remaining positions of need:
fullText:
The Michigan Wolverines have a solid 2027 recruiting class assembled up to this point in the year. Depending on where you look, Kyle Whittingham and company have a borderline Top 10 overall class, and there are still players left for the taking.

While spots are filling up, there are still a few positions of need for Michigan before the December early signing period. Here are the top three needs.

Four-star Quentin Burrell is the only wide receiver committed to Michigan’s 2027 class. The Wolverines were able to get three wide receivers last cycle, but there’s no denying they could use at least one more — but preferably two — wide receivers before it’s all said and done.

Both Trey Pierce and Enow Etta could head to the NFL after this season, and there are plenty of unproven commodities waiting in the wings. Michigan’s 2027 class is strong with edge rushers, but outside of four-star Xavier Muhammad, there is a pretty sizable gap on the defensive front.

A true nose tackle would help beef up the class and combat some of those strong, Big Ten interior offensive linemen down the road. Adding some bulk would, in theory, open up pass rushing opportunities for the edge rushers that Michigan already has committed, and continue the Wolverines’ tradition of powerful, tenacious defensive lines.

Michigan’s 2027 class is loaded in the secondary with guys like four-star Monsanna Torbert, four-star Blake Jenkins and four-star Darius Johnson all have starter ceilings. Four-star safety/nickel Tavares Harrington and three-star safety Charles Woodson Jr. make this probably the biggest strength of the 2027 bunch.

But the current starting five are all older, as Zeke Berry and Rod Moore are redshirt seniors, Smith Snowden is a true senior, and both Jyaire Hill and Chris Brady are redshirt juniors. Between sophomore Shamari Earls, junior Mason Curtis and freshman Jamarion Vincent, there is still talent in the pipeline. Yet, there will be heavy turnover in the coming year or so, and replenishing that back five should be among the staff’s checklist.

Would these adds complete the 2027 class? Who else do you want Whittingham to go after? Let us know down in the comments section below.

title: We built a video ingestion pipeline for 60× scale headroom
description: Building a high-volume video ingestion system for a scale target that refused to hold still, and the three times it pushed back and taught us something.
fullText:
Most systems are built for the load they have. This one had to be built for a load nobody could name yet. When we started, the target was “around 30 million items a day.” By the time we were in production it had been re-baselined to 2 million, with the 30M number still standing as the direction of travel. Somewhere in that range was the real system, and we had to build something that didn’t need rewriting when the number moved.

This is a note on how we did it: the architecture, the decisions that created the headroom, how we knew it worked, and three moments where the system pushed back. We were a small mixed team, a couple of platform consultants plus the client’s own engineers. Everything below is “we”; the hindsight at the end is mine.

The domain, in one line: ingest high-volume public video content from across the open web, enrich it (metadata, downloaded media, machine transcription), index it, and expose search over it.

The job was a searchable, near-real-time index of public video: not a crawl-once dataset but a continuously updating one. As videos are published across the open web, the system finds each one within seconds, downloads the video and pulls its metadata, works out whether anyone is speaking and in what language, transcribes the speech to text, and makes the whole record (caption, transcript, metadata) searchable within about five minutes of the video going live. A user can then query “show me recent videos that mention X” and get answers off a corpus that’s minutes old.

Three forces pull against each other the entire time: volume (a firehose that could reach tens of millions of new items a day), freshness (minutes, not hours), and a scope that kept moving as the product found its shape. Almost every decision below is about holding those three in tension, so that when one of them changes (the volume target changed by more than an order of magnitude mid-project) the design bends instead of breaking. And the volume was a guess. We were building for a number nobody could pin down, which is a different problem from building for a big one.

The pipeline is six stages joined by queues: discover → fetch → detect-language → transcribe → index → search. Each stage is its own service (containers on ECS/EC2) with its own input queue and its own autoscaling policy, and it knows nothing about its neighbours beyond a message schema. Services physically can’t import each other’s code; a build rule fails the compile if they try. That reads like a style rule; it’s the decision everything else depends on. Because the only coupling between stages is a queue, each one scales on its own backlog and a slow stage becomes a growing queue rather than an outage propagating upstream.

Stages talk through queues fed by fan-out topics, so a producer can add consumers without knowing they exist. Message schemas are versioned as discriminated unions, so two versions can coexist on a queue during a rolling deploy. Autoscaling is driven off queue depth, not CPU. The honest signal for a pipeline is how much work is waiting, and CPU-based scaling lags it badly.

We chose managed queues over a streaming log and containers-on-VMs over Kubernetes. The language call was a real bake-off: a colleague wrote the scanner in Go, I wrote it in Node. Go came out about 15% faster on the hot path. We shipped Node anyway. Our stack is Node, and a 15% edge on one service didn’t justify carrying a second language. Every one of these was a “smaller team, fewer moving parts” call.

Four decisions carry the headroom, and none of them is “add more machines.” That part is easy once the design lets you.

Ingestion volume is governed by a single configuration value that sets how much of the available stream we take in, read live each cycle, held completely separate from how many workers run. One knob is coverage, fleet size is speed; they’re orthogonal. Moving between operating points is one value changed live: no redeploy, no effect on in-flight work. That single indirection is most of why the scale target could move without the architecture moving with it.

Two properties make retries safe end to end. First, the discovery→fetch hop runs on FIFO queues keyed per video for both grouping and deduplication, so a duplicate discovery inside the window is collapsed before anyone pays to fetch it. Second, as the diagram shows, the indexer’s document is assembled by three producers arriving in any order, any number of times. So writes are scripted upserts keyed to the same document, with nulls stripped so a late partial can’t clobber a field that’s already there:

Create-then-merge and merge-then-create converge to byte-identical documents. Once every write is order-independent and replay-safe, you can retry aggressively, and aggressive retries are what let the pipeline ride out a flaky upstream instead of dropping data.

Between fetch, audio, transcription and index, a queue absorbs every rate mismatch. Long units of work keep their lock alive with a visibility heartbeat that re-extends at a third of the timeout, and interrupted work is never deleted; a shutdown mid-unit just lets the message redeliver. But discovery is deliberately not back-pressured by downstream: if it falls too far behind real time, it advances its cursor and sheds the backlog rather than queue work that’s already going stale. For a freshness product, current-but-incomplete beats complete-but-late. We picked which property to protect, on purpose.

Every queue has a dead-letter queue at three attempts. Every service but the orchestrator is stateless and disposable. The services themselves own almost no durable state; the one exception is a small cursor record, and everything heavy lives in the object store and the search cluster, which are built to be stateful. The CPU-bound stages run competing-consumer worker pools (N loops each doing pull-one, process, repeat) instead of pulling a batch and awaiting it, so one slow item can’t stall the nine behind it. When something breaks, it breaks in one lane.

One thing worth saying plainly, because it took us a while to accept: the ceiling was never the scanning. Scanning compute you scale by adding tasks. The real limit is the shared egress out to the open web. That’s finite in a way compute isn’t, and every scaling conversation came back to it.

A pipeline that fans out across six services and three storage systems can’t be verified by unit tests that mock their way around the hard parts. So we didn’t mock. Across roughly 550 test cases, vi.fn, vi.mock and vi.spyOn appear zero times; the rule is enforced, not aspirational. Verification is built from the outside in.

The safety net that matters is the tests that stand up the real thing in containers: real message queues, a real object store, a real search cluster, and the actual service Docker images, not test doubles. About 180 tests run this way, of which the heaviest 30-odd are full end-to-end system tests, backed by a dedicated internal package whose only job is a container factory per service. The search acceptance test seeds a synthetic corpus into the queue, runs the real indexer image to apply the schema, boots the real indexer service to consume and write into a real search cluster, then queries the API over HTTP and asserts the result. It was written before the search service existed; its own header calls it “the test that guides the service: RED until the service is built inward.” The acceptance test was the specification.

Two habits sat on either side of that net. Every service began as a design doc committed to the repo (roughly 2,900 lines of them across system design, capacity model, index mapping and the search contract), reviewed and “signed” on a fixed four-phase rhythm (design, review, PR plan, implement) before a line of service code, then built as a dependency-ordered sequence of PRs rather than discovered in the editor.

And we validated against real data, not just synthetic fixtures. We ran the actual mapping code across a real staging dump to measure things you can’t guess. That corrected a vendor’s 50 KB-per-document cluster-sizing assumption down to a measured ~2 KB, which changed the hardware. A field-presence audit over a couple thousand real records shaped the index mapping and exposed two schema bugs (a field that was a string where we’d typed a number; a duration in milliseconds we’d read as seconds). And we checked search correctness by planting a known set of real posts and comparing results side-by-side against a reference store, where they diverged became tickets, not opinions.

The acceptance test came first. Building the service was making it go green.

We wrapped the discovery worker’s outbound validation call in a circuit breaker, the textbook move, tuned conservatively: trip after five requests at a 50% error rate, reset after thirty seconds. What the textbook omits is that our workers shared one pool of egress infrastructure. When it degraded, every worker’s breaker saw the same failure rate and tripped in the same second. On open, our handler aborted the whole assignment. The abort returned the message to the queue; the next worker leased it, hit the same degraded dependency, aborted again, and on the third receive it dead-lettered.

The fix had two halves. Stop treating “circuit open” as “fail the work”; treat it as “wait”:

The jitter matters: without it, “wait then retry” just moves the synchronised stampede a second to the right, so every worker still wakes together and re-trips the breaker in lockstep. Jitter spreads the wake-ups, and the breaker’s reset is a single half-open trial rather than the whole fleet firing at once. Then retune so it fires on a real outage, not on the ambient error rate of a dependency that fails a fraction of calls by nature: threshold to 75% over a thirty-second window with a volume floor of a hundred requests, reset probe every five seconds. The retry budget stopped being spent on a dependency that was going to fail the same way three times in a row.

Load-testing search, the cluster began returning 429 across the board: “too many point-in-time contexts.” It read like we’d outgrown the search tier. We hadn’t. Deep pagination opened a point-in-time reader per result page to mint a stable cursor, released only if the caller paged all the way to the end. Almost nobody pages to the end. Each reader lived for its keep-alive window, and under load the single-page searches (the overwhelming majority) opened them faster than they expired, until we hit the cluster-wide cap and every query started failing, regardless of size.

We deleted the point-in-time approach entirely and made the cursor stateless: an opaque token carrying only the sort key of the last hit, resolved against the live index on the next call:

Zero server-side state, so nothing to leak and unbounded concurrent paginators. The tradeoff we accepted out loud: this gives best-effort consistency, not a frozen snapshot, so a document indexed mid-traversal can shift a page boundary. For an append-mostly index that’s fine, and a strict point-in-time export was deferred to a separate internal path.

Language detection gates the expensive transcription step; only allowed-language clips go on to transcribe. We’d implemented it by running a general speech model on CPU, and under load it pinned at ~95% and became the pipeline’s bottleneck. The obvious fix was GPUs, alongside transcription. We built that migration and measured it before committing, and the GPU sat ~94% idle. Per message ran ~2.6s end to end, but the model forward pass was ~0.3 to 0.6s of it; the rest was audio decode, voice-activity detection, and feature extraction, all on the CPU. Which meant the GPU couldn’t keep up either: two nodes cleared maybe 290 clips a minute against a firehose north of 700 a minute. A fleet of mostly-idle GPUs isn’t an answer.

So we went the other way. The model that finally kept pace I found at about 2am, once it was clear the GPU path was a dead end: a small ~85 MB classifier built for exactly one job, on cheap CPU. I cut the input work feeding it, too. It cleared the inbound stream (roughly 125K clips in under five hours, dead-letter rate under 0.03%), kept pace on commodity cores, and handed the entire GPU pool back to transcription, where the forward pass dominates and a GPU earns its cost. The CPU classifier that replaced the GPU fleet we were about to provision runs at a fraction of the cost. Measuring the migration before funding it is what stopped the spend.

I’d model the shared-dependency failure mode before reaching for the circuit breaker; the correlated-trip behaviour is obvious once you say “shared” and “fleet” in the same sentence. I’d have caught the point-in-time leak with one test: issue a single-page search and assert the server-side reader count returns to baseline. And I’d have killed the “provision a database and a cache for now” reflex sooner. Both were deleted unused, and while they sat there they were a false signal that the system was more stateful than it is. The real shape (queues, object store, search index, one tiny cursor) was there from the start.

Make one config value your global throttle and keep it independent of fleet size. Put a queue between every pair of stages and decide, per boundary, whether overload should wait or shed; don’t let it be an accident. Make every write order-independent and replay-safe before you let yourself retry aggressively, because aggressive retries are your cheapest availability. Verify from the outside in against real infrastructure, and validate against real data: the design doc settles the arguments, the system test catches the bugs, and real data catches the assumptions. And when a stage is slow, profile where the milliseconds go before you buy the resource that looks scarce; the bottleneck is usually one layer over from where it hurts.

None of this is exotic. Most of it is a refusal to couple things that don’t need coupling, which is what lets one number move without dragging the rest of the system along with it.

Doron Tsur leads platform and data-infrastructure engagements at Codo: distributed systems, search, and the infrastructure underneath them.

title: We're open sourcing our privacy proxy CLI
description: pvcli is a curl-like tool designed to simplify the testing of complex privacy protocols like OHTTP.
fullText:
Debugging privacy-preserving protocols is hard. Oblivious HTTP has several different steps across four different parties, not to mention binary HTTP encoding and details spread across many draft RFCs. We've taken what we've learned operating protocols like Oblivious HTTP at the scale of millions of requests per second, and wrapped it up in a nice, clean CLI tool — that we are open sourcing today.

We call it our privacy-client, or pvcli. We’re releasing it under the Apache-2.0 License, and it is open for contributions.

Here’s a single line of code that executes a full Oblivious HTTP request with a relay, gateway and origin. Don't worry if you don't know what that means, we'll cover it below.

We’ll explain why we built this tool, and show just how handy it can be.

Let’s take a closer look at our motivation for creating pvcli. Over time, the Privacy team’s product suite and customer base grew. We added products like Privacy Proxy and Privacy Gateway, which power Apple’s Private Relay, Microsoft’s Edge Secure Network VPN, Flo Health’s Anonymous Mode, and more. With it came an increasing amount of special customer requirements, domain knowledge, and complexity. As a result, we saw increased friction in development and incident response.

To see this in action, let’s look at how one of our products implements Oblivious HTTP, also known as OHTTP. First, a quick primer. OHTTP provides users with a privacy guarantee: no one can know both who made a request and what they’re requesting. To achieve this, OHTTP requires two servers, a relay and a gateway, operated by two non-colluding parties.

Below is a sequence diagram of OHTTP, where our customer owns the relay and Cloudflare owns the gateway. At a high level, OHTTP can be broken down into these steps:

It involves quite a bit of back-and-forth, as you can see:

Each step is a potential point of failure that we have to consider while debugging!

In particular, we saw certain kinds of problems when debugging OHTTP.

As a result, we decided to place all of our privacy protocols in one tool. It has a clean interface that’s already familiar, displays every single step of the protocol in order, and is flexible enough to support new protocols and architectures.

To see the difference this makes, let’s see an OHTTP debugging scenario — before and after pvcli.

Say we operate an OHTTP relay that sits in front of a customer's gateway. The customer has asked us to do an end-to-end test with a request:

Recall the OHTTP steps from earlier. The first step is to fetch the public key from the gateway. We use curl to fetch it from the customer gateway and get this back:

That’s a big binary string in hex. To make sense of it, we look at OHTTP RFC 9458 §3 and parse it manually:

We repeat this process for however many public keys are in the binary string.

Next, we convert our original HTTP request into binary HTTP, referencing RFC 9292. We manually craft the binary with the help of some bespoke scripts:

Finally, we form a wrapper HTTP request that will hold our OHTTP request. To do so, we spend some more time writing another makeshift script that encrypts the binary HTTP request in the manner OHTTP specifies, using the public key from earlier. We create a header, which is the concatenation of public key ID, asymmetric encryption method ID, and symmetric encryption method IDs. Then, we concatenate header and encrypted binary HTTP request, resulting in:

We put those bytes into the body of our wrapper HTTP request, and send it to our relay. We get back a response.

What does that mean? We reach out to the customer to ask if they can share logs from their gateway. In the meantime, we double-check the bits we've crafted. The decoded public keys look fine. The binary HTTP request... Oh! We see:

BHTTP is length prefixed. That means we specify a length (0x0a is 10 in decimal), and then 10 bytes follow. But here, 11 bytes follow. There is an extra 20 before the 00. 20 represents a space character, so we must have accidentally added that when building the body. We remove the extra character, resend, and it works!

With pvcli, all of that is now a single command:

It handles all the binary parsing and encrypting for us, and prints logs in case we want to dive deeper:

What used to be a fragile process — involving manipulating bits, gluing together scripts, and referencing long RFCs — is now one command.

pvcli takes a lot of inspiration from curl. We designed it with the “principle of least surprise” in mind. As a result, a lot of the arguments are the same as curl’s! Try a quick GET request to our cdn-cgi endpoint:

If you’re curious about what is happening under the hood, you can use -v to get detailed logs:

Now, about that OHTTP command from earlier: you use --ohttp to tell pvcli to construct an OHTTP request. You pass in the relay as the --first-hop and the gateway as the --proxy. The target will be an echo server, so you can see what the target would see. In this command, we filled in the arguments with a relay, gateway, and target from ohttp.info.

Try running the command yourself!

We’ve encountered many cases where we wanted to pass headers to the relay, rather than the target. You are able to do that with --first-hop-header:

Similarly, we’ve also had cases where we wanted to authenticate to the relay with mTLS, to ensure that the correct client is talking with the correct relay. To do that, you can use --first-hop-client and --first-hop-key.

And it just works. Need to test a full Oblivious HTTP request with a relay, a gateway, arbitrary headers, and mTLS? Or perhaps only request through a gateway? Or maybe you just want to see the OHTTP key configuration? pvcli can do it with a single command, debugging included.

There are some great tools for OHTTP that already exist. Martin Thomson’s Rust implementation and Chris Wood’s Go implementation were incredibly helpful when we built out our original OHTTP implementation a few years ago. But pvcli is not only focused on OHTTP. We’re looking to add as many privacy-preserving protocols as we can to the tool. So while there are other OSS tools out there for debugging OHTTP, nothing combines OHTTP, CONNECT proxying, MASQUE and Privacy Pass (coming soon) all in one place.

Oblivious HTTP is an amazing protocol, and we would love to see you use it. We hope that this tool helps people debug OHTTP and write their own OHTTP implementations.

We are accepting contributions! To get started, clone the repo at https://github.com/cloudflareresearch/pvcli, and submit a pull request.

If you're looking for ways to contribute, here are some things on our to-do list. For MASQUE, we plan to add support for proxying TCP over HTTP/3, and UDP and/or IP over HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. For OHTTP, we plan to support post-quantum cryptography, add timing/latency information, support Chunked OHTTP, and improve logging.

Contact us if you are interested in using Cloudflare’s OHTTP Relays and Gateways.

title: Impressions of Teal
description:
About two months ago, I found the Teal programming language, which describes itself as a statically-typed dialect of Lua. It transpiles to Lua and runs typecheck on the developer’s machine, so it fills roughly the same niche as TypeScript. It’s used by quite a few projects, including LuaRocks and inspect.
For better or worse, I am trying to write Lua without feeling like it’s year 2010, and Teal promised to be suitable for this purpose.
This post is a retrospective on my experience: what went right and what, in my opinion, could be improved.
fullText: About two months ago, I found the Teal programming language, which describes itself as a statically-typed dialect of Lua. It transpiles to Lua and runs typecheck on the developer’s machine, so it fills roughly the same niche as TypeScript. It’s used by quite a few projects, including LuaRocks and inspect. For better or worse, I am trying to write Lua without feeling like it’s year 2010, and Teal promised to be suitable for this purpose. This post is a retrospective on my experience: what went right and what, in my opinion, could be improved. Mostly the latter. Disclaimer: while I stumbled upon multiple issues, I deeply respect everyone who works on this project, and I consider it a valuable tool. No offence intended.Annotations I think the main selling point of Teal is just how simple its annotations are. Look at the example on the website:local function add(a: number, b: number): number return a + b end local s: number = add(1, 2) print(s) It’s concise and non-intrusive, like TypeScript. Compare it to LuaLS annotations, which offers a competitive Lua typing project:---@param a number ---@param b number ---@return number local function add(a, b) return a + b end ---@type number local s = add(1, 2) print(s) This is where its obvious advantages end, though. As we’ll find out in a bit, the simplicity is quite fragile. I’m a Rust-pilled developer, so I expect some degree of soundness from type systems. “Soundness” means that if the type checker says the program is fine, you shouldn’t encounter type errors in runtime. Sounds easy? But soundness is fundamentally difficult to achieve in dynamic languages due to variance. The issue arises when mutability and subtypes collide. Here’s an example:Suppose that some function f takes a parameter x: number[].Outside the function, create a list a: integer[]. You should seemingly be able to pass it as an argument to f, since every integer is a number: f(a).From the perspective of f, x is number[], so it can append 1.5 to the list.But this causes the variable a: integer[] to contain a non-integer value 1.5! The only real way to solve this is with readonly annotations, like in TypeScript. Teal doesn’t offer anything of similar functionality. It also doesn’t have nil safety, not even opt-in, so e.g. all table accesses return T, not T | nil. I won’t hold this specific issue against Teal, as even TypeScript supports bivariance by default and doesn’t have nil safety for arrays, but it does hint that Teal considers soundness – which I’d call the main point of typing – an afterthought.Unions Teal has very rudimentary support for discriminated unions (or sum types, or enums with fields). For comparison, here’s what that looks like in Rust:enum Enum { Variant1 { a: String, }, Variant2 { a: i32. b: i32, }, } …and in TypeScript, which simulates them with union types:interface Variant1 { type: "variant1" a: string } interface Variant2 { type: "variant2" a: number b: number } type Enum = Variant1 | Variant2 Note that we have to explicitly add a field of a literal type to disambiguate types in runtime. Teal supports neither first-class sum types, nor literal types, so you have to tell it how to disambiguate variants explicitly – otherwise you can’t make a type union:local record Variant1 where self.type == "variant1" type: string a: string end local record Variant2 where self.type == "variant2" type: string a: number b: number end local type Enum = Variant1 | Variant2 where denotes a type predicate. It can contain arbitrary code, and the compiler doesn’t validate that the definition actually makes sense. So you have to write the equivalent of unsafe code every time you want to define a discriminated union! Furthermore, Teal can’t validate that newly created instances of Variant* have the right types, because type is just a string.
