fullText:
The debut from Scandinavian outfit Dead Astronauts promises shooting, survival, and, in a shake-up to the genre, seeds that terraform its pristine world right before your eyes

The wilds of the sub-Arctic north: towering pine trees, flashes of psychedelic-yellow lichen, and a sun that never wholly sets during the summer months. This land is gorgeous, yes, but also unforgiving, yet in Haex (pronounced “hex”) you have an unusual tool at your disposal to make it a little more hospitable: a cube that fits snugly in the palm of your hand out of which grows a plant. You plant this so-called Seed in the earth and – voilà – the world around you transforms: new vegetation and topography but also narrative threads to follow, and, naturally, enemies. Wield these small-but-mighty kernels of change at your own peril.

“Your adventure and your world is player-shaped,” says Haex’s creative director Tobias Nyman. He explains that everyone starts a campaign with a unique, procedurally generated world. Each Seed then contains further procedural data that causes it to terraform before your eyes. “You change the world as you go,” he says. “It becomes even more unique.”

The singularity of each game world is crucial for keeping not just you but other players on their toes. That’s another of Haex’s wrinkles: it is an online co-operative game, meaning your friends may join you on this ever-transforming survivalist adventure.

Teaming up, you play as a group of research scientists sent to investigate an anomaly in the rugged Scandinavian landscape. You come across odd, shapeshifting objects and beasts: for example, an ash-grey humanoid creature with spikes protruding from its face that would make even Pinhead from Hellraiser wince; also, a sentient wall so supermassive that it scrapes the clouds. There is a further layer to these spatial and, perhaps, alien mysteries: an unknown language of arcane sigils that must be decoded.

Nyman talks effusively of influences: sci-fi movies such as Annihilation and Arrival (as is clear from the trailer); the weird fiction thrillers of author Jeff VanderMeer, too. Unexpectedly, the creative director cites the niche music genre known as cosmic black metal as a touchstone. “There is the wild, grim, frostbitten north, an extraterrestrial entity and a thing that traverses the mist,” says Nyman, hinting at a shared emotional effect between his beloved music genre and the game: a mingling of dread and awe, and of seeking transcendence in nature.

Nyman co-founded Haex’s studio Dead Astronauts (another nod to VanderMeer), in 2024, having previously worked at Ubisoft Massive, where he helped make recent open-world blockbusters, Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora and Star Wars Outlaws. Yet where those titles’ settings are gorgeous and gigantic (“monumental,” stresses Nyman), they are also somewhat static. By contrast, Haex’s game world is more dynamic, and it is being made by just 12 developers. The theory is that its morphing, geo-engineered space should foster more fluid, interesting experiences, despite Haex’s focus on somewhat familiar-feeling shooting and survival mechanics.

Taking the leap to independence has also enabled Nyman to make a game that is more personal to him. As a youngster, he split his time between Stockholm and the far north of Sweden. He recalls looking up at the night sky blanketed with constellations as his father explained Einstein’s theory of relativity. Another memory: gazing out at an expansive crop of cloudberries – a “field of gold,” says Nyman, by virtue of the small fruit’s colour. What has stuck with him most, however, is the region’s silence – a silence so great that it was “almost screaming at me”, he says. That feels like an apt summation of Haex’s aims: an experience that is miraculous and malicious; a setting that is beautiful yet can feel as if it is bearing down on you with cruel intensity.

title: AI can fuel biological weapons. We must harness its power for defense | Annie Jacobsen
description:

As artificial intelligence rapidly transforms the biological sciences, it is pushing the future of biology in two opposing directions. AI can help bad actors generate recipes for biological weapons with just a few keystrokes and computational prompts. fullText:
The offensive potential is no longer theoretical. We need to develop systems to strengthen public health as quickly as AI is accelerating biological design

As artificial intelligence rapidly transforms the biological sciences, it is pushing the future of biology in two opposing directions. AI can help bad actors generate recipes for biological weapons with just a few keystrokes and computational prompts. At the same time, AI can track disease outbreaks and deliver critical public health information to millions of people in real time – potentially stopping a deadly outbreak in its tracks. What we are dealing with in this moment is profound: a race between offense and defense. Between the proliferation of dark biology, where deadly pathogens are engineered in secret, and the promise of a new era of collective global health.

Every infectious disease outbreak begins with a handful of cases. Public health wins by learning about an outbreak before it spreads wide, before hospitals fill and a crisis starts to spiral out of control. As transmission rates explode, options shrink. One of AI’s greatest values is its ability to compress the timeline between outbreak and detection. Speed can mean the difference between containing an outbreak and confronting an epidemic, or another global pandemic.

The World Health Organization (WHO) now uses AI to track the spread of infectious disease. At the WHO’s Hub for Pandemic and Epidemic Intelligence, in Berlin, Germany, computational systems leverage artificial intelligence and pathogenic surveillance to track and monitor infectious disease outbreaks around the world. At the center of this new way forward sits a computer-based system called Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources, or Eios (“EE-oss”), which acts as a giant filter for the world’s minute-by-minute health information.

For decades, traditional epidemic intelligence has relied on official case counts. But data from hospitals, labs, research groups and other formal reporting systems takes days or weeks to register and input into official databases. Eios leverages the colossal power of modern computing and social media to get a more immediate picture of a disease outbreak. Eios focuses on unofficial reports, citizen chatter, local news reports, social media posts and more. Proficient across multiple languages, Eios scans millions of websites, feeds and platforms, searching for outbreaks as they happen. It scrapes, filters and ranks information. The goal of Eios is to pull signal from noise.

AI is a force multiplier, changing the biological sciences every day. The real question is not whether AI can do catastrophic harm in the realm of biological sciences – it most certainly can – but whether public health officials can figure out how to deploy AI as a defensive tool faster than malicious actors deploy it as an offensive one.

The offensive potential is no longer theoretical. AI systems can already help researchers navigate enormous bodies of biological knowledge that once required years of specialized training. They can explain complex laboratory techniques, locate obscure scientific literature, troubleshoot technical problems and suggest experimental designs. None of these capabilities is inherently dangerous. Together, however, they lower the barrier to entering what was once a highly specialized field.

The greatest concern is that AIs can help humans create genuinely novel, or new, forms of biology. Scientists are already exploring these possibilities, from mirror-image life to organisms designed with capabilities that do not already exist in nature. Until recently, these possibilities were largely confined to theory or science fiction. Biology is unlike any other technology because what it produces can reproduce, spread across borders, mutate, and evolve on its own. A software bug crashes a computer. A biological mistake can become self-propagating. Once a living organism is released into the world, it cannot simply be switched off or recalled. That biological weapons are alive is what makes them fundamentally different from every other class of weapon, from the arrow to the ICBM.

The race has already begun. As I cover in my forthcoming book Biological War, and this recent New York Times article outlines, biological weapons have an extremely low barrier to entry. Unlike nuclear weapons, which require tightly controlled fissile material and complex delivery systems, biological weapons can be built with widely available laboratory tools, aided by increasingly powerful AI systems.

The technology to engineer life is advancing faster than the existing laws, treaties and safeguards meant to govern it. This widening gap is where existential danger lives. The point is pressure, not panic. We need to develop AI systems to strengthen public health, accelerate disease detection and help build biological defenses as quickly as AI is accelerating biological design. Because once biology outruns our ability to contain it, there is no recalling what has already been unleashed upon the world.

Annie Jacobsen is the author of Biological War, to be published on 28 July by Dutton. She also wrote the Pulitzer prize–finalist in history The Pentagon’s Brain and the New York Times bestsellers Nuclear War, Area 51 and Operation Paperclip

title: Boss of startup hacked by rogue OpenAI agent urges ‘radical transparency’ in investigation
description: Artificial intelligence firm should provide $100m for cyber defences, says Hugging Face...
fullText:
Artificial intelligence firm should provide $100m for cyber defences, says Hugging Face CEO

The boss of the startup hacked by an OpenAI agent has called for the investigation into the incident to show “radical transparency”.

Clément Delangue, the chief executive of Hugging Face, said the “unprecedented” attack on his business required a similar response.

Writing on X after OpenAI revealed that its technology had gone rogue during a cybersecurity test, Delangue also called on the company to provide $100m (£75m) worth of computing power to help build defences against such attacks.

“The first autonomous agent cyber-attack is an unprecedented event. It deserves an unprecedented response!” he wrote.

OpenAI revealed on Wednesday last week that Hugging Face had been hacked by an agent – an AI tool that can carry out a series of tasks autonomously – powered by a combination of its latest publicly available model, GPT-5.6 Sol, and an even more capable model that was yet to be released. This occurred during a test of the models’ hacking abilities, which included deploying them in a supposedly safe “sandbox” – an enclosed digital laboratory – with lower safety guardrails.

Once they had gained the open internet access needed to exit the sandbox, the models targeted Hugging Face, according to OpenAI, because they “inferred” the startup had the information needed to “cheat the evaluation”. Hugging Face first reported the hack on 16 July but at the time was not aware OpenAI had inadvertently carried out the attack.

Delangue, whose company provides a database of AI models to developers, called for a fully transparent review of the incident, which has led to expressions of concern over safety standards at OpenAI and within frontier AI labs.

Writing that he had asked for “radical transparency” from OpenAI, Delangue said: “Let’s release the traces from the ‘rogue’ agents so the entire research community can study what happened.” Calling for extra funding from OpenAI to build protection against AI, he added: “Let’s commit $100M in compute from OAI to help the Hugging Face community build powerful cyber defenses with the best open and closed models.”

Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at the University of Surrey, said Delangue’s call should be heeded.

“It’s too easy to ‘blame’ the AI as having gone rogue whereas this is all about how OpenAI were running the tool. What is required is that OpenAI give full details of their setup and how that failed,” he said.

OpenAI has been approached for comment.

title: Microsoft and Amazon Are Both Introducing New Cloud Gaming Options
description: Microsoft's is testing ad-supported Xbox cloud gaming, while Amazon Luna brings free streaming games to Fire TV.
fullText:
Two tech giants, Microsoft and Amazon, took steps last week to move gaming further into the cloud, with each company aiming at a different part of the (gigantic) gaming demographic.

Microsoft is testing a free (albeit ad-supported) cloud-gaming model for Xbox games. Starting today, gamers who signed up for Microsoft's Xbox Insider Program will be able to play games from their library that are cloud-compatible, without paying for a Game Pass Ultimate subscription. They will, however, have to watch ads at the beginning of the session. Microsoft is currently capping playtime at one hour per session; use up your time and you'll have to watch more ads. There's no word yet on how long the test will be running.

Meanwhile, Amazon announced it is going to embed its Luna cloud gaming service directly into Prime Video—but only if you have a Fire TV device. Fire TV users will see a dedicated "Games" tab next to "Movies," "TV shows" and "Sports." They will be able to play titles like Hogwarts Legacy, EA Sports FC 26 and Clue for the cost of their Prime membership.

The two companies clearly have different targets in mind. Microsoft is catering to the kind of "core" gamers who already own a library of titles but might want to play them on secondary devices like phones and laptops. Amazon is going after more casual gamers, and is trying to put their gaming offerings in front of as many eyeballs as possible. It plans to package its games on the same pages as the movie entries for well-known IP like Harry Potter, so someone might decide to play a little game with their remote before they watch a movie.

If you have an Xbox, here's how to check out some ad-supported cloud gaming.

Download the Xbox Insider Hub app on Xbox Series X|S, Xbox One, or Windows PC.

Enroll in the Xbox Insider Program. It's free.

That's it! Now you can stream select cloud-compatible games you own (after you check out some commercials, of course.)

If you have Prime, you can already try Luna. The company isn't adding any extra content for Fire TV users; it's just changing the way it presents the games it offers. Here's how to check it out.

First, you'll need a n Amazon Fire device. That means Fire TV stick, Fire TV Cube, or a smart TV running the Fire TV operating system.

On the main menu, you should see the new "Games" tab.

Click it and go to town. Pro tip: Play Indiana Jones and the Great Circle because it is fantastic.

You can play Luna games with any Bluetooth controller or use your phone as the controller.

title: How many midfielders do Rangers need after busy summer?
description: Rangers have a team full of central midfielders, but are they good enough to provide enough ammunition for their strikers?
fullText:
Cammy Devlin could not hide a wry smile when asked if he was confident of being a surefire starter for Rangers following his summer switch from last season's title rivals, Heart of Midlothian.

If the Australia 28-year-old did not know it before his return from the World Cup, his first couple of training sessions were a reminder of the plethora of players already competing for the central midfield berths with the Ibrox side.

And media questions at his first public press conference also emphasised the number of players in his position still being linked with a possible summer transfer to the Scottish Premiership club.

New manager Derek McInnes hopes to complete a couple more deals - not necessarily midfielders, though - before they start their season away to Dundee United in the top flight on Friday evening.

So who are Devlin's rivals in the Ibrox engine room?

McInnes teases Rangers signing within 48 hours

Who has your Premiership club brought in & let go this summer?

Devlin opens up on 'too stressful' Hearts exit for Rangers

Three of Rangers' seven summer signings - and none of their 11 departures - are central midfielders.

Yet they already had six on their books - nine if you include three who were out on loan.

Considering they are attacking midfielders, you can discount Thelo Aasgaard, who has just been to the World Cup with Norway, and Nedim Bajrami, who has failed to become a regular starter in his two years at Ibrox, as competition for the more defensively minded Devlin.

Likewise, Jose Cifuentes, Lyall Cameron and 20-year-old Paul Nsio, considering they have returned from Toronto, Aberdeen and Raith Rovers, respectively, without having suggested they are ready to make the step up.

Ivory Coast international Mohamed Diomande, whose form dipped in his second full season at Ibrox, is more a box-to-box man.

Meanwhile, Nicolas Raskin has looked more effective pushing forward for Rangers despite preferring to play just in front of the defence.

It was, though, in that latter role that the Belgium international received rave reviews at the World Cup, making it ever more likely that Rangers will look to cash in this summer on a player who has expressed his desire to move to a top-five league.

Given Raskin's anticipated exit, it was no surprise McInnes would look to snap up Devlin given the Australian was a key player in their title challenge together with Hearts - especially as he was available for free.

However, Rangers have also added two more defensive midfielders - Dan Neil, who was out of contract with Sunderland, and Vanja Dragojevic, purchased from Partizan, where he was captain at the age of just 20.

That is before considering two more defensive midfielders already on Rangers' books.

Scotland cap Connor Barron must have been relishing the arrival of his former Aberdeen manager as he seeks more regular starts, while Tochi Chukwuani is still bedding in after his January arrival from Sturm Graz.

Meanwhile, Rangers continue to be linked with a current Sturm Graz defensive midfielder, Ryan Fosso.

At least Jens Hjerto-Dahl, for whom Rangers have reportedly had bids rejected by Tromso, is more attack minded.

No wonder Devlin insists he is taking nothing for granted despite his close relationship with McInnes.

"It is a massive challenge when you come to a club of this size with a history of winning," he said.

"Not that at Hearts I expected to play every week - that definitely wasn't the case.

"There will definitely be challenges. There's a lot of great midfielders.

"I've only just been here a couple of days training with the boys, but the quality in the squad, which I already knew because I played against them, is really high."

Devlin was asked if he was surprised Rangers continue to be linked with midfielders.

"It's normal to be linked with good players that are costing a lot of money," he said.

"If you come here and don't expect that, you're probably not in the right head space."

Devlin had been offered a new contract to extend his five years at Tynecastle and had options elsewhere, including Major League Soccer.

However, when McInnes moved to Ibrox, the same man who had been trying to persuade him to stay at Hearts was able to convince him to move along the M8 despite potentially greater competition for a starting place.

"I've never got anywhere in life without just fighting as hard as I can," Devlin said.

"It wasn't easy to get here. The same as the national team - it's hard to get there, but it's even harder to stay there.

"That's something I pride myself on - my hard work, treating every training session and every game like it might be my last."

It was Devlin who anchored the midfield, with Diomande and Aasgaard in front, in Rangers' final pre-season friendly - a goalless draw with West Ham United on Sunday.

No matter who wins the battle for places, former Rangers midfielder Andy Halliday questions whether his former club have so far improved in that area of the pitch.

"Last season, there was a real lack of creativity from midfield," he told BBC Radio Scotland's Sportsound.

"They have 11 midfielders at the club right now and, for me, none of them can dictate a game.

"They are all very much in the same mould, dogged out of possession, tidy players, but none that can score goals or create chances."

For that reason, Halliday expects McInnes to add to his midfield further.

"They still have so much business to do," he added.

"The manager has got characters in to improve the mentality and then they can sprinkle a bit of stardust with the next three or four signings."

However, speaking after the Ibrox draw with West Ham, McInnes hinted it would be a yet-to-be signed winger to whom he would look to provide extra ammunition for his strikers.

"The one area of the pitch we are really strong is through the middle of the park just now," he said.

"Nico will be back this week, but after so many games played and his World Cup exploits, we never planned for Nico to be back for Dundee United - but I've got good options in there and it's an area we are particularly strong."

title: O'Donoghue's 'pride and relief' after banishing ghosts of 2021
description: Ryan O'Donoghue tells the BBC of his "pride and relief" after starring in Mayo's All-Ireland win five years after missing a penalty in the final.
fullText:
Mayo's emotional All-Ireland triumph on Sunday brought a collective release to everyone associated with the county, but victory on Gaelic football's biggest day also provided Ryan O'Donoghue a measure of redemption.

In the 2021 final, O'Donoghue missed a penalty that would have given Mayo the lead over Tyrone in the second half.

While O'Donoghue top-scored on the day with 0-8, Tyrone won the game, leaving the spot-kick failure - which came 12 months after the 2020 final loss to Dublin - to eat away at him for five years before he got another crack at the final.

And against Kerry on Sunday, the 27-year-old set the tone for a furious Mayo performance as he pressed and hassled the Kingdom defence from the first minute in a man of the match performance.

"The two main emotions are pride and relief," he told The GAA Social.

"After 2020 and 2021, if I'm being honest, I was never over 2021 until about a half-hour ago [at full-time on Sunday].

"Now I'm an All-Ireland champion, we're All-Ireland champions and I'm over it. I'm a firm believer that everything happens for a reason.

"There are a lot of things that have happened in the past couple of years on the pitch - 2020, 2021 and the Roscommon game [a 10-point loss in this year's Connacht semi-final]. I don't think today would have happened if we didn't go through those things."

Pride and emotion as Mayo end 75-year wait for glory

Mayo beat Kerry in thriller to end 75-year All-Ireland wait

O'Donoghue, who made his senior inter-county debut in 2020, had enjoyed a superb season for Andy Moran's side prior to Sunday's final.

But his indefatigable display - in which he scored 0-5 and launched the move that ended with Darragh Beirne's 40th-minute goal - has installed him as the frontrunner for the Footballer of the Year award (he would be the first Mayo winner since Moran in 2017).

It would be a remarkable achievement for a multi-talented sportsman, who fought in two All-Ireland boxing finals in his youth and played for the Republic of Ireland soccer team at underage level.

And like so many of his team-mates, Belmullet club-man O'Donoghue was able to savour the epic celebrations at Croke Park with his family, including his father Michael and County Down-born mother Brenda.

"What my mother and father have done for me since I was 11 years of age. Boxing, my dad used to leave at 4 o'clock in the morning to take me to Dublin to the National Stadium for Ireland training," explained O'Donoghue.

"Up and down the road to Castlebar when I was playing Kennedy Cup with Mayo, up and down the road, under-14, Minor. It's a long journey from Castlebar to Belmullet.

"My father worked two jobs. I was playing with Sligo Rovers 2014 to 2016. I didn't get paid, we had to pay our own diesel. There were bills to be paid and my father worked to get me up and down the road to Sligo.

"They've given me every opportunity, whether it's boxing, soccer or Gaelic. This is for them. That's the pride and the emotions in mum and dad. I'm so happy to have repaid them. There's been so many sacrifices. I'm so glad we've done it."

title: How do you score points in artistic gymnastics?
description: Our Ask Me Anything team looks at how athletes can score big in artistic gymnastics.
fullText:
It's been a strong start for Team Scotland in the 2026 Commonwealth Games artistic gymnastics, with Reuben Ward making history by winning the nation's first ever gold medal in the men's all-around.

England also clinched bronze with Wales in fourth place in the women's all-around team event.

And there could be many more medals to come for the home nations this week, with several individual events taking place.

As one of only two events at this year's Games where winners are decided solely by judges applying a scoring scale - the other being boxing - how are points allocated to gymnasts to separate the medallists from the rest?

Firstly, it's important to note that men and women compete in slightly different events across artistic gymnastics.

This applies to both individual and all-around disciplines, meaning in the men's all-around contest athletes are judged on six events, and for the women's all-around the scores are based on four events.

Women are judged on their top eight highest-scoring skills, and men on 10.

There is further variation when women receive marks for 'artistry' on floor and beam, including 'expression, confidence and personal style' incorporated into the routine and a varied tempo throughout.

Men are not scored under such criteria, especially as the floor event contains no music, but can still add in elements to show originality and creativity.

The women's vault event also has the apparatus set to a lower height than the men's.

Like many judged sports, there are two main factors to balance when scoring an artistic gymnastics routine - difficulty and execution.

The two scales being used to allocate points are the 'D-score' for difficulty and the 'E-score' for execution, each having a dedicated panel of multinational judges who have been approved by the International Gymnastics Federation (FIG).

The scores produced by each of these panels - following any 'neutral deductions' - are then combined to give the gymnast a final score, either as a standalone result for the individual events or a combined score across multiple events for the all-around contests.

The biggest difference between how the two scores are decided upon is that the Difficulty Score starts at zero and racks up depending on how challenging the routine is deemed to be - with no upper limit to the scoring.

However, the question with E-Scores should perhaps be 'how are points lost' instead of 'how are points scored', as each athletes begins their routine with a perfect 10 which decreases as mistakes are made.

Points are deducted in increments of 0.1, 0.3, 0.5:

0.1 points deducted for small errors such as a minor loss of balance

0.3 points deducted for medium errors like significant loss of balance

0.5 points deducted for large errors – deep squats on landing an example

1.0 point deducted for major errors such as falls

D-Scores arise from predetermined values set for different elements in the FIG Code of Points, set from difficulty ratings A through to H-J.

For example, the Code of Points allocates 0.1 points for A-grade 'basic' skills such as a forward roll or handstand, and up to 0.8-1.0 points for H-J grade 'exceptional' named pioneering moves.

There are also difficulty points available for the composition of the routine showing balance of skill types, and connection points for how well the skills are linked together to produce a flowing display.

The only exception to the dual E-Score and D-Score system is the vault event, where each routine has a pre-determined D-Score and so only the E-Score is judged.

Neutral deductions are applied to the combined E and D-Scores, and take into account errors unrelated to the routine itself.

These include stepping out of bounds, going over allocated routine time, or outfit violations.

For a medal-winning result, athletes will be aiming for points in at least the 14s and into the 15s.

A world-class routine may reach into the high 15s or low 16s.

For example, during her dominance of the 2016 Olympics, US gymnast Simone Biles scored 15.866 on vault, 14.966 on uneven bars, 15.433 on balance beam, and 15.933 on floor exercise to produce an overall score of 62.198 for the gold medal, which was more than two points clear of the runner-up.

Artistic gymnastic team events are judged on the same basis as individual events, but the scores are spread slightly differently.

At least two athletes from a nation take part in each apparatus event, with individual scores added together for the overall team score.

If three athletes take part in any of the disciplines, the two highest-scoring routines count towards the team's overall score.

title: Robertson receives first Scotland call-up as Ihsan & Jones return
description: Lyle Robertson receives a first senior Scotland call-up for August's ICC Men's Cricket World Cup League 2 series against Canada and the United Arab Emirates.
fullText:
Lyle Robertson has received a first senior Scotland call-up for August's ICC Men's Cricket World Cup League 2 series against Canada and the United Arab Emirates.

Falkland's Robertson is one of three changes to the squad that toured Nepal in May, with Zainullah Ihsan and Michael Jones also returning.

Meanwhile, Michael Leask drops out, while the injured duo of Brad Currie and Owen Gould are unavailable.

"It's great to welcome back Zainullah Ihsan and Michael Jones to the squad for this series," said Scotland head coach Owen Dawkins.

"Zainullah has shown excellent progress across the summer with his performances in training, in club cricket for GHK and in regional cricket with Western Warriors.

"Michael missed our previous two tours due to his Lancashire commitments, so it's exciting to have a player of his quality available again for a home series.

"We're also pleased to award a first senior international call-up to Lyle Robertson. As a young player he represented Scotland at the ICC Under-19 World Cup in the Caribbean and since then he's continued to show steady development."

The upcoming series will be Scotland's final CWCL2 fixtures, taking place at Forthill in Broughty Ferry.

The Scots currently sit second in the table, alongside the Netherlands, and are five points behind leaders United States.

ITV will show next year's Rugby World Cup in Australia, extending the broadcaster's coverage of the tournament to a 10th successive edition.

All 52 matches from the event, which features 24 teams and a last-16 knockout round, will be shown live.

"This is much more than a new agreement with a trusted partner, it is a statement of intent to ensure that everyone in the UK can experience and be inspired by one of the world's iconic sporting events, its action, drama and personalities," said World Rugby chief executive Alan Gilpin.

The broadcaster, a rights holder for every men's World Cup since the 1991 edition, has previously secured the 2026 and 2028 editions of the new Nations Championship, and the majority of Six Nations fixtures up to and including the 2029 tournament in a shared-rights deal with BBC Sport.

ITV will show every England men's game currently scheduled until summer 2029, while Scotland, Wales and Ireland's matches will also be free-to-air in the United Kingdom over the same period.

title: Pirlo out of running for Italy job over link to Russian betting company
description: Andrea Pirlo says he is no longer a candidate to coach Italy following days of controversy over his link to a Russian betting company.
fullText:
Andrea Pirlo has said he is no longer a candidate to coach the Italian national side following days of controversy over his ties to a Russian betting company.

His appointment as Italy's next head coach had not been confirmed by the Italian Football Federation (FIGC) yet was being treated as all but certain.

But over the weekend several Italian politicians criticised the FIGC's choice, noting that Pirlo, 47, had taken up a role as global ambassador for Russia's Fonbet last October.

The betting company has sponsored several sporting events involving veterans of Moscow's war in Ukraine and has organised events in Russia at which Pirlo appeared alongside pro-Kremlin figures.

"Anyone who is or has been promoting Russia after 2022 should not hold national office," said Carlo Calenda of the centrist Azione party.

"After learning last night that I am no longer a candidate for the Italian national team, I feel it is my duty to clarify some aspects," Pirlo, a former Internazionale, Juventus, AC Milan and Azzurri midfielder, wrote in an Instagram post on Monday morning.

"Over the last few days I watched, with great bitterness, the debate that swirled around my name," he said, adding that any "professional collaboration" he undertook in his capacity as coach for United FC in Dubai "was exclusively of a commercial and sporting nature".

"To assign a political meaning to that collaboration means ascribing to me beliefs which I have never expressed and that do not belong to me," Pirlo wrote.

Pina Picierno, a vice-president of the European Parliament, said at the weekend that Italian football "desperately needed a cultural, ethical and managerial revolution" but that the choice of Pirlo "goes in the exact opposite direction".

In contrast, Pirlo was offered support by the Russian ambassador in Rome, Aleksey Paramonov, who said that it was "saddening" to note that, "despite [Pirlo's] extraordinary contribution to world sport and to Italy's image around the world, in your own country, you are now being ostracized".

Scrutiny of Pirlo's ties to Fonbet and Russia intensified last spring, when he took part in a Fonbet event held in Moscow, which saw him and former teammate Marco Materazzi sign autographs at Luzhniki Stadium.

Nationalist pro-Kremlin pop star Shaman, who has repeatedly expressed his support for the Russian invasion of Ukraine, also performed at the event.

At the time, Ukrainian skeleton slider Vladyslav Heraskevych - who was disqualified from the Winter Olympics over his helmet depicting fellow athletes killed in the war - noted the Luzhniki event had taken place on the same day as a large Russian attack on Ukraine.

Heraskevych also criticised Pirlo for appearing next to Russian footballer Artem Dzyuba, who in the wake of the war in Ukraine posted on social media that he was "proud to be Russian".

"It's sad to see childhood legends turn into moral bankrupts," Heraskevych said.

The debate now risks engulfing new FIGC technical director Paolo Maldini, who has only been in post since 11 July and who Italian media say may resign over Pirlo's failed appointment.

Maldini and his adviser, former AC Milan teammate Leonardo, were tasked with finding a new head coach to navigate Italy through a Nations League group that includes France, Belgium and Turkey in the autumn and then try to qualify for Euro 2028.

The Italian football community has been undergoing much soul-searching after the team failed to qualify for a third World Cup earlier this year. Italy's loss on penalties to Bosnia-Herzegovina in April led to coach Gennaro Gattuso stepping down as well as a reshuffle of the FIGC echelons.

Earlier this month, Pep Guardiola and Carlo Ancelotti were both unsuccessfully approached ahead of Pirlo.

According to Italian media, other names currently being considered are Antonio Conte and Roberto Mancini - who led Italy to Euro 2020 glory before failing to qualify for the World Cup in Qatar and unceremoniously stepping down from the Italy bench to coach Saudi Arabia.

title: Kalpana's King George win 'number one' for Balding
description: British trainer Andrew Balding won £1.3m in two hours on Sunday as Kalpana took UK racing's biggest prize fund.
fullText:
British trainer Andrew Balding labelled his King George VI & Queen Elizabeth stakes race victory with Kalpana at Royal Ascot as "number one" of the 2,000 career winners he has registered.

After finishing second 12 months prior, Kalpana held off a surge by last year's winner Calandagan to win by one and a half lengths on Saturday.

The Kingsclere trainer was in no doubt where the win ranked in his illustrious 25 years of training.

"This is probably number one and It is an emotional win for lots of reasons," Balding told BBC Radio Berkshire.

"She [Kalpana] is a high-class filly and deserved her moment to win a race like this, it's a big deal as she's been with us a long time and everyone is so fond of her.

"We actually thought the field this year was stronger than last year, so I'd have probably settled for third."

The filly beat off the best from around the world over a mile and a half with the win coming six months after the death of Balding's father, legendary trainer Ian Balding.

He won the prestigious race in 1971 with Mill Reef and the Park House Stables in Hampshire have now produced a second King George winner.

Turning the tables on French-trained Calandagan was especially sweet for the 53-year-old trainer.

The win, combined with Item's win at York in a Group Two race, catapults Balding up in the trainer's title race, within striking distance of leader Aiden O'Brien.

Balding won £1.3m in just under two hours, as the King George is the UK's most valuable race of the year.

Kalpana is expected to feature in the Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe in October.

title: Record Spurs spend shows new ambition - Van de Ven
description: Micky van de Ven says Tottenham's record spending highlights a "new ambition" after an "unacceptable" season.
fullText:
Micky van de Ven says Tottenham's record spending highlights a "new ambition" after an "unacceptable" season - and backed the team to play "more enjoyable" football under Roberto de Zerbi.

Tottenham have finished 17th in the Premier League in back-to-back years and only narrowly avoided relegation on the final day of last season.

Under De Zerbi, who was appointed in late March, Spurs have spent a club record £237m this summer.

Defender Van de Ven is in talks over a new contract, having joined Tottenham in 2023 on a six-year deal.

"It's really good that you can see the club has made some changes," the 25-year-old told BBC Sport in Sydney, where the club are on their pre-season tour.

"You can see the club has a new ambition. It's something that's really important for players who have been here for a long time.

"Last season was a stressful season, unacceptable from our side, so to leave all of that behind and go into the new season fresh means a lot."

Richarlison scores as Spurs beat Auckland at Eden Park

Unhappy Tottenham players should leave - De Zerbi

Tottenham had three managers last season, with Thomas Frank managing less than eight months in charge before being sacked after a dismal start to the season.

Interim manager Igor Tudor left the club after 44 days before De Zerbi took over with seven games of the season remaining.

Frank struggled to connect with the Tottenham fans and was criticised for playing with a "safety-first" approach.

Van de Ven believes De Zerbi will have the team playing better football, helped by the new signings and a full pre-season to drill the squad.

"It's going to be different compared to the manager we had last season," Van de Ven said.

"It's going to be more with the ball, I think, more about playing football. I think it's also going to be more enjoyable for people to watch because we'll be playing offensive football.

"You can see he [De Zerbi] has brought a lot of passion into our group, a lot in terms of mentality and passion on the pitch.

"It is something we needed because everybody was a little bit down.

"He brings a lot of good energy and, from pre-season, we have really had the time to bring his football into the team. That's really enjoyable."

Earlier this month Spurs broke their transfer record twice in two days, first signing midfielder Mateus Fernandes from West Ham for £85m before bringing in Sandro Tonali from Newcastle for £100m.

Jan Paul van Hecke, Van de Ven's Netherlands team-mate, has also joined from Brighton in a £52m deal, alongside the free transfers of experienced trio Marcos Senesi, Andrew Robertson and Martin Dubravka.

"The feeling of the team is really good, to be honest," Van de Ven added.

"I have really enjoyed working with him [De Zerbi]. That's what we have been doing in this pre-season, and the guys who are coming in have been unbelievable as well.

"They have fit in well to the group."

title: York appoint Lindsey after shock Maynard sacking
description: York City appoint former Crawley Town boss Scott Lindsey as their new head coach, one day after sacking title-winning Stuart Maynard.
fullText:
York City have appointed former Crawley Town boss Scott Lindsey as their new head coach, one day after sacking title-winning manager Stuart Maynard.

Maynard led the Minstermen to promotion as National League champions last season but was relieved of his duties on Sunday because of what the board called a "difference in direction and vision for the football club".

Lindsey, 54, took Crawley up to League One in his first spell in charge in 2024 but his second spell was brought to an end in March after a 10-game winless run in League Two left them one point above the relegation zone.

His first game as York boss will be against his former side in an EFL Cup preliminary tie on Monday, 3 August.

Maynard was appointed in August last year when York's owners Matt and Julie-Anne Uggla sacked Adam Hinshelwood, who had led them to second place in 2024-25 and had the team unbeaten from their first five games.

However, the decision was ultimately vindicated last season as Maynard guided the club to the National League title with 108 points and ended their 10-year EFL exile.

They won the division with a dramatic last-minute equaliser at Rochdale - who would have taken the sole automatic promotion spot instead.

York described Lindsey, who has also had stints in charge of Swindon Town and MK Dons, as having "a vast wealth of experience working across the EFL".

He will be assisted by Joao Alves, while Gary Elphick, who worked under both Hinshelwood and Maynard, will stay on as first team coach.

York start the League Two season with a home game against Bristol Rovers on Saturday, 15 August.

title: England's Langton feared for gymnastics future after fall
description: England's Gabriel Langton says he feared for his future in gymnastics after his horror fall at the Commonwealth Games.
fullText:
England's Gabriel Langton said he feared for his future in gymnastics after his horror fall at the Commonwealth Games, but will "definitely be back to it" soon.

The 19-year-old spent 20 hours in a neck brace before being discharged from hospital, having fallen from three metres directly on to his head in Friday's competition.

Langton said it was a move on the high bars he had competed "1,000 times and it is once that has happened".

He said he initially felt frustrated and embarrassed before coming to realise the severity of the situation.

"I knew I could speak and move my fingers and toes so my main thing was 'hopefully I can do gymnastics again'," Langton told the BBC.

"That question was in my head for the 20 hours until I got the MRI scan results. That was eating away at me."

Langton's scans showed swelling and bruising, results which meant he was allowed to leave hospital on Saturday night.

"A little bit sore and a little bit stiff but that is to be expected," he said of his condition.

"I can't really complain too much."

Before his fall, Langton was attempting to move into a handstand position on the high bar but lost his grip and fell head first on to the mat.

There was a lengthy delay to the competition before Langton was taken away on a trolley and then a stretcher.

"Once I went up and both hands have left the bar that is not the best," he said.

"From that moment, I knew 'oh this isn't going to be comfortable'."

The England team went on to secure a silver medal behind Canada in the competition.

The teenager did not receive his medal until he returned to the team hotel on Saturday evening, with the other members of the team gathering to applaud him.

"That was incredible," he said.

"Seeing all of the team-mates, coaches and getting my medal. I saw my personal coach from Birmingham. It was so nice."

With no further competition of his own, Langton was back in the arena on Sunday to support team-mates in the men's all-around final.

He said he will "take it easy for a couple of days and do the rehab" before returning to training in the near future.

"I trust in my gymnastics capability," he said.

"It was really just a freak accident."

title: Brighton captain Symonds signs new 'long-term' deal
description: Brighton captain Maisie Symonds signs a new contract, described by the club as long-term.
fullText:
Brighton captain Maisie Symonds has signed a new contract, described by the club as long-term.

The 23-year-old midfielder, who joined from Chelsea in 2021, is Albion's longest-serving player and has made 103 appearances in all competitions.

Head coach Dario Vidosic said: "Maisie is a massive influence both on and off the pitch and since becoming captain last season she has developed both as a player and as a person.

Former Brighton keeper Baggaley joins Birmingham

What's working - and what's not - for WSL fans?

Brighton reached the Women's FA Cup final at Wembley for the first time in May, with Symonds skippering the side against Manchester City.

Symonds has represented England up to under-21 level and received her first senior call-up in March 2025.

On signing her new deal, she added: "I'm very happy. I feel so at home here. It's the only club I've ever played for professionally and I feel I've grown so much over the last six years along with the club and the women's team.

"It really felt like we are setting high standards for ourselves with what we've been building in the last two years.

title: Real Madrid contract talks and Arsenal interest - what is Vinicius Jr's future?
description: With Real Madrid renewing contract talks and Arsenal showing interest, there may be no more intriguing transfer situation right now than Vinicius Jr's future.
fullText:
There may be no more intriguing situation in the transfer landscape right now than Vinicius Jr's future.

The Real Madrid forward is unquestionably one of the most high-profile footballers on the planet.

The Brazil international joined Real as an 18-year-old in 2018, winning 14 trophies and scoring 128 goals in 375 matches for the Spanish giants.

To think they have allowed him to enter the final year of his contract is perplexing - but that is where we are.

In normal circumstances, according to industry sources, Vinicius' market value would exceed £200m.

On the pitch, that amount of money would get you a world class left-winger who is also adept at playing centrally, as well as a player who, aged 26, is reaching his peak years.

Off the pitch, you would be signing a global icon whose commercial value would be financially lucrative.

What now for Vinicius Jr after Mourinho signs Real Madrid deal?

Has Vinicius Jr brilliance just papered over the Brazilian cracks?

Real Madrid have tried to renew their attacker's contract and opened further talks with him on Monday - but, as of yet, to no avail.

His potential availability has alerted Arsenal, who are among the clubs to have internally explored exploiting the contractual impasse. Teams in Saudi Arabia are also monitoring his situation closely.

Gunners manager Mikel Arteta wants to sign proven talent - and Vinicius fits the bill.

Sources close to Arsenal insist he is just one of a number of options the club are exploring in their search for a left-sided attacker, after missing out on Morgan Rogers to Chelsea.

However, BBC Sport understands Arteta has become so smitten with the notion of signing Vinicius that he is viewed internally as the club's number one target.

As Arsenal discovered with Rogers, there are no guarantees clubs attract their priority targets.

Indeed, Arsenal are realistic about their chances of landing Vinicius Jr. They know it is a long shot.

Similarly, there is a sense from those close to Vinicius Jr that any move to Arsenal would be difficult.

For most South American footballers, playing for Real Madrid or Barcelona is a lifelong ambition. Leaving the Spanish capital - even for a club as illustrious at Arsenal - would be viewed as, at best, a sidewards step.

With Real being arguably the biggest club on the planet, there is a sense that leaving the Bernabeu would also impact the player's commercial brand.

Talks over a new Real deal for Vinicius are expected to ramp up in the coming days.

It is claimed the forward is still very receptive to renewing at the Bernabeu but "wants to feel loved". Recent reports have stated that new manager Jose Mourinho wants to keep all his big names at the club.

But there is serious jeopardy for Real if they keep Vinicius without renegotiating his contract. The scenario of the Brazilian leaving for nothing in 2027 would represent a financial catastrophe, even for a club as cash rich as them.

With that in mind, resolving the situation one way or another is understandably viewed as a priority for Real before the transfer deadline.

As it stands Vinicius can start speaking to rival clubs about a free transfer move away from Real at the turn of the year. Leaving on a free will be far more lucrative in terms of wages to the attacker than leaving this summer, when the buying club has to find a transfer fee.

Additionally, how much would Real demand for Vinicius?

Their move for Eden Hazard seven years ago may provide us with clues. The club signed the Belgian in 2019 in a deal worth up to £130m. He was 28 at the time and in the final year of his contract at Chelsea.

Vinicius is two years younger and has a commercial value that exceeds Hazard's - and that is not to mention the seven-year cost of inflation.

It is clear that Arsenal would almost certainly need to obliterate the British transfer record of £125m, from Alexander Isak's move from Newcastle to Liverpool last summer.

Then there are Vinicius' wages to factor in. Reports suggest he earns in the region of £450,000 a week at Real Madrid, although sources indicate it is considerably more.

At Arsenal, that would immediately make him the club's top earner by some distance, with Bukayo Saka currently earning up to £400,000-a-week.

But, with Vinicius a year away from his Real contract expiring, it is not simply a case of merely matching - or even slightly improving - his money if he was to leave this summer.

The nature of free transfers means Vinicius could conceivably double his money next year.

With that scenario now within reach, it is safe to assume the forward will almost certainly request a significant pay increase if he moves this summer.

Having to find what is likely to be a minimum £130m plus wages will be a hard push for any club, no matter how rich, in the era of financial regulation.

Arsenal, nevertheless, have analysed the numbers and believe they have the financial means to fund a move for Vinicius. It is understood the signing has widespread backing across the club.

In the past, Arsenal have offered players very generous image rights deals. This would be a key component of any agreement to take Vinicius to the Premier League.

The winger's advisors at agency Roc Nation will be fully aware of these factors.

The fact Roc Nation also represent Arsenal attacker Gabriel Martinelli - whose chances would be left severely limited by Vinicius' arrival - also makes for an intriguing subplot.

It is understood that Martinelli, who has up to two years left on his contract, is happy at Arsenal and will only consider leaving for an opportunity that suits him.

Effectively, the leverage is almost entirely with Vinicius.

Arsenal are unquestionably one of the most attractive projects in European football. They will be one of the favourites to lift the Champions League next season, having lost on penalties in last season's final. They are in a very strong financial position, too.

But a move to north London would require Vinicius to relinquish the sort of leverage that most players, even of his standing, do not have.

Perhaps most importantly of all, it would mean him giving up on being a Real Madrid footballer.

Is he prepared to do that? We should have the answer soon.

title: English football agrees trial to end goalkeeper tactical timeouts
description: English football is set to implement a radical trial to try to eradicate the goalkeeper tactical timeout this season, BBC Sport can reveal.
fullText:
English football is set to implement a trial to try to eradicate the goalkeeper tactical timeout this season, BBC Sport can reveal.

The Football Association, Premier League, English Football League, National League and Women's Super League have agreed on the measure, pending permission from the International Football Association Board (Ifab).

Earlier this year, Ifab decided against changing the law and invited leagues to volunteer for trials.

Pro Ref, led by chief refereeing officer Howard Webb, has been in discussions with the leagues to determine how to tackle the issue. It settled on a team having to remove an outfield player from the field.

If a referee signals that the physio can come on to treat a goalkeeper, the coach will have 10 seconds to nominate another player to leave the pitch for one minute, telling the fourth official of their choice.

If no player has been selected within 10 seconds, the captain must leave the field.

If clearance is received by the Ifab in time, the first game to feature the trial will be the Carabao Cup preliminary round tie between Tranmere and Rochdale on Saturday, 1 August.

BBC Sport understands that the Australian A-League will trial a variation with the captain always having to leave the field.

The tactic of gaining a timeout as the keeper is treated has become increasingly common and controversial in recent seasons.

It has not been uncommon for the goalkeeper to sit on the turf and signal for the physio, with all the other players rushing to the technical area for a team talk. As soon as the coach has delivered their instructions, the keeper gets up to play on.

Goalkeeper treatment has also been used to disrupt the opposition's momentum when they are on top.

In November, Leeds United boss Daniel Farke accused Manchester City goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma of feigning injury to "bend the rules" and break up play.

At the Ifab's AGM in February, head of referees Pierluigi Collina said that finding a solution to stop the goalkeeper tactical timeout was a priority.

At the 2026 World Cup, Collina told his officials to prevent players from going to the technical area on all stoppages.

The effectiveness of the measure is open to debate, as the three-minute hydration breaks in each half created a natural opportunity for a team talk.

In its own discussions, English football felt that merely stopping players going to the technical area would not deter coaches from using goalkeepers to break up play.

English football chose this trial as it follows the logic applied to outfield players, who must themselves leave the field for one minute if the physio comes on.

It is intended to be proactive as a deterrent rather than reactive to a team talk as it happens.

Match of the Day pundit Danny Murphy suggested last season that lawmakers could act to close the loophole in this exact way.

"I think they can change it really quickly," Murphy said. "If a keeper goes down injured, instead of him having to go off, one of the outfield players should go off then it's fair all round.

"It's a little change that makes a world of difference."

Officials will not prevent players from visiting the touchline as an injury is treated but it is hoped the prospect of playing with 10 players for a minute will act as an adequate disincentive.

This is especially the case in the final minutes of games, when teams trying to hold on to a result would use the goalkeeper to kill momentum. Now they would have to play with 10 players.

There are a few exemptions when a team-mate will not have to go off.

Where a goalkeeper says they do not need the physio and they have not caused play to stop

The goalkeeper and an outfield player have collided

If a goalkeeper is fouled and needs immediate treatment

If there is a serious injury (has to be substituted) or concussion.

There have been some concerns that a requirement to leave the field for one minute could lead to players, both goalkeepers and outfield, attempting to play on with an injury.

The results of the trials will be assessed by Ifab at its meetings throughout the seasons, and this could lead to a permanent law change globally from 2027-28.

title: Second again - why has Scheffler stopped winning?
description: World number one Scottie Scheffler has not won a tournament since January, but what's the reason?
fullText:
It has been six months since world number one Scottie Scheffler won a golf tournament.

Given he earned 14 victories over the previous two seasons, it is a drought few could have conceived when he triumphed at the American Express Open on 27 January 2026.

The four majors have passed without a Scheffler victory - he won both the US PGA Championship and The Open in 2025 - while two weeks ago he missed his first cut in 78 events, ending the longest unbroken streak on the PGA Tour.

On Sunday, he was runner-up in Minnesota to PGA Tour rookie Jackson Koivun.

So is the world's best player past his peak?

Was it mere hyperbole to compare him favourably with Tiger Woods when he was racking up the victories on tour?

Or does his consistency suggest the floodgates are about to re-open?

Woods comparisons continue after Scheffler wins again

How 'Tiger-like' Scheffler is conquering golf

At the top of his powers, Scheffler, 30, is a front-running machine.

Of his 20 victories on tour, 75% have come when he has held the lead going into the final round, albeit his most recent three victories have been when trailing after 54 holes.

This season however, he has not even been joint leader after the third round and therefore always been chasing on a Sunday.

Take the 3M Open this weekend. He shot an eight-under 63 to finish second behind exciting new talent Koivun, but was still three shots back.

Twice in 2026 he has lost in a play-off, to Matt Fitzpatrick and Viktor Hovland. Both times Scheffler trailed going into round four and duly reeled in the leader, only to fall short on the extra hole.

Early in his career, Scheffler coughed up the lead after 54 holes a number of times, including when leading Rory McIlroy by six shots at the Tour Championship in 2022.

Since then, when in front with 18 to play, he has ruthlessly converted. This season, he has not given himself that chance.

Failing to put everything together at once?

At his best, there is an inevitability to Scheffler winning - but over the course of any tournament, a dip in one element can cost him.

For instance, The Open at Royal Birkdale was won brilliantly by New Zealand's Ryan Fox but, if Scheffler's putter had worked during the week, he would have reclaimed the title he took at Royal Portrush last year.

In his second round alone, he missed seven birdie putts from 15 feet or less - four inside 10 feet - and was ranked 60th in the field on the greens.

It is an Achilles' heel that has dogged Scheffler before, but the PGA Tour has him as fifth-best putter, external on tour in 2026 - so it is certainly not a problem every week.

Or perhaps slow starts are costing him. On nine occasions this season, including at the Masters and the US Open, he has begun with a round of 70 or over, leaving himself playing catch-up for the rest of the tournament.

A glance at Scheffler's record shows metronomic consistency across all facets of his game.

Winning a golf tournament is just really, really hard to do.

How Fox kept cool at baked Birkdale to win The Open

Winning does not matter to him?

Before The Open, Scheffler doubled down on previous comments he had made about there being "more to life than playing golf".

Despite being ranked as the world's best player for more than three years, the Texan told reporters the thought of making history "just isn't that important".

A devout Christian and now with two young children, Scheffler has made it clear he would happily walk away from the game if it harmed his family life.

However, before speculating that such a perspective would harm his competitive edge, it is worth evaluating the on-course demeanour of a player who is expressive when his game is not going as well as he would like.

Any suggestion Scheffler does not care about winning would be dismissed within seconds by his caddie Ted Scott, who said earlier this year:, external "If Scheffler was playing a nine-year-old girl in ping pong, he would want to beat her 21-nothing!"

If wins are the only currency, both Matt Fitzpatrick and Cameron Young have three on tour this season, while Wyndham Clark has a regular victory and a US Open.

But a glance at the FedEx Cup's season-long rankings reassert Scheffler's dominance.

Players are awarded points for where they finish in a tournament - and Scheffler has 795 more than Fitzpatrick in second.

That is because even though he has not win since January, he has done everything but.

Sunday's second place at the 3M Open was his fifth runners-up finish - only the second golfer in 40 years to have at least five second places in a season on the PGA Tour.

He has also finished third on two occasions, and in the top five 11 times across 17 starts in 2026. It is a body of work that dwarfs anything put together by his rivals.

"I think I've been really close to winning some tournaments and that can be frustrating," Scheffler said before the Scottish Open.

"At the same time, I've had some good results - a fourth and a second are not bad results by any means. Margins in golf are really small and I just keep trying to do my best."

The lack of wins has not prevented him stretching his lead at the top of the Official World Golf rankings, external either.

In fact, the distance between him and second-placed Rory McIlroy is equivalent to between McIlroy and America's Matt McCarty (in 67th).

Scheffler has been world number one since 21 May 2023 - nearly 166 weeks. Woods' unbroken record stands at 281 weeks, between June 2005 and October 2010.

That intimidating record is still more than two years off for Scheffler, but current evidence suggests knocking him off top spot will be extraordinarily difficult.

title: Jaguars 53-man roster projection as training camp approaches
description: How will the Jaguars' 53-man roster shake out? We take a look ahead of the start of training camp.
fullText:
Training camp is around the corner.

The Jacksonville Jaguars will soon be embarking on the month long journey to prepare themselves for the regular season and beyond.

Ahead of the start of training camp and the preseason, here's a look at the potential 53-man roster based on what we've seen from the offseason.

Rank Em!: 5 most important Jacksonville Jaguars for 2026 include the big names

While Travis Hunter will be listed twice on this roster, he is counted only once (cornerbacks).

Projected on roster: Trevor Lawrence, Nick Mullens

Cuts: Carter Bradley, Joey Aguilar (R)

Observations: Lawrence's job is safe and it'll take a lot for Bradley or Aguilar to usurp Mullens as the backup. However, the battle for third string QB could heat up throughout training camp. Bradley is the incumbent but the Jaguars promote competition at all levels. It'll be something to watch, especially during joint practices and preseason games.

Projected on roster: Chris Rodriguez Jr., Bhayshul Tuten, LeQuint Allen, DeeJay Dallas

Cuts: Ameer Abdullah, J'Mari Taylor (R)

Observations: We have yet to see Rodriguez on the field after his injury sidelined him during offseason workouts. The thought is that the Jaguars will use a by committee approach to their running game. Tuten and Allen are expected to step into larger roles in their second season with the team. An underrated battle might be between Dallas and Abdullah as the team's kick returner. Whoever wins that battle will secure their spot on the roster.

Projected on roster: Jakobi Meyers, Brian Thomas Jr., Parker Washington, Travis Hunter, Josh Cameron (R), CJ Williams (R)

Cuts: Brady Boyd (R), Chandler Brayboy, Tim Jones, Ben Patterson, Trebor Pena (R), Austin Trammell, Michael Wortham (R)

Observations: What a crowded room. Meyers, Thomas and Washington are surefire starters. Hunter's defensive usage might bring his offensive snaps down some, opening the door for someone to get some extra reps. Williams had an impressive offseason and will likely carve out a role with the team. Cameron has special teams value as a returner, likely cementing his spot.

Projected on roster: Brenton Strange, Nate Boerkircher (R), Quintin Morris, Tanner Koziol (R)

Cuts: Patrick Herbert, Hunter Long, Ethan Conner (R)

Observations: Are philosophical changes coming for Coen's offense? That's a joke, but I am curious if we'll see a set with all four of these players on the field at the same time. This position is pretty straightforward with both rookie tight ends making the team in addition to the two guys who received contract extensions from the team this offseason.

Projected on roster: Cole Van Lanen, Ezra Cleveland, Robert Hainsey, Patrick Mekari, Anton Harrison, Walker Little, Emmanuel Pregnon (R), Jonah Monheim, Wyatt Milum, Chuma Edoga

Cuts: Jerome Carvin, Trystan Colon, Ricky Lee, Jimto Obidegwu, Garrett DiGiorgio (R)

Observations: I think the team will opt to keep 10 offensive linemen. As they try to solidify the five best starters, they'll need several players who can play multiple positions in reserve spots. As Van Lanen returns from his injury, we'll likely see different combinations across the line throughout camp.

Projected on roster: Josh Hines-Allen, DaVon Hamilton, Arik Armstead, Travon Walker, Ruke Orhorhoro, Albert Regis (R), BJ Green II, Danny Striggow, Wesley Williams (R)

Cuts: Keivie Rose, Matt Dickerson, Zach Durfee (R), T.J. Bollers (R), Quinton Bohanna, Jalen Hunt (R), Quindarius Dunnigan, Bryan Thomas Jr. (R)

Observations: This group has heavy expectations placed on their shoulders. With a healthy Travon Walker back in the ranks, position flexibility is key here as well. Several of the players here can play inside or out, giving the team the bodies needed should injuries arise.

Projected on roster: Foye Oluokun, Ventrell Miller, Dennis Gardeck, Branson Combs, Jack Kiser, Jalen McLeod

Cuts: Yasir Abdullah, Parker Hughes (R)

Observations: Another position group that's pretty straightforward. With McLeod back in the mix Abdullah is on the outside looking in. Hughes is the last man in, so he's first man out. He'll be a practice squad candidate though.

Projected on roster: Travis Hunter, Montaric Brown, Jourdan Lewis, Jarrian Jones, Jabbar Muhammad

Cuts: Keni-H Lovely, Christian Braswell, Preston Hodge (R), Devon Marshall (R), Dane Jackson

Observations: Muhammad had as good of a camp as any player on the roster. It's with that logic that the 2025 UDFA makes the team. Lewis and Hunter missed the entire on-field portion of offseason workouts, but they're projected starters. Brown was brought back to be a starter and Jones could find himself amongst the starters depending on how Lewis' recovery goes. Braswell would likely need to have a better camp than Muhammad to make the roster. Lovely and Hodge are longshots who could find themselves in a competition if the team keeps an extra corner.

Projected on roster: Eric Murray, Antonio Johnson, Caleb Ransaw, Rayuan Lane III, Jalen Huskey (R)

Cuts: Devin Neal Jr. (R), Cam'Ron Silmon-Craig, Trevian Thomas

Observations: Murray and Johnson are the likely starters here with Ransaw potentially pushing his way into a starting role. Lane is a special teams ace and Huskey is a Day 2 pick from this year's draft. It'd take a something terrible for him to be cut from the roster. Neal, Thomas and Silmon-Craig are likely battling for a practice squad spot after roster cuts are made.

Projected on roster: Logan Cooke, Cam Little, Ross Matiscik

Observations: The kicker who has the two longest field goals in league history is safe. The highest-paid long snapper in league history is safe. The player with the highest net punting average in league history is safe. This is the most clear cut position grouping.

title: Marquis Clark talking trash to get playing time with Tennessee basketball
description: Tennessee basketball freshman guard Marquis Clark knows playing time may be hard to come by this season. He's developed a plan to get on the floor.
fullText:
Tennessee basketball freshman Marquis Clark wants to be annoying.

It's nothing personal. But as Clark sits behind a roster full of guards and ball-handling wings, he's trying to find ways to get on the court.

His solution? Talking trash. It's an old trick he and fellow Chicago native Dai Dai Ames have relied on during the Vols' summer practices.

"I'd say Dai Dai," Clark said on July 23 about who else talks the most trash. "We're from Chicago, so we like to talk stuff and get in people's head. That's what gets us going. Yesterday, Dai Dai was going at Miles (Rubin), talking smack to him. That's what we do."

Clark is a smaller, 6-foot-1 guard with a penchant for scoring. At Whitney M. Young High School, he broke the all-time scoring record with 1,983 career points, surpassing the previous record set by NBA first-round draft pick Quentin Richardson.

Scoring alone, though, won't get Clark on the floor on a Rick Barnes roster.

"Defense for sure," he said about where his game has developed most. "Being a pest, that's how I'm going to get on the court, so I've got to keep that up. I feel like that's been the best thing I've picked up."

Clark isn't the only player that has had to work on his defense. Barnes has had to teach his schemes to an almost entirely new group, a group that was specifically recruited for its scoring prowess.

"I think that guys have started to understand more and more what we're looking for, and way more defensively than anything," Barnes said. "What made it so difficult is that we had so many new guys. The only really active player from last year was DeWayne (Brown II), with Troy (Henderson) being out. In the past, our older players helped us with that guys came in. Every player we've recruited to come in here has had to come in and learn to do what we want to do."

Adjusting to Barnes, and college basketball, hasn't been easy for Clark. In one previous practice, he was punished to the Versaclimber, an intense cardio machine, between "six or seven" times, he recalled.

Clark has leaned on Brown and Henderson as the two returners from last season who also dealt with Barnes as freshmen.

"I've learned a lot," he said. "When I came in, I didn't really know what to expect. They were the first two guys I went to since they were here last year. I've definitely learned a lot, and I keep asking questions."

Clark is jostling with the other freshmen to be this season's Brown. Barnes said he thought about redshirting Brown last fall before the forward became the "biggest surprise" on the roster and quickly carved out a spot in the rotation.

Clark may be slotted behind other experienced guards like Ames, but he wouldn't have it any other way.

"We signed up to play against the best of the best," Clark said about the freshman class. "For all of us, we came in with the mindset that we want to get on the court, so we're going to compete against whoever."

title: USA250: The 10 greatest Nevada college athletes ranked
description: Nevada and UNLV are the two prominent colleges in the state and they lead our list of 10 best college athletes from the Silver State.
fullText:
In choosing the 10 greatest collegiate athletes to play in the state of Nevada, we’re pretty much limited to two schools - the University of Nevada and the University of Nevada-Las Vegas.

That isn’t to say there aren’t plenty of worthy candidates from those institutions, but the biggest names who played their home games in the Silver State did so for the most part in the traditional revenue sports, and wound up either heading south to Las Vegas or north to Reno.

With apologies to Wolf Pack fans, this list is going to favor the Rebels bit thanks to its hoops pedigree. But we think we’ve chosen the top candidates from both locales.

The brightest of the stars from UNLV’s glory days was enshrined in the National Collegiate Basketball Hall of Fame in 2019. Over his two seasons with the Runnin’ Rebels that included the 1990 NCAA championship and a Naismith Player of the Year honor a season later, he averaged 21.6 points and 11.2 rebounds before embarking on his NBA career.

USA 250 LISTS: Alaska | Alabama | Arizona | Arkansas | California | Colorado | Connecticut | Delaware | Florida | Georgia | Hawaii | Idaho | Illinois | Indiana | Iowa | Kansas | Kentucky | Louisiana | Maine | Maryland | Massachusetts | Michigan | Minnesota | Mississippi | Missouri | Montana | Nebraska | Nevada | New Hampshire | New Jersey

While football often took a back seat to basketball at UNLV, Cunningham nevertheless left his mark in college before his lengthy NFL tenure. He threw for 8,020 yards and 59 touchdowns while also doubling as the punter from 1982-84. In his senior season, Cunningham threw for 24 scores as the Rebels set a school record with 11 wins.

Nevada’s innovative pistol offense needed the right man at the controls, and Kaepernick did it better than anyone. From 2007-10 he amassed 14,200 yards of total offense and surpassed 2,000 yards passing and 1,000 rushing for three consecutive seasons with the Wolf Pack.

The power forward known as "The Hammer" was a first-team All-American during the 1986-87 season while leading the Rebels to the Final Four. He set a single-season scoring record with 903 points that year and led the school to 93-11 record in his three seasons with three NCAA Tournament appearances before being selected No. 2 in the NBA draft.

PROGRAM RANKINGS: Top 25 | Big Ten | SEC | ACC | Big 12

Inducted into the Nevada hall of fame in 2025, Snyder led the Wolf Pack to the Western Athletic Conference regular season and tournament titles and the school's first Sweet 15 appearance as a senior in 2004. He was named WAC player of the year that season and scored 1,404 career points during his Reno days before being selected in the first round of the NBA draft.

The floor general for those UNLV Final Four squads also has a place in the school’s hall of fame. He handed out 838 assists and snared 275 steals over his four seasons with the Rebels. Anthony was a three-time, all-Big West selection and a third-team All-American in his senior season.

A standout infielder with the Rebels, Williams compiled 58 home runs and 217 RBI during his three seasons at the school. His best campaign was his final year when he hit 25 long balls and drove in 89 runs while being a first-team All-American selection. Williams was the No. 3 overall pick in the 1986 MLB draft and would go on to a 17-year career with 378 home runs.

Moore had one of the great seasons in men's collegiate golf in 2004 as he won the NCAA individual championship in addition to taking the U.S. Amateur title and victories in the the U.S. Amateur Public Links and the Western Amateur. The following year as a senior, Moore won the Haskins and Nicklaus Award with a scoring average of 69.29, the second-lowest in NCAA history.

UNLV’s all-time scoring leader in women’s basketball, Frohlich averaged 21.2 points and 10.1 rebounds with the Rebels from 1998-2002. She was a three-time Western Athletic Conference player of the year and third-team All-American as a senior. Frohlich competed for her native Germany on the national team and now operates a sports academy in California.

Kaepernick’s running mate in the Wolf Pack backfield was arguably just as instrumental to the team’s success during its epic 13-1 season in 2010. A third-team All-American as a senior, e recorded 5,159 yards from scrimmage, 4,588 of those rushing, and scored 53 total touchdowns for his Nevada career.
